modules.cost: [`sign_of_det2`], at most [`ITERATIONS`] passes of a few comparisons, subtractions and one Euclidean division each. [`sign_of_det3`], at most [`DET3_PASSES`] passes, each at most about 480 calls of [`sign_of_det2`]; its search keeps up to 119 lattice points in a fixed array of 2,856 bytes. No allocation, no recursion.
modules.does: [`sign_of_det2`] finds the sign of x1·y2 − y1·x2 from the four entries without ever forming a product: it compares, subtracts and divides, keeping every value within the entries' own magnitude, and [`orient2d`] applies it to the three points' translations, as the generated `orient2d` does. [`sign_of_det3`] finds the sign of a 3 × 3 determinant the same way, by a walk in the lattice its first two rows span whose every test is a [`sign_of_det2`], and [`orient3d`] applies it to the four points' translations, as the generated `orient3d` does. A product is never computed, so no value needs more bits than a few entries: the method answers in 64-bit arithmetic where the exact paths need 128 bits.
guarantees: **The exact sign.** For every four entries of magnitude at most [`ENTRY_MAX`], the result is the sign of x1·y2 − y1·x2 (tested against 128-bit products and against the generated `orient2d` in this crate's `tests/avnaim.rs`, and against big integers by geom-fuzz's `variants` target). For every nine entries of magnitude at most [`DET3_ENTRY_MAX`], the result of [`sign_of_det3`] is the determinant's sign (tested against big integers here, and against the generated `orient3d` in this crate's `tests/avnaim.rs` and geom-fuzz's `variants` target). An entry past its bound is refused with `None`, never answered.

**Checked and bounded.** Every step is a checked method. [`sign_of_det2`]'s loop runs at most [`ITERATIONS`] times: each pass either answers or replaces the second row by one whose entries are below half the first row's, so the entries halve at least every two passes. [`sign_of_det3`] runs at most [`DET3_PASSES`] passes, each with a lattice search of at most 119 doublings and 118 halvings, kept in a fixed array.
modules.job: The signs of 2 × 2 and 3 × 3 integer determinants in single-precision arithmetic, by Avnaim, Boissonnat, Devillers, Preparata and Yvinec's method: chapter 23.3's reference for the exact paths of orientation (piece G42). It lives here, in a development crate, because it is a reference to measure against, not a path the kernel ships: G42's report measured it and did not adopt it, so it is outside the foundation set's coverage and mutation gates (28.8), which its pass limits, never reached, could not meet by test.

method.text: Avnaim, Boissonnat, Devillers, Preparata and Yvinec, "Evaluating signs of determinants using single-precision arithmetic", Algorithmica 17 (1997), sections 2 and 3, doi:10.1007/BF02522822 (the authors' report: <https://inria.hal.science/inria-00090613>). Signs first: an entry of zero leaves one product, and entries of mixed signs settle the sign or are made positive by negating rows and columns. Then, with the rows ordered so that x2 ≥ x1 and y2 ≥ y1, the Euclidean step x2 = k·x1 + xr, yr = y2 − k·y1 keeps the determinant (|x1 y1; xr yr|), and the halves of the first row settle it or give a smaller second row: (xr, yr) when both lie in the lower halves, (x1 − xr, y1 − yr) when both lie in the upper, which negates the determinant. The paper writes that last determinant without the change of sign; it is −|x1 y1; xr yr|, as expanding both shows, and this module follows the expansion.

modules.cost: reading and parsing every summary, linear in their size; then O(n log n) for n benchmarks, which are kept in an ordered map.
guarantees: **Exact, for every count.** Every limit is tested in integers ([`Change::rose_over`]): 100 · head > (100 + p) · base, and a count resolves p% exactly when it is at least ⌈100 / p⌉. Percentages are computed, as floating point, for display only.

**Every benchmark judged, or no verdict.** Every benchmark the run lists has exactly one summary, every summary is a benchmark the run lists and of the schema version the gate's Gungraun writes, and every summary carries a whole count for each of the eight judged measures, from the pull request and, for a benchmark the merge base has, from the merge base; anything else is an error, never a pass.
**Deterministic reports.** Benchmarks are judged and reported in name order, and measures in the order of [`JUDGED`], the same on every run and every platform.
**Totality.** No input makes [`parse_summary`], [`judge`] or [`read_summaries`] panic.
modules.job: The instruction-and-cache gate's verdict, read from Gungraun's machine-readable summaries: instructions and estimated cycles are gated at the gate's percentage on every benchmark, and each L1 and last-level miss count is gated at that percentage only where its merge-base count can resolve it; a smaller miss count is listed and judged through estimated cycles.

method.text: the hard cases of elementary-function implementations, each a separate path through libm (which `geom_num::math` wraps): arguments that need the longest trigonometric argument reduction (Payne and Hanek 1983, <https://doi.org/10.1145/1057600.1057602>), results near overflow and underflow, subnormals, and arguments next to the ends of each domain.

modules.cost: building a batch takes O([`BATCH`]) generator draws (at most `ATTEMPTS` = 64 · [`BATCH`] candidates, so it always ends), once per benchmark, outside every measured run.
guarantees: every batch is a pure function of its operation and class, the same on every target and in every build profile; every catalogued batch is full ([`BATCH`] inputs; the tests check it) and is what its class claims; a class an operation lacks gives an empty batch; and no builder panics.
modules.job: The inputs every benchmark runs on: fixed batches, built the same way on every target.

method.text: the input categories robust-geometry work tests and times separately, because each takes a different path through the code: general position, nearly degenerate, exactly degenerate (all three are Shewchuk's, 1997, section 6: <https://doi.org/10.1007/PL00009321>), and the extremes of the number range. Exactly degenerate points on circles and spheres come from Pythagorean triples and quadruples (<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pythagorean_triple>, <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pythagorean_quadruple>): integer points at one exact distance from a centre. Nearly degenerate triangles and tetrahedra with huge coordinates are unimodular lattice bases (<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unimodular_matrix>), built with the extended Euclidean algorithm (Knuth, *The Art of Computer Programming*, volume 2, section 4.5.2): their area or volume is the smallest nonzero one the grid allows.

modules.cost: the exact predicates' inputs and N keys per input, once per batch.
guarantees: every batch is full, the same on every target, and its classes are what they claim (`tests/inputs.rs`); the keys within an input are distinct and their order rotates from input to input, so every argument position holds the smallest key in turn.
modules.job: Inputs for the perturbed predicates (G30): [`orient2d`], [`orient3d`], [`incircle`] and [`insphere`] of `geom_num::perturb`, each point with a distinct key.

method.text: the exact predicates' own input classes ([`super::predicate`], after Shewchuk, <https://doi.org/10.1007/PL00009321>, section 6), drawn with this operation's seed, with keys attached.

modules.cost: a few draws of [`crate::rng::SplitMix64`] per input, once per batch, outside every measured run.
guarantees: every batch is full, the same on every target, and its classes are what they claim (`tests/inputs.rs`); every result is checked against exact cross products, Cramer's rule and exact rounding by `tests/attack_g06.rs`.
modules.job: Inputs for plane-based geometry: [`through`] (`Plane::through`), [`side`] (`Plane::side`), [`tpi_new`] (`Tpi::new`), [`tpi_homogeneous`] (`Tpi::homogeneous`), [`side_of_tpi`] (`Plane::side_of_tpi`), [`to_grid`] (`Tpi::to_grid`), and for the point where a line meets a plane (G29) [`lpi_new`] (`Lpi::new`), [`lpi_homogeneous`] (`Lpi::homogeneous`), [`side_of_lpi`] (`Plane::side_of_lpi`) and [`lpi_to_grid`] (`Lpi::to_grid`).

method.text: the degenerate cases of plane-based geometry as `Tpi::new` documents them (after Campen and Kobbelt 2010, <https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8659.2009.01609.x>), with Shewchuk's input classes (<https://doi.org/10.1007/PL00009321>, section 6) and unimodular bases (Knuth, volume 2, section 4.5.2) for the nearly degenerate ones.

modules.cost: a few draws of [`crate::rng::SplitMix64`] per input, once per batch, outside every measured run.
guarantees: every batch is full, the same on every target, and its classes are what they claim (`tests/inputs.rs`, against exact determinants and Shewchuk's filter bounds); every sign is checked against an exact determinant by `tests/attack_g06.rs`.
modules.job: Inputs for the exact predicates: [`orient2d`], [`orient3d`], [`incircle`] and [`insphere`].

method.text: Shewchuk's three input classes (random, nearly degenerate, exactly degenerate; 1997, section 6, <https://doi.org/10.1007/PL00009321>) and the extremes of the frame; unimodular bases from the extended Euclidean algorithm (Knuth, volume 2, section 4.5.2); Pythagorean triples and quadruples for integer circles and spheres (<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pythagorean_quadruple>).

modules.cost: a few draws of [`crate::rng::SplitMix64`] per input, once per batch, outside every measured run.
guarantees: the batch is full, the same on every target, and holds both zeros in both orders and every ordering (`tests/inputs.rs`); every result is checked against `f64::total_cmp` by `tests/attack_g06.rs`.
modules.job: Inputs for finite doubles in total order: [`total_max`], [`total_min`] and [`cmp`] on `Real`.

method.text: IEEE 754-2019 totalOrder (section 5.10) as Rust's `f64::total_cmp` implements it (<https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.f64.html#method.total_cmp>); one input per case of the ordering, including the signed zeros.

modules.cost: a few draws of [`SplitMix64`] per input, and at most four `next_u32` draws to place a stream, once per batch, outside every measured run.
guarantees: every batch is full and the same on every target, and takes the paths listed (`tests/inputs.rs` checks each claim); every result is checked against an independent Philox4x32-10 and independent draw definitions by `tests/attack_g06.rs`.
modules.job: Inputs for the counter-based random numbers of `geom_num::rng`: the Philox4x32-10 block function ([`philox4x32_10`]), a stream started at a block ([`stream_from`]), the five draws ([`next_u32`], [`next_u64`], [`next_f64`], [`below`], [`range_inclusive`]) and the two ways a stream range hands out streams ([`range_philox`], [`chunk`]).

method.text: boundary-value analysis (<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boundary-value_analysis>) on the paths `geom_num::rng` documents: the block refill of `next_u32`, the end of a stream's 2^66 words, the rejection in Lemire's method (2019, <https://doi.org/10.1145/3230636>), whose probability is (2^64 mod n) / 2^64, and the checked steps of a stream range.

modules.cost: a few draws of [`crate::rng::SplitMix64`] per input, once per batch, outside every measured run.
guarantees: the batch is full, the same on every target, and takes all three branches and both ends of `i128` (`tests/inputs.rs`); every result is checked against an exact sign by `tests/attack_g06.rs`.
modules.job: Inputs for the sign of an exact integer: [`of_i128`] (`Sign::of_i128`).

method.text: one input per branch of a three-way comparison, at both ends of the type (boundary-value analysis, <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boundary-value_analysis>).

modules.cost: a few draws of [`crate::rng::SplitMix64`] per input, once per batch, outside every measured run.
guarantees: every batch is full, the same on every target, and its classes are what they claim (`tests/inputs.rs`); every result is checked against exact integers by `tests/attack_g06.rs`.
modules.job: Inputs for fixed-width integers, `Wide<L>`: [`add`], [`sub`], [`mul`], [`neg`], [`cmp`], [`signum`], [`to_i128`], [`from_i128`] and [`resize`], for any width `Wide` allows (two limbs or more; the catalogue uses I256, I320, I384 and I512, and 2, 4 and 8 limbs for the growth checks). Where a class cannot exist at a width its batch is empty, as for any class an operation lacks: typical products need four limbs (two typical operands make up to 252 bits), and at two limbs every value fits an `i128`, so nothing overflows `to_i128`.

method.text: the operand classes that take each path of schoolbook multiple-precision arithmetic (Knuth, *The Art of Computer Programming*, volume 2, section 4.3.1, <https://www-cs-faculty.stanford.edu/~knuth/taocp.html>): short operands, full-width operands, carries out of the top limb.

modules.cost: the `Wide` batch's draws and one pass to split it, outside every measured run.
guarantees: every batch is full where its class exists, and the same on every target; each value is the value of the `Wide` input it was split from, so its class is that input's (`tests/inputs.rs`); every result is checked by `tests/attack_g06.rs`.
modules.job: Inputs for the fixed-width integers in 32-bit limbs, `Wide32<M>` (piece G42): for each operation, the batch of the `Wide` operation of the same bit width ([`super::wide`]), drawn from the `Wide32` benchmark's own seed, each value split into twice as many 32-bit limbs; and pairs of `i64` for [`Wide32::product_i64`].

method.text: the operand classes of schoolbook multiple-precision arithmetic, as [`super::wide`] (Knuth, *The Art of Computer Programming*, volume 2, section 4.3.1, <https://www-cs-faculty.stanford.edu/~knuth/taocp.html>); a value's 64-bit limb k is its 32-bit limbs 2k and 2k + 1.

modules.cost: one call of the operation per input, plus the loop above; no allocation, because the buffer already holds one result per input.
guarantees: each kernel calls exactly the `geom-num` function it is named after, once per input and in order, and stores every result (`tests/attack_g06.rs` recomputes each benchmark's results by calling `geom-num` directly); it allocates nothing when the buffer has room for the batch, as every harness gives it.
modules.job: The measured code: one function per operation, which runs the operation on every input of a batch and stores each result.

method.text: the batch-of-independent-calls microbenchmark with an optimisation barrier per input, as divan documents it (<https://docs.rs/divan/0.1.21/divan/fn.black_box.html>), with the results written to memory instead of folded into a checksum.

modules.cost: a benchmark is one pass of its operation over [`inputs::BATCH`] inputs (two passes under the instruction-count gate, whose first pass warms the caches; one and two runs under the fuel gate, whose difference is one pass). Building a batch takes O([`inputs::BATCH`]) generator draws and hashing it O([`inputs::BATCH`]) SHA-256 blocks, once per benchmark, outside every measured region.
guarantees: Every benchmark runs the operation it is named after (`tests/attack_g06.rs`), on inputs that are what their class claims (`tests/inputs.rs`).
Inputs and results are pinned by golden digests that must match in every build profile and on wasm32 (`tests/golden.rs`, and the fuel gate).
The gate, the catalogue and `geom-num`'s public functions agree (`tests/coverage.rs`).

The library has no `unsafe` code, no panicking calls or indexing outside tests, no recursion, no hash maps of its own (Gungraun's summary model keeps counts in an insertion-ordered `IndexMap`, which [`callgrind`] only looks up by key, so no result depends on its hashing), no randomness (inputs come from fixed seeds) and no platform maths.
modules.job: Spare Kit geometry kernel, development only: benchmarks, and the count gates that block a regression over 5%.

method.text: deterministic count gates in place of timing, as chapter 23.13 sets them out: Valgrind's Callgrind and DHAT through Gungraun (<https://github.com/gungraun/gungraun>), Wasmtime's fuel (<https://docs.wasmtime.dev/api/wasmtime/struct.Config.html#method.consume_fuel>), the doubling test for growth (<https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/14analysis/>), and SHA-256 golden digests of canonical outputs (NIST FIPS 180-4, <https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/180-4/upd1/final>).

modules.cost: a few wrapping integer operations per draw, and one per byte of a seed's name.
guarantees: every draw is a pure function of the seed and the number of draws before it, in wrapping 64-bit integer arithmetic only, so the sequence is the same on every target, in every build profile and with overflow checks on or off; [`SplitMix64::range`] stays inside its range for every pair of `i64` bounds, and no method panics.
modules.job: A fixed-seed generator for benchmark inputs: the same numbers on every target, every run.

method.text: SplitMix64, from G. L. Steele, D. Lea and C. H. Flood, "Fast splittable pseudorandom number generators", OOPSLA 2014 (<https://doi.org/10.1145/2660193.2660195>), with the constants of Vigna's reference code (<https://prng.di.unimi.it/splitmix64.c>, public domain). Seeds are derived with 64-bit FNV-1a (<http://www.isthe.com/chongo/tech/comp/fnv/>). The tests check both against their published values.

provenance.name: Vigna's SplitMix64 reference code
provenance.purpose: for the constants and steps of SplitMix64, which the tests check against its published outputs. No code copied.

modules.cost: one compression of 64 rounds per 64-byte block, so linear in the message; the state is `sha2`'s fixed block buffer, and nothing is allocated except the string `Display` writes.
guarantees: **The digest FIPS 180-4 defines**, whatever pieces the message is fed in: `sha2`'s, which the tests check against the standard's own examples, a million bytes in uneven pieces and every padding length.

**The same digest on every target**: SHA-256 is fully specified integer arithmetic, and `sha2`'s portable and processor-specific back ends compute the same function (the tests run on every target the gates run on, wasm32 included).
**A hexadecimal digest reads back as itself**: [`Digest::from_hex`] takes exactly 64 digits, either case, and refuses anything else; [`Digest`]'s `Display` writes 64 lowercase digits.
No method panics.
modules.job: SHA-256, the hash of every benchmark's golden digests: the `sha2` crate's, with the golden digest type the gates compare and the hexadecimal form `golden.txt` stores.

method.text: the Secure Hash Standard, NIST FIPS 180-4 (<https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/180-4/upd1/final>), as the `sha2` crate implements it (<https://docs.rs/sha2/0.11.0/sha2/>), checked against the standard's example values (<https://csrc.nist.gov/projects/cryptographic-standards-and-guidelines/example-values>).

errors.name: BvhError

invariants: Every box is rounded outward to whole grid steps and never misses what it should contain; boxes around certified or Tolerant geometry are padded by their bound (19.9, 23.7).

Built top-down in one pass by the binned surface-area heuristic with integer costs; every split is a pure function of the node's contents, ties broken by entry key, so the tree is the same on any number of threads (19.9).
Answers never depend on the tree's shape: every query returns its set sorted by key (19.9, 23.7).
Traversal uses an explicit stack with a depth limit, never recursion, and checks cancellation at fixed steps (19.9, principle 13).
Parallel only through `geom-run`'s helper (23.4).
crates.job: The one tree of integer boxes, 2D and 3D.

modules.cost: constant per box; no allocation.
modules.does: an [`Aabb`] holds a lower and an upper corner of whole grid steps. It comes from `geom-math`'s grid boxes exactly ([`Box2`], [`Box3`]), or from a box of doubles in grid units rounded outward ([`Aabb::from_float`], [`FBox2`], [`FBox3`]), and [`Aabb::inflated`] pads it by its holder's class (chapter 23.7): nothing for Exact geometry, the bound ε for Certified(ε), the tolerance for a Tolerant import, each rounded up to whole steps. The tree measures a box by [`Aabb::area`], the surface-area heuristic's measure in whole numbers.
guarantees: **Never misses what it holds.** Grid boxes convert exactly. A float box's lower corner is rounded down and its upper corner up, each to a whole step, and a padding is the bound rounded up, so the result holds every point within the bound of the float box.

**Bounded, so every cost is exact.** Every coordinate lies within ±[`LIMIT`] = 2^43 (the 2^40 frame of chapter 6 with room for padding), so an extent plus one is at most 2^44 + 1 < 2^45, a 3D area (three products of two) is below 3·2^90 < 2^92, and an area times an entry count (below 2^32) is below 2^124: the tree's costs are exact in `u128`.
**Closed.** Boxes that touch overlap, as `geom-math`'s do.
modules.job: The box tree's boxes: closed boxes of whole grid steps in two or three dimensions, padded by the exactness of what they hold.

method.text: chapter 23.7 of the kernel architecture ("Boxes that never miss", padding by exactness) and section 19.9 ("Boxes are whole grid steps"); the area measure is the surface area of I. Wald, "On fast construction of SAH-based bounding volume hierarchies", IEEE Symposium on Interactive Ray Tracing (2007), <https://doi.org/10.1109/RT.2007.4342588>, counted in grid points so a point's box has a positive measure, and in two dimensions the perimeter, the plane's analogue (the chance a random line meets a convex region is proportional to its perimeter).

modules.cost: O(n·D) per level of the tree, about log₂ n levels for spread boxes and at most [`MAX_DEPTH`]; memory: the nodes, the order, one centre per entry, and per subtree task a copy of its range's order. No recursion.
modules.does: [`build`] takes the entries sorted by key and returns the tree's nodes and the order of the entries along its leaves. Each node's entries are split by the plane, among b − 1 planes per axis between b bins of their boxes' centres (b = min(entries, [`BINS`])), that minimises area(left)·count(left) + area(right)·count(right), or kept as a leaf once there are at most [`LEAF_MAX`]. The top of the tree is built on the calling thread until every unbuilt range holds at most [`GRAIN`] entries; those subtrees are then built as one phase of the helper, one task each, and spliced in task order.
guarantees: **One tree for one set of entries.** Every split is a pure function of the range's entries: the bins and the costs are whole numbers ([`crate::bound`] bounds them), ties between planes go to the lower axis and then the lower plane, and the partition is stable, so each range keeps its entries in key order. Which ranges become subtree tasks depends on their sizes alone. So the nodes, their order and the entries' order are the same for any thread count, pool and chunking, and for any input order of the same entries.

**Depth at most [`MAX_DEPTH`].** From depth [`MEDIAN_DEPTH`] = 32 on, every split is at the median in key order. A range there holds fewer than 2^32 entries, and halving reaches at most [`LEAF_MAX`] entries within 31 more levels, so no leaf is deeper than 63.
**No recursion.** Ranges wait on an explicit stack; ranges where all centres coincide are split at the median in key order.
**Charged.** Each node charges its entry count to the meter before its work, so a build stops at the same node for the same budget on every machine.
modules.job: The box tree's construction: top-down, by the binned surface-area heuristic with whole-number costs, in parallel only through `geom-run`'s helper.

method.text: I. Wald, "On fast construction of SAH-based bounding volume hierarchies", IEEE Symposium on Interactive Ray Tracing (2007), <https://doi.org/10.1109/RT.2007.4342588> (binning centroids into a fixed number of bins per axis and sweeping the bin boundaries), with costs counted in whole grid points and ties broken by axis, plane and key (section 19.9 and chapter 27's `geom-bvh` row); the subtree phase follows chapter 23.4's helper.

modules.cost: building is O(n log n): a sort by key when the input is not in key order, n codes, the runs' sorts and ⌈log₂(n/32,768)⌉ rounds of merges, with a copy of the points in key order and two buffers of n slots (24 bytes each) at the peak of a round. A search is two binary searches per cell (at most 27 cells) and one exact test per point in those cells. The pairs are one search per point.
guarantees: **The same answer everywhere.** The order (code, key) is unique for distinct keys, so the index, its bytes and every answer are the same for any input order, pool and target; every answer is sorted by key.
**Exact.** Distances are compared as squared integer distances in `i128` (each coordinate difference below 2^41 + 2^42, so the sum of squares stays below 2^88), never in floating point.
**Bounded and cancellable.** No recursion; the meter is charged one unit per point a search scans, so a cancelled or over-budget search returns an error and no keys.
**Safe.** No `unsafe`, no panics, no unchecked indexing; allocations are fallible.
modules.job: The Morton-sorted cell index (piece G55): grid points in a linear octree, for point searches such as welding and envelopes (chapter 19.9).

method.text: the Morton order (G. M. Morton, "A computer oriented geodetic data base and a new technique in file sequencing", IBM Ltd., Ottawa (1966)) and the linear octree, the leaves of an octree kept as a sorted list of location codes (I. Gargantini, "An effective way to represent quadtrees", Communications of the ACM 25(12) (1982), 905–910, <https://doi.org/10.1145/358728.358741>). The bits are spread by the mask-and-shift sequence for 21-bit coordinates, applied to the low 21 and the high 20 bits of each.

modules.cost: constant.
modules.does: [`BvhError`] names each failure of the tree's construction, refit and queries, and maps `geom-run`'s stops and phase errors onto them, so a caller sees one error type.
guarantees: **Typed, never partial.** Every failure is one of these kinds and returns no tree or answer; a tree that fails to refit is left exactly as it was before the call.
**Stops keep their reason.** A meter's stop (budget, cancellation, memory) and a phase's budget failure keep `geom-run`'s own record of it.
modules.job: Why the box tree could not build, change or answer.

method.none: an error enum and its conversions, with `geom-run`'s stops (chapter 23.10).

modules.cost: O(nodes visited + answers·log answers); memory: the answer.
modules.does: each query walks the tree from the root with an explicit stack, skipping every node whose box misses, and charges one unit of its meter per node, or pair of nodes, it visits. It collects the keys it finds and sorts them.
guarantees: **The answer of brute force.** A query returns exactly the keys (or key pairs) whose boxes meet, as testing every entry (or every pair) would, sorted ascending: a pair within one tree as (smaller key, larger key), a pair between trees as (this tree's key, the other's). So the answer does not depend on the tree's shape, a refit, a rebuild or the thread count it was built with.

**No recursion, bounded stacks.** A tree is at most [`MAX_DEPTH`] deep, so a walk of one tree holds at most `MAX_DEPTH + 1` nodes on its stack, of two trees at most `2·MAX_DEPTH + 1` pairs (each step descends one side, pushing two), and of one tree against itself at most `4·MAX_DEPTH + 1` (a node against itself pushes three). The stacks are vectors with room for [`MAX_DEPTH`] reserved, grown fallibly beyond it.
**Cancellable, never partial.** The meter polls the caller's cancellation at fixed charges; a stopped query returns [`BvhError::Stopped`] and no keys.
modules.job: The box tree's queries: the entries whose boxes meet a box, the pairs of entries whose boxes meet within one tree, and the pairs between two trees.

method.text: depth-first traversal of a bounding-volume hierarchy, and the simultaneous traversal of two hierarchies for overlapping pairs, as in G. van den Bergen, "Efficient collision detection of complex deformable models using AABB trees", *Journal of Graphics Tools* 2(4) (1997), 1–13, <https://doi.org/10.1080/10867651.1997.10487480>, with the larger node descended first; answers sorted by key (section 19.9 and chapter 23.7).

modules.cost: building as [`crate::build`], plus a stable sort by key; a refit O(updates·log n + nodes); the bytes O(entries + nodes). Memory: the entries, the nodes and the key index.
modules.does: [`BoxTree::build`] sorts the entries by key, refuses a repeated key, and builds the nodes ([`crate::build`]). The entries are then stored in leaf order, each leaf a range of them, beside an index from key to position. [`BoxTree::refit`] gives entries new boxes and passes the change up to every node. When the tree's cost ([`BoxTree::cost`], the surface-area heuristic summed over its nodes) passes [`REBUILD_FACTOR`] times the cost it was built with, the refit rebuilds the tree from its entries instead. [`BoxTree::to_bytes`] writes the tree in a canonical form, for goldens and caches.
guarantees: **A function of its entries.** A tree is built from the set of its entries alone: their input order, the pool, the thread count and the chunking change nothing, down to the last byte of [`BoxTree::to_bytes`]. A rebuild equals a fresh build of the same entries.
**Every node holds what is below it.** A node's box is the union of its children's, a leaf's the union of its entries', after a build and after a refit.
**All or nothing.** A refit checks every update before it changes anything, so a refused refit, or one stopped by its meter while rebuilding, leaves the tree as it was.
**Children after parents.** A node's children have larger indices than it has, so one pass from the last node to the first refits the tree.

modules.does: [`Entries::of`] reads a [`TypedTransform`]: an exact grid transform and a rational one through their exact integer entries (m / d), a certified one through its own doubles. [`Entries::image`] maps a homogeneous point w·P (weight w) to M·(w·P) + w·t, once in doubles in a fixed order and once in intervals, and returns the doubles with the distance between them, an upper bound on how far the double image lies from the exact image under the exact transform.
guarantees: **Exact entries enclosed.** An integer entry whose double is not exact (beyond 2^53) is widened by its rounding; each quotient m / d is an outward-rounded interval division; a certified transform is exact in its own doubles (`geom-math`'s `transform` header).

**The image's error bounded.** The interval image holds the exact image of the exact point, and the double image is computed from the doubles of the same entries, so the returned distance bounds their difference.

**Exact images report 0.** When every entry is exactly its double (grid and certified transforms), each coordinate is also summed exactly, as exact products in `geom-num`'s superaccumulator, and an image equal to its double reports an error of 0: interval arithmetic widens every result and could never say so.

modules.does: [`check`] runs a kind through every law of [`Law`] at the parameters given and returns the first law broken, with where. The laws compare certified objects with each other: two enclosures of one exact value must overlap, so a bound, an enclosure, a conversion, a split, a reversal or a transform that is wrong by more than its own stated error is caught wherever a sample lands on it. Evaluation in doubles is compared with the certified enclosure within a relative 2^−30, which catches a wrong formula, not rounding.
guarantees: **Sound.** A law reported broken is broken: two certified enclosures of one exact value that do not overlap (after widening by the stated deviations) prove that one of them is false, and a refusal the law requires that did not come is a broken refusal.
**Deterministic.** The checks run in the order of the parameters given, each law in the order of [`Law`]; the same kind and parameters give the same verdict.

modules.does: implements [`ParamCurve`] for [`Curve`]. Points and derivatives are A3.1, A3.2 and A4.2 (`geom-nurbs`). Enclosures, bounds and derivative bounds come from the curve's Bernstein forms in interval arithmetic (piece G59): the piece holding the parameter, or each piece meeting the span cut down to it by de Casteljau subdivision at interval parameters, its box from the convex hull; derivatives from hodographs, and for a rational curve by Leibniz's rule on W·C = A, C^(k) = (A^(k) − Σ C(k, i)·W^(i)·C^(k−i)) / W, in interval boxes. Conversion to NURBS is the curve itself, exactly. A split inserts the parameter until its multiplicity is the degree (A5.1) and parts the control points there. Reversal negates and reverses the knots, which is exact. A transform maps the control points (affine invariance) with the weights kept.
guarantees: **Certified.** Every enclosure and bound holds the exact value; a split's deviation is the certified rounding of the knot insertion; a transform's is the largest certified error of a control point's image, which bounds the curve's because a NURBS point is a weighted average of its control points with weights `N_i`·`w_i` ≥ 0 (The NURBS Book, P4.3 and P4.4).
**Exact where the operation is.** Conversion and reversal change no bit (deviation 0).
**Refused outside the domain.** A parameter or span outside it is an error, never clamped.

method.text: The NURBS Book, 2nd ed. (<https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-59223-2>): A3.1, A3.2, A4.2, A5.1, de Casteljau subdivision (section 1.3), hodographs (section 3.3) and affine invariance (P4.10), on `geom-nurbs` (pieces G56 and G59).

modules.does: [`ParamCurve`] is the trait chapter 12.1 names for this behaviour, implemented by each kind and by [`CurveKind`], the storage enum with one variant per kind, which dispatches to it. Operations that make a new curve (split, reverse, transform) return a [`CurveKind`], because a transform may change a kind (a non-uniform scale turns a circle into an ellipse, chapter 7), wrapped in `geom-nurbs`'s [`Changed`]: the result and a certified bound on how far it lies from the exact result of the operation on the exact input, 0 when it is exact.
guarantees: **Certified, or refused.** Every bound and enclosure holds the exact value for the curve the stored data define; every [`Changed`] deviation bounds the distance between the returned curve and the exact result. **Typed transforms.** A transform is a `geom-math` [`TypedTransform`]: exact, rational or certified, and the result's deviation accounts for its entries as the variant holds them.

method.text: [`Finding::new`] leaves a finding's detail unwritten under Kani, as Kani's own `std` leaves the messages of `assert!` and `panic!` unformatted during verification (<https://github.com/model-checking/kani/blob/0d2328a93f0e0ff66132d6bfa1a7d884877cf862/library/std/src/lib.rs>, credited below): Kani reports a failed proof with a trace of every value, and formatting symbolic values would only enlarge the problem it solves. The rest of this root is the [`Finding`] type, its `Display` and `Error` implementations and the [`Harness`] alias, whose shape 28.5 gives. Each harness module names the method it follows.

modules.cost: per case, 6 checked `i128` products and 5 checked sums for the reference, one call each to the predicate, the exact path and the filter (each constant time), and at most [`MAX_INPUT_BYTES`] bytes read by [`decode`]. No allocation unless a finding is reported.
modules.does: [`check`] takes three grid points a, b, c and computes [`reference`], the determinant of the 3 × 3 matrix whose rows are (a.x, a.y, 1), (b.x, b.y, 1) and (c.x, c.y, 1), expanded along its third column in `i128`: (b.x·c.y − b.y·c.x) − (a.x·c.y − a.y·c.x) + (a.x·b.y − a.y·b.x). That determinant is orient2d's definition (Shewchuk 1997, section 4.1); this module computes it with no code shared with `geom-num`, and by another formula than `geom-num`'s (b − a) × (c − a), so the two agree only if both are right. Against it, `check` holds `geom-num` to three claims:
guarantees: **Any bytes are a case.** Every byte string, the empty one included, decodes to three valid grid points, reading at most [`MAX_INPUT_BYTES`] = 73 bytes; the bound is derived on the constant and a unit test builds the input that reaches it.

**The oracle cannot overflow on the grid.** Each coordinate has magnitude at most M = 2^40 − 1, so each of the six products is at most M² < 2^80, each 2 × 2 minor at most 2M² < 2^81, and the determinant at most 6M² < 2^83, far inside `i128`. Every step is a checked method all the same, and a step that failed would be reported as a [`Finding`] naming this harness as the defect, never a panic and never a wrapped value.

**A wrong answer is a [`Finding`]**, naming the claim, the points, the reference value and what `geom-num` gave. An error from the predicate, or a `None` from the exact path, is a finding too, never read as a sign: `geom-num` proves every grid input answers.
**A panic is a failure.** Nothing is caught: a panic in `geom-num` fails the run, and the engine reports the input.

**What is proven and what is tested.** For every case [`proof_case`] can give with bound [`PROOF_BOUND`] (every coordinate within `PROOF_BOUND` steps of 0 or of an edge ±(2^40 − 1) of the frame, in any combination), Kani proves that all three claims hold and that nothing on the way panics or overflows (`tests/orient2d.rs`, `orient2d_proof`; Kani checks every arithmetic step, index and unwrap by default). Near the edges the filter's products round, so the proof covers the filter's error bound, not only exact arithmetic. Everywhere else in the frame the claims are tested, by fuzzing and the property tests, not proven.
modules.job: Fuzz target and bounded proof: `geom-num`'s orient2d agrees with the exact determinant of its definition, computed here from scratch.

method.text: an exact oracle for a predicate, the first of chapter 28.6's checks (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/28-testing.md`), with bounded Kani proofs of sign agreement with an exact integer reference, as evidence report 08 recommends for predicates (`projects/kit/notes/G01-evidence/08-standards-coverage-testing.md`, "Recommended test architecture", item 1). The reference is the 3 × 3 determinant of the definition, expanded by cofactors along the column of ones, in Shewchuk's paper: J. R. Shewchuk, "Adaptive Precision Floating-Point Arithmetic and Fast Robust Geometric Predicates", *Discrete & Computational Geometry* 18 (1997), 305–363, <https://doi.org/10.1007/PL00009321>.

modules.cost: 4 + 3 + 6 + 6 + 10 = 29 predicate calls per input, each constant time, and at most [`MAX_INPUT_BYTES`] bytes read.
modules.does: [`decode`] turns a fuzzer's bytes into grid points with `geom-test`'s [`GridSampler`] (four 2D points, then five 3D points). [`check`] calls every exact predicate on them: `orient2d`, `incircle`, `orient3d` and `insphere`. For each, it checks that the predicate answers, then swaps every pair of points and checks that the sign flips, `Zero` staying `Zero`. [`harness`] is `decode` then `check`, the function every fuzzing engine drives (the crate README sets out the layout).
guarantees: **Any bytes are a case.** Every byte string, the empty one included, decodes to valid grid points (magnitude at most 2^40 − 1), aimed at the hard cases: extremes of the frame, repeated and one-step-apart points, collinear points and coarse sub-grids (see `geom_test::grid`).
**A bounded input.** [`decode`] reads at most [`MAX_INPUT_BYTES`] bytes; longer inputs only add bytes nobody reads. The bound is derived below and a unit test builds the input that reaches it.
**A panic is a failure.** The harness does not catch panics: a predicate that panics fails the run, and bolero reports the input and its seed.

**An error is a failure.** Each predicate returns `Result<Sign, NumError>`, and `geom-num` proves that for grid points it is always `Ok`: its bit budgets are derived for every grid input and checked when it compiles, so `NumError::BudgetExceeded` can only be a defect in `geom-num` (`geom_num::predicate`'s module documentation). Every point the harness decodes is a grid point, so an error, on the first call or after any swap, is a [`Finding`] naming the predicate, the error and the points. It is never read as a sign, so a defect can never pass for an exact degeneracy or for a sign that flipped.
**A broken law is a [`Finding`]** naming the predicate, the swap and the points.
modules.job: Fuzz target: `geom-num`'s exact predicates never panic, and swapping two points flips their sign.

method.text: the algebraic laws of section 28.6 of the kernel architecture (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/28-testing.md`, "Swapping two points flips the sign"). Each predicate is the sign of a determinant with one row per point (the points lifted onto the paraboloid z = |p|² for in-circle and in-sphere), as in Shewchuk, "Adaptive Precision Floating-Point Arithmetic and Fast Robust Geometric Predicates", Discrete & Computational Geometry 18, 1997 (<https://doi.org/10.1007/PL00009321>), which `geom_num::predicate` follows. Exchanging two points exchanges two rows, and by the Leibniz formula an exchange of two rows negates a determinant, so every transposition must flip the sign. The board names orient2d's swap; the same law is checked on the other three predicates, whose points the harness decodes anyway.

modules.cost: `cases` runs of the harness, plus one `SplitMix64` word per eight bytes drawn and one or two words per length.
modules.does: [`run`] resolves a seed with `geom_test::seed::resolve` (the test's default, or `SPAREKIT_SEED`; printed as `seed: <hex>`), then for each case draws a length in `0..=max_len` and that many bytes from `geom-test`'s `SplitMix64`, and runs the harness on them.
guarantees: **The same cases every run.** One seed gives the same byte strings on every target, so a pull request runs a fixed set of cases (28.17) and any failure replays exactly with the printed seed.

**A failure says how to keep it.** [`Failure::Finding`] carries the case number, the seed, the bytes in hexadecimal and the broken law. Saved as a file in the target's `tests/__fuzz__/<target>/crashes` folder, the bytes become a case bolero's test mode replays on every run (28.16).
**Panics are not caught.** A harness that panics fails the test, and the seed line printed before the first case shows which seed to replay.
**Every seed is printed**, by [`run`] as `geom_test::seed::resolve` prints it and by [`run_with_seed`] as `geom_test::seed::fixed` does, before the first case.

modules.cost: per input, the registered descriptions parsed and evaluated once each in big integers, and three exact-path calls per predicate; at most [`MAX_INPUT_BYTES`] bytes read.
modules.does: [`decode`] turns a fuzzer's bytes into the inputs the predicates take: six 2D and five 3D grid points from `geom-test`'s [`GridSampler`], and twelve plane-normal coordinates of 83 bits and four plane offsets of 125 bits, each an extreme, zero, a small value or a value of a random bit length. [`check`] evaluates each registered predicate's description (geom-gen's `PREDICATES`, read by its `predicate_lang::parse`) on those inputs in big integers, and compares the shipped `value`, the plain-`i128` variant (`geom_num::generated::plain`) and the width-aware limb variant (`geom_num::generated::limbs`) with that exact value, and Avnaim et al.'s signs of orient2d and orient3d (`geom_bench::avnaim`) with its sign. [`harness`] is `decode` then `check`, the function every fuzzing engine drives (the crate README sets out the layout).
guarantees: **Any bytes are a case.** Every byte string, the empty one included, decodes to inputs inside every predicate's domain: grid points (magnitude at most 2^40 − 1), aimed at the frame's extremes and at degenerate configurations, and rounded inputs within their declared bits.
**A bounded input.** [`decode`] reads at most [`MAX_INPUT_BYTES`] bytes; longer inputs only add bytes nobody reads.

**An independent oracle.** The exact value is the description's own arithmetic in `num-bigint`'s arbitrary-precision integers, read from the description's text, not from the generated code or the fixed-width integers it uses.
**A wrong or missing value is a [`Finding`]** naming the predicate, the variant, the inputs, what the variant returned and the exact value. Every input is in the domain, so a `None` is a finding too.
modules.job: Fuzz target: every variant of every generated exact path returns the exact value (chapter 23.3; piece G42).

method.text: differential testing against an exact oracle, as chapter 23.3 asks of every variant ("the differential fuzzer checks every variant against a rational oracle"), `projects/engines/geometry/architecture/23-performance.md`, with `num-bigint`'s integers; the descriptions' integer values need no rational.

modules.cost: one operation on `Wide` and one on `BigInt` per input, at most O(L²) for a product of L ≤ 12 limbs, plus up to seven `resize` targets; at most [`MAX_INPUT_BYTES`] bytes read.
modules.does: [`decode`] turns a fuzzer's bytes into a [`Case`]: a width, an operation and two operands of that width (and, for `resize`, a second width). [`check`] runs the operation on `geom_num::wide::Wide` and on `num-bigint`'s `BigInt`, an arbitrary-precision oracle that shares no code with it, and compares: the exact result when it fits the width and `None` exactly when it does not, for `checked_add`, `checked_sub`, `checked_neg` and `checked_mul`; the order (`Ord`, `==`); the sign (`signum`, `is_negative`, `is_zero`); `resize` to every other width; and the `i128` conversions both ways. [`harness`] is `decode` then `check`, the function every fuzzing engine drives (the crate README sets out the layout).
guarantees: **Any bytes are a case.** Every byte string, the empty one included, decodes to a case. Each limb is read through a rule byte that makes the values at every width's limits common: 0, 1, −1, the top bit alone, all bits but the top one, a copy of the limb below, or a word read from the input. So the most negative and most positive values, their neighbours, and carries that run the whole length come up all the time, not once in 2^64.

**Every width the kernel uses, and the two reserved ones.** `I128` as `Wide<2>`, `I256`, `I320`, `I384`, `I512`, and `Wide<9>` and `Wide<12>`, the 576- and 768-bit widths chapter 6.2 reserves for later predicates (the board's G26; whether they are named is an owner's decision, G240), through the same generic code.
**A bounded input.** [`decode`] reads at most [`MAX_INPUT_BYTES`] bytes, derived below; a unit test builds the input that reaches it.
**A panic is a failure; a disagreement is a [`Finding`]** naming the operation, the width, the operands and both answers.
modules.job: Fuzz target: `geom-num`'s wide integers agree with a big-integer oracle on every operation.

method.text: differential testing against an independent arbitrary-precision implementation, the big-integer oracle chapter 29.3 names for the wide integers (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/29-sources-licences.md`), here `num-bigint` 0.4.8 (<https://docs.rs/num-bigint/0.4.8/num_bigint/struct.BigInt.html>). Two's complement in `L` limbs holds exactly −2^(64L−1) ..= 2^(64L−1) − 1 (the module header of `geom_num::wide`); the oracle reads a `Wide`'s limbs with `BigInt::from_signed_bytes_le`, the same two's-complement reading, computes exactly, and writes a result that fits back with `to_signed_bytes_le`.

invariants: **Pure generators.** A generator reads nothing (no files, no environment, no clock) and gives the same bytes on every target, so `check` means the same everywhere; `tests/purity.rs` checks the generator modules' source, and each generator's unit test compares its output with the committed file on every target CI runs, wasm32 included. A generator's seed is fixed in the registry; `SPAREKIT_SEED` never applies to generators, whose outputs are committed and must reproduce.

**Exact.** Generators compute with integers and exact fractions ([`exact`], and [`bignum`]'s naturals and polynomials in the unit roundoff), never with rounded floating point, unless an output is defined as rounded (the filter constant, rounded up once).
**Bytes, exactly.** Outputs use `\n` line ends, and each generated folder's `.gitattributes` turns off line-ending conversion for them, so a Windows checkout compares the committed bytes.
**Development only**, so it may use `std` (chapter 27); `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`; no `unwrap`, `expect`, `panic!` or indexing outside tests.
crates.job: several chapters generate code or data that is checked in (predicate filters and their certificates, subdivision tables, EXPRESS tables, the native format's field tables, `MAP.json`, `PROVENANCE.md` and `NOTICE`)

modules.cost: linear in the number of limbs for addition and shifts, quadratic for multiplication; the generator's numbers have at most a few dozen limbs.
modules.does: [`Nat`] is a natural number of any size (little-endian 64-bit limbs) with exact addition, multiplication, shifts, comparison and a decimal form; the predicate generator's bit-range certificate holds every bound as one. [`UPoly`] is a polynomial in u with non-negative whole coefficients: every bound of the filter's error analysis is one, because the analysis only adds, multiplies, and multiplies by u or by 1 + u. [`UPoly::round_up_to_f64`] gives the smallest `f64` at least the polynomial's exact value at u = 2^-53, as its bits, and [`Nat::nearest_f64`] the `f64` nearest a natural number, as the number it is: the largest a rounded input's `f64` copy can be.
guarantees: **Exact or nothing.** Every operation is exact. One whose result would not fit (a coefficient beyond `u128`, a shift beyond `u32` bits, a value beyond the largest `f64`) returns `None`, never a rounded or wrapped value; nothing panics.
**Canonical.** A [`Nat`] has no zero top limb and a [`UPoly`] no zero top coefficient, so equal values compare equal and print the same.

**Rounded only on purpose.** [`UPoly::round_up_to_f64`] rounds towards +∞, so the `f64` it gives is never below the exact value; [`Nat::nearest_f64`] rounds to nearest with ties to even, exactly as the filters convert a rounded input. Nothing else here rounds.
modules.job: Exact numbers for the predicate generator: natural numbers of any size, and polynomials in the unit roundoff u = 2^-53 with whole coefficients.

method.text: schoolbook addition and multiplication on limbs with 128-bit intermediates (Knuth, *The Art of Computer Programming*, volume 2, section 4.3.1, <https://www-cs-faculty.stanford.edu/~knuth/taocp.html>); decimal digits by repeated short division by 10^19 (Knuth 4.4). The `f64` encoding is IEEE 754-2019's binary64 (<https://standards.ieee.org/ieee/754/6210/>): a normal value is m · 2^e with 2^52 ≤ m < 2^53, stored as the biased exponent e + 52 + 1023 above the 52 fraction bits of m.

modules.cost: O(log n) steps for each greatest common divisor; a decimal is O(number of digits).
modules.does: [`Ratio`] is a non-negative fraction of two `u128`s, always in lowest terms, with checked multiplication and division. [`Ratio::decimal`] writes its exact decimal expansion when it has a finite one, and [`Ratio::fraction`] writes it as `n/d`.
guarantees: **Exact or nothing.** Every operation is exact; one whose result does not fit in `u128` returns `None`, never a rounded or wrapped value. A decimal is written only when it terminates, and then with every digit.
**Canonical.** Lowest terms and a positive denominator, so equal values compare equal and print the same.
modules.job: Exact non-negative fractions for generators, and their exact decimal form.

method.text: Euclid's algorithm for the greatest common divisor (Knuth, *The Art of Computer Programming*, volume 2, section 4.5.2, Algorithm A; <https://www-cs-faculty.stanford.edu/~knuth/taocp.html>), with cross-cancellation before multiplying (Knuth 4.5.1), so intermediate products stay as small as the result allows. A fraction in lowest terms has a finite decimal expansion exactly when its denominator is 2^a × 5^b, and then it has max(a, b) digits after the point (Hardy and Wright, *An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers*, section 9.2); the unit tests check both facts on every denominator that divides 6,400.

modules.cost: every generator once, plus reading or writing each output and listing each generated folder (at most [`MAX_FOLDER_DEPTH`] folders deep, without recursion). Validation compares every pair of outputs and of folders: O(n²) in their number, times their length.
modules.does: [`validate`] checks a registry's rules. [`write()`] produces every output and writes each one whose bytes changed. [`check`] produces every output in memory and compares it with the file, byte for byte, reporting each as current, different (with the first line that differs) or missing. Both also report every orphan: a file in a generated folder that no generator owns. Both work on a workspace root given by the caller, so tests can use a scratch copy.
guarantees: **Byte for byte.** `check` compares bytes, not text: a changed line end, a trailing space or a missing final newline is a difference.

**Validated and generated before anything is written.** `write` validates the registry and runs every generator before it writes any file, so a broken registry or a failing generator leaves every file as it was. An I/O error part-way (a full disk, a folder where a file should be) can leave the outputs before it written; `write` returns the error, and running it again once the cause is fixed finishes the job, because it rewrites only what differs.
**Every file is reported.** `check` does not stop at the first difference: the report names every output that differs or is missing, and every orphan.

**No orphans.** Every output lies inside one of the registry's generated folders ([`Folder`]), and every file in such a folder must be the output of a registered generator or on the folder's keep list. So the old output of a renamed or removed generator is reported as [`Status::Orphan`] until someone deletes it. Neither `write` nor `check` deletes anything.

**One file per output, on every system CI runs.** An output path is relative, uses `/`, and has only plain components of the portable filename character set (`A`–`Z`, `a`–`z`, `0`–`9`, `.`, `_`, `-`), none longer than 255 bytes, none starting with `-` or ending with `.`, and none a Windows device name (`CON`, `PRN`, `AUX`, `NUL`, `COM0`–`COM9`, `LPT0`–`LPT9`, in any case, with or without an extension); the whole path is at most [`MAX_OUTPUT_LEN`] bytes. No two outputs are equal when letter case is ignored (Windows and macOS file systems ignore it), and no output lies inside another. So two generators can never write one file on any runner, and every output can be a file.
modules.job: Writing every generator's output, and checking that every committed output is current.

method.text: regenerate-and-compare, the way CI keeps generated code honest (chapter 27 of the kernel architecture, `projects/engines/geometry/architecture/27-crates-folders.md`: "CI reruns every generator and fails on any difference"). File names follow POSIX's portable filename character set (<https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/basedefs/V1_chap03.html#tag_03_282>) and Microsoft's file naming rules (<https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/fileio/naming-a-file>).

modules.cost: whatever the generator's function costs.
modules.does: [`Generator`] describes a generator; [`Generator::run`] produces its output in memory; [`Generator::seed_line`] is the line every command prints for it.
guarantees: **A seed is explicit, and printed.** A generator that uses randomness is [`Generate::Seeded`], with its seed fixed beside it in the registry, and its function receives that seed. One that uses none is [`Generate::Plain`], and its function receives no seed. Every command prints every generator's line, `seed: <16 hex digits>` or `seed: none`, before it runs any generator.

**No hidden seed: a checked rule, not a type rule.** Rust's types cannot stop a generator's function from building its own seed, because `geom_test::Seed` and `geom_test::SplitMix64` are public. So `tests/purity.rs` reads the source of every generator module and fails if one names a seed, builds a generator or another source of randomness, or reads the environment, a file or a clock; only `registry.rs` may write a seed, and only as a `Generate::Seeded` entry.
**Pure.** The function is a plain `fn` with no captured state: the same bytes every call.
modules.job: One generator: its name, the one output file it owns, its seed if it has one, and the pure function that produces the file's bytes.

method.text: the committed-output pattern of chapter 27's proposed `geom-gen` rule (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/27-crates-folders.md`, "Generated code and data have one home"), with the seed discipline of sections 28.5 and 28.17 (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/28-testing.md`).

modules.cost: constant; a few hundred exact operations.
modules.does: [`generate`] writes a Markdown file, [`OUTPUT`], with three tables:
guarantees: **Exact.** Integers and exact fractions only ([`crate::exact`]); a decimal is printed only when it terminates, with every digit, and a fraction otherwise. Every integer operation is a checked method or an exact fraction operation, so an overflow is an error, never a wrapped value.

**From the code.** Every number comes from `GridStep::quarter_nm`, `grid::COORD_MAX`, `grid::COORD_BITS`, the unit constants (`grid::QUARTER_NM_PER_MM` and the others), the `ladder` constants and `ladder::quarter_nm`, or from the exact unit definitions below. The steps are found by walking `GridStep::coarser` to the coarsest step and then `GridStep::finer` to the finest, so a new step gets its row and column without an edit here. `geom-num` has no list of its unit and ladder constants, so `UNITS` and [`LADDER`] name them, and `tests/drift.rs` reads `geom-num`'s `ladder.rs` and `grid.rs` and fails if any public constant there is missing from the output.

**Checked against the code.** The generator fails rather than print a table that contradicts `geom-num`: each step's name is `Q<rung>`; each step is 25 times finer than the one above, as `grid.rs` states; each unit constant is its unit's exact size, and `GridStep::steps_per` gives exactly the whole counts the table shows, and `None` where the table says "not whole"; each ladder length agrees with `ladder::quarter_nm`; each commit-distance ceiling bounds the exact distance committing can move a point, √n half steps in n dimensions; `ladder::ANGULAR` is exactly 2^`ladder::ANGULAR_LOG2`, bit for bit; and the angular bound is the fit bound divided by 2^`grid::COORD_BITS`.
**No randomness**, no input, `\n` line ends: the same bytes on every target. A unit test compares the output with the committed file, built into the test, on every target CI runs, wasm32 included.
modules.job: Generator `grid-steps`: the grid steps, common units on each step, and the tolerance ladder, exactly, from `geom-num`'s own constants.

method.text: the definitions. 1 mm = 10^6 nm = 4,000,000 quarter-nanometres. The inch is 25.4 mm exactly and the US survey foot 1200/3937 m exactly, as NIST Special Publication 811 (2008 edition), appendix B, states (<https://www.nist.gov/pml/special-publication-811>). An `f64` is exactly 2^e (for a normal e) when its fraction bits are zero and its biased exponent is e + 1023, by the binary64 format of IEEE 754-2019 (<https://standards.ieee.org/ieee/754/6210/>). A point whose n coordinates each move by at most h moves by at most √n · h, by Pythagoras: √(n · h²).

modules.cost: one run of every generator and one read or write of each output ([`geom_gen::files`]), or a listing of the registry.
guarantees: every command prints each generator's seed (`seed: <hex>`, or `seed: none` for a generator that uses no randomness) before it runs any generator, so the seeds are printed even when a generator fails. `--root` names the workspace root to work in; by default it is the workspace this binary was built in. Exit codes: 0 success; 1 an output differs or is missing, or a generated folder holds an orphan (`write` too reports orphans, and never deletes them); 2 a usage, registry, generator or file error.
modules.job: `geom-gen`: write, check or list every committed generator output.

method.none: it parses its arguments and calls [`geom_gen::files`], whose module header carries the method.

modules.cost: linear in the description's steps times the ways its scale's larger-ofs resolve (one per case); no allocation beyond the text.
modules.does: a generated filter computes the description's steps in `f64` on its inputs (coordinates, their differences, and the `f64` copies of wider integers), the scale S from the groups' maxima, and the bound `fl(C · scale)`, and answers when the computed value is beyond the bound. [`gappa_problem`] states exactly that computation in Gappa's binary64 with rounding to nearest, beside the same steps evaluated exactly, on whole-number inputs bounded by their groups' maxima, and asks Gappa to prove that the error is within K · S and the computed bound within a relative error R of C · S, with K = C · (1 − R): together, |error| ≤ K · S ≤ bound, so an answer has the exact sign. Where the result's scale has several monomials (the larger of `m_x^3 m_y` and `m_x m_y^3`, say), one problem cannot state it: [`gappa_case_problem`] states one problem per case ([`gappa_cases`]), the case where one group's maximum is the largest when the monomials share one degree, and otherwise where one monomial is the largest of the result's, each with S that monomial and the hypotheses the case implies. [`fptaylor_problem`] states the normalised problem for `FPTaylor`, each step divided by its scale S(v), the largest of its monomials at the group maxima, so every input is in [−1, 1] and the result's scale is 1, with a ratio parameter in [0, 1] where a sum's operand has a smaller scale set; one problem covers every input, with the same K, which HOL Light compares the certificate's bound with. [`proof_sentence`] is the label: proven, naming the problems, when the Gappa problems state the filter in every case, and otherwise "checked, not proven" with the open issue [`UNPROVEN`] gives it. Every problem carries Gappa's hints and HOL Light's bound in its text, so the tools' runs need nothing else.
guarantees: **The shipped steps.** Each problem holds one rounded definition per operation of the filter, in the generated code's order, with its operands and operation, and the constant and the scale's product order as the code has them; `tests/certificate_problems.rs` holds the committed problems to the committed filters statement by statement.

**Every input covered, nothing assumed that fails.** A filter's cases together cover every input, one problem for each way its scale's larger-ofs resolve, and each hypothesis holds for every input of its case; `tests/certificate_problems.rs` justifies each one independently.

**Exact numbers.** R = (k + 1)u, for the k roundings between the maxima and the bound, bounds the bound's relative error ((1 + u)^k − 1 < (k + 1)u for u = 2^−53), and K = C · (1 − R) is computed exactly from the constant's bits: both are dyadic, written exactly. A rounded input's largest copy is its bound rounded to the nearest `f64`, exactly ([`crate::bignum::Nat`]).

**Refused, never approximated.** A filter the Gappa problems cannot state (a scale term formed from more than two inputs, say) is refused with the reason, and its label says "checked, not proven" with its issue; with no issue in [`UNPROVEN`] its module cannot be generated.

**Ratios, never more.** Each ratio parameter of an `FPTaylor` problem is S(operand) / S(sum) for the pairs of scale sets named in the problem's header, each the same ratio once their common factor is cancelled, and every use of it is one of those pairs: the problem's box holds every input's normalised values, never fewer.
modules.job: The problems that machine-check a predicate filter's error bound (chapter 28.6 of the kernel architecture; pieces G35 and G40): the filter's claim stated for Gappa, whose proof Rocq checks, and for `FPTaylor`, whose certificate HOL Light checks; and the label each generated module carries, proven or "checked, not proven".

method.text: Melquiond and Pion's certified semi-static filters, Gappa proofs of a homogeneous predicate's error as a multiple of the product of its inputs' maxima (*Formally certified floating-point filters for homogeneous geometric predicates*, RAIRO Theoretical Informatics and Applications 41 (2007), <https://doi.org/10.1051/ita:2007005>), with Gappa's `LIN` predicate (`a // b`) in place of their special rounding operators, which current Gappa no longer has, and a case split for a scale that takes a larger-of; and `FPTaylor`'s symbolic Taylor forms on the normalised problem (Solovyev et al., *Rigorous Estimation of Floating-Point Round-off Errors with Symbolic Taylor Expansions*, ACM TOPLAS 41 (2018), <https://doi.org/10.1145/3230733>).

modules.cost: linear in the number of steps, times the size of the numbers (a few limbs, a few dozen coefficients) and of the scale sets (a few monomials).
modules.does: [`derive`] takes a description ([`crate::predicate_lang`]) and returns a [`Derivation`]: for every step, a [`StepCert`] (the bound on its exact value over the input domain, its bits, the integer type the exact path computes it in, and the filter's scale, unit bound and unit error for it), the scale expression the filter evaluates at run time, the number of roundings in it, and the error constant, exactly and as the `f64` the filter uses.
guarantees: **The certificate.** For every input in the domain (grid coordinates |v| ≤ 2^40 − 1 = `geom_num::grid::COORD_MAX`; rounded inputs |v| ≤ 2^bits − 1), every step's exact value v has |v| ≤ `bound` < 2^`bits`, and its exact-path type holds every value of that magnitude.

**The filter.** With M(g) the largest |x̃| over the computed scale variables x of group g, S the largest product Π M(g)^e(g) over the monomials e of the result's scale, and ṽ the result computed in `f64` in the steps' order: |ṽ − v| ≤ E · S, where E is the result's unit error. The generated filter computes S in `f64`, at least S · (1 − u)^r with r = [`ScaleExpr::roundings`] (every product's rounding and its operands', since relative errors multiply), and multiplies it by the constant, one more rounding: k = [`Derivation::roundings`] = r + 1. The constant is at least E · (1 + 2u)^k, so the computed bound is at least E · S, and a computed value beyond it in magnitude has the exact value's sign. If S is zero the exact value is zero.

**No overflow, no underflow, no NaN.** Every value the filter computes is a whole number (inputs are whole numbers or `f64` copies of them, and the correctly rounded sum or product of whole numbers is whole), so none is subnormal; and every computed magnitude, and the bound, is checked here to stay below 2^1000, far from `f64::MAX`.
modules.job: The derivation behind each generated predicate: the bit-range certificate of every intermediate, the width of the exact path, and the filter's error constant, all exact.

method.text: Meyer and Pion, *FPG: A code generator for fast and certified geometric predicates*, Real Numbers and Computers 2008 (<https://inria.hal.science/inria-00344297>), as Geogram's PCK uses it (Lévy, *Robustness and efficiency of geometric programs: the Predicate Construction Kit (PCK)*, Computer-Aided Design 72, 2016, <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cad.2015.10.004>; generated headers such as <https://github.com/BrunoLevy/geogram/blob/16843b4804de35f14ef54667950ab4c8acdd0062/src/lib/geogram/numerics/predicates/orient3d.h>, BSD-3-Clause, read for method; no code is ported). Shewchuk's stage-A bounds (<https://www.cs.cmu.edu/afs/cs/project/quake/public/code/predicates.c>, `exactinit`) are the comparison in the generated headers.

provenance.purpose: for its compile-time bit counting, a cross-check of the certificate here. No code copied.

modules.cost: linear in the number of steps.
modules.does: [`predicate_module`] writes a predicate's module from its [`Derivation`]: a header with the description, the bit-range certificate and the error analysis, the error constant, `filter` (the `f64` evaluation and its decision), and `value` and `exact` (the checked integer evaluation). [`parent_module`] writes the module that declares them and holds the helpers they share. Both are formatted as rustfmt formats them, so `cargo fmt --check` passes on the committed files. [`verus_twin`] writes a Verus-annotated twin of a predicate's exact path (chapter 28.7; piece G36): a model of the grid's types, the description's value over the integers, and `value` written by the same function as the module's, with a `#[verus_spec]` attribute and a `proof!` hint before each product, so with those removed it is the shipped `value` token for token.
guarantees: **The code is the derivation.** `filter` performs exactly the derivation's steps, in their order, one `let` per step, so the error analysis is about the code that runs; it computes the scale by the derivation's scale expression, whose roundings the constant accounts for. `value` performs the same steps, each in the integer type the certificate gives it (the narrowest of `i64`, `i128`, `I256`, `I320`, `I384` and `I512` that holds its bound), with operands widened to that type and checked arithmetic (`checked_add`, `checked_sub`, `checked_mul`, and `resize` between `Wide`s), so a certificate that was wrong would show as `None`, never as a wrapped value. A product in a `Wide` whose operands fit `i128` is `product_i128`, and one with one such operand `checked_mul_i128` (piece G29): the same exact product or `None`, without widening the narrow operand to every limb. The certificate's rows name the same steps.

**Width-aware, as chapter 23.3 asks.** A step that fits 63 bits is computed in `i64`, so a product of two such steps is `i128::from(a).checked_mul(i128::from(b))`: two sign-extended 64-bit operands, whose product the compiler proves cannot overflow `i128` and emits as one 64 × 64 → 128-bit multiply, where a product of two general `i128`s is a long overflow-checked sequence. The value is the same either way; only the cost differs.

**Only the domain the analysis assumes.** A point input is a `P2` or `P3`, whose coordinates are within the grid, so no caller can pass a value outside it. A rounded input is passed as its exact integer, an `i128` (a description's rounded input of more than 127 bits is refused here: no correctly rounded conversion of a wider integer to `f64` exists in `geom-num` yet); `filter` converts it to its nearest `f64` and both functions return `None` for one outside its declared range, before any bound is relied on.

**Names that cannot collide.** Every name the module binds is checked here against every other and against the module's items, imports and Rust's keywords, so a description that slipped past the language's rules ([`crate::predicate_lang::reserved`]) is refused, never emitted as code that shadows a value or does not compile.

**Kernel rules.** No native integer arithmetic and no casts beyond the exact conversion of a grid coordinate to `f64` and the correctly rounded conversion of a rounded input (each with its reason written beside it), no `unsafe`, no panics, no allocation; every public item documented.

method.text: the straight-line predicate programs of Meyer and Pion's FPG input language (a subset of C with `group` declarations; Meyer and Pion, *FPG: A code generator for fast and certified geometric predicates*, Real Numbers and Computers 2008, <https://inria.hal.science/inria-00344297>) and of Geogram's PCK `.pck` files (BSD-3-Clause; for example <https://github.com/BrunoLevy/geogram/blob/16843b4804de35f14ef54667950ab4c8acdd0062/src/lib/geogram/numerics/predicates/orient2d.pck>), cut down to what the kernel's predicates need: one expression per line, no preprocessor, no symbolic perturbation. modules.cost: each generator derives one predicate, or all eleven for the parent module and each variant: a few hundred exact operations each.
modules.does: holds the description of each predicate on explicit grid points (chapter 6.2: orientation in 2D and 3D, in-circle and in-sphere), of the side of a plane, whose coefficients are wider integers whose `f64` copies are rounded (chapter 23.2), and of the predicates on implicit points (chapter 6.3, piece G29): the sign of the weight of a three-plane point, of a line-plane point and of a 2D crossing point, and which side of a plane (or, in 2D, of a line) each lies on, in the language of [`crate::predicate_lang`], and the generators that derive each one ([`crate::predicate_derive`]) and write its module into `geom-num` ([`crate::predicate_emit`]): [`OUTPUT_DIR`]`/<name>.rs` for each predicate and [`OUTPUT_DIR`]`/mod.rs` for the module that holds them, and [`PLAIN_OUTPUT`] and [`LIMBS_OUTPUT`] for every exact path in plain `i128` and in width-aware 32-bit limbs, two of chapter 23.3's variants (piece G42), which the benchmarks compare with the shipped paths. `geom-num`'s `predicate.rs` calls the four explicit-point ones, `plane.rs` the side of a plane and the three-plane and line-plane ones, and `crossing.rs` the 2D crossing ones.
guarantees: **The same formulas as `predicate.rs`, `plane.rs` and `crossing.rs`.** Each description evaluates the determinant that `geom-num`'s hand-written fast path evaluates, term for term and with the same signs, so the generated exact value equals the hand-written one (tested in `geom-num`), and the generated filter's sign, when it gives one, is that value's sign. In-sphere shares the three cross products its four 3 × 3 determinants need instead of recomputing them; the values are the same. `plane_side` evaluates n · p + d as `geom-num`'s `Plane::side` does, term for term; `tpi_weight` and `tpi_side` evaluate the three-plane point's weight and its classification as `Tpi::homogeneous` and `Plane::side_of_tpi` do, except that the classification subtracts n · (−X) where `plane.rs` adds n · X, the same value; and the line-plane and crossing descriptions evaluate what `plane.rs` and `crossing.rs` document for them, step for step.
**Pure.** No input but the descriptions and `geom-num`'s constants; the same bytes on every target.

modules.cost: a few seconds natively: for every node, a few hundred halvings, each an exact evaluation of a polynomial of degree at most 2n + 1 ≤ 61 at a dyadic point.
modules.does: writes `geom-num`'s `src/quadrature_rules/mod.rs`, the tables `geom_num::quadrature` integrates with: the Gauss–Legendre rules of 1 to [`GAUSS_MAX`] points, and the Gauss–Kronrod rules of 2n + 1 points that extend the n-point Gauss rule for each n of [`KRONROD_N`] (QUADPACK's six). Every number is computed in exact rational arithmetic and rounded to the nearest `f64`, ties to even, only once an exact enclosure of it lies inside one rounding cell, so each entry is the correctly rounded value of the true node or weight.
guarantees: **Correctly rounded.** Every node and weight is the `f64` nearest to the exact value, ties to even (dashu-ratio's `to_f64`, which its documentation guarantees correctly rounded, and the unit tests check against both neighbours), decided from an exact enclosure, never from an approximation.

**Exact or nothing.** Every step is exact rational arithmetic; a bracket that does not round to one value within [`MAX_HALVINGS`] halvings, or an isolation that fails, is an error, never an approximate table.
**Pure.** No input but the constants here; the same bytes on every target.
modules.job: Generator `quadrature-rules`: the Gauss–Legendre and Gauss–Kronrod rules on [−1, 1], computed exactly and each node and weight rounded once to the nearest `f64` (piece G51; chapters 12 and 29.4).

method.text: G. H. Golub and J. H. Welsch, *Calculation of Gauss quadrature rules*, Mathematics of Computation 23 (1969), <https://doi.org/10.1090/S0025-5718-69-99647-1>; G. H. Golub and C. F. Van Loan, *Matrix Computations*, 4th ed., Johns Hopkins (2013), section 8.4.1 (bisection by Sturm count); A. S. Kronrod, *Nodes and Weights of Quadrature Formulas*, Consultants Bureau (1965); G. Szegő, *Über gewisse orthogonale Polynome, die zu einer oszillierenden Belegungsfunktion gehören*, Mathematische Annalen 110 (1935), <https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01448041> (the interlacing); the rule set is QUADPACK's (R. kinds.name: NotFinite

kinds.doc: The matrix is singular: a zero pivot (LU, triangular, tridiagonal).
kinds.name: Singular

kinds.doc: The matrix is not symmetric positive definite (Cholesky).
kinds.name: NotPositiveDefinite

kinds.doc: The work budget cannot cover the factorisation's cost.

kinds.doc: An allocation could not be made.
kinds.name: OutOfMemory
