errors.name: LinalgError

invariants: Bit-identical results on every target and thread count: plain scalar loops in a fixed order, no SIMD chosen at run time, no `mul_add`, and no threads inside one factorisation (15.6, 21).
Least-squares steps come from QR or the complete orthogonal decomposition, never from the normal equations, which square the condition number (15.6).
The least-change step is the limit of the damped steps as damping goes to zero, so an under-determined system never jumps to a pivot-order basic solution (15.6).
Column ordering follows COLAMD (Davis, Gilbert, Larimore and Ng 2004), written in safe Rust, with ties broken by variable order (15.6).
No platform maths: every maths function comes from `geom_num::math` (21).
crates.job: Deterministic dense and sparse linear algebra: QR, the complete orthogonal decomposition, triangular solves, column ordering.

modules.cost: one allocation of len · count doubles; access is constant time, copies linear.
modules.does: [`Cols`] holds `count` columns of `len` doubles each, one after another, so a column is one contiguous slice and two columns can be borrowed together for a rotation. [`Cols::to_matrix`] copies chosen columns, in a chosen order, into a row-major [`Matrix`].
guarantees: **No panic, no abort.** Every index is checked and every index sum and product too; a bad one is [`LinalgError::Defect`]. The storage is allocated fallibly.
**Exact copies.** Moving values between [`Cols`] and [`Matrix`] copies them unchanged.
modules.job: Matrices stored by columns, for the factorisations that work column by column (the SVDs and the symmetric eigensolver), and checked index arithmetic for them.

method.text: column-major storage as LAPACK uses it (E. Anderson et al., *LAPACK Users' Guide*, 3rd ed., SIAM (1999), <https://www.netlib.org/lapack/lug/>).

modules.cost: (4/3)·n³ for the reduction and 2·n³ for its accumulation, charged first as 4·n³; each QR step then charges (block + 1)·(4n + 12). One working copy, the tridiagonal and Q.
modules.does: [`SymmetricEigen::factor`] reduces a symmetric n × n matrix to tridiagonal form T by n − 2 Householder similarity transformations (Golub and Van Loan's algorithm 8.3.1), then applies implicit QR steps with Wilkinson's shift (algorithm 8.3.2), chasing the bulge down T with Givens rotations, until every subdiagonal entry is negligible (|`b_i`| ≤ 2^−52·(|`a_i`| + |`a_(i+1)`|)); the diagonal is then Λ, and the accumulated transformations Q. Eigenvalues come smallest first, each with its unit eigenvector as a column of Q.
guarantees: **Symmetric or refused.** A matrix that is not square is [`LinalgError::Shape`]; one whose entries are not exactly symmetric, `a_ij` ≠ `a_ji` for some pair, is [`LinalgError::NotSymmetric`]. Only the lower triangle is read after that check.

**Deterministic.** Fixed order of reflections, rotations and deflation tests; the shift from the trailing 2 × 2 block, computed on the block scaled to magnitude 1; IEEE 754 operations in the order written and the correctly rounded square root; a stable sort of the eigenvalues with ties broken by position.

**Accuracy, checked against exact rationals.** The method is backward stable: Q·Λ·Qᵀ is a symmetric matrix within a small multiple of u·‖A‖ of A, so each eigenvalue is within that of an exact one (Golub and Van Loan, section 8.3.6). The tests check the residual and Q's orthogonality exactly and bracket each eigenvalue by exact inertia counts of A − x·I.
**Bounded.** At most 30·n QR steps, then [`LinalgError::NoConvergence`]; each step charges its work before it runs, the reduction its own first.
modules.job: The symmetric eigenproblem: A = Q·Λ·Qᵀ for a symmetric matrix, by Householder tridiagonalisation and the implicit symmetric QR algorithm with Wilkinson's shift.

method.text: G. H. Golub and C. F. Van Loan, *Matrix Computations*, 4th ed., Johns Hopkins (2013), algorithms 8.3.1 (Householder tridiagonalisation), 8.3.2 (the implicit symmetric QR step with Wilkinson shift) and 8.3.3 (the symmetric QR algorithm), and section 8.3.6 (accuracy); J. H. Wilkinson, *The Algebraic Eigenvalue Problem*, Clarendon Press (1965), chapter 8, for the shift; B. N. Parlett, *The Symmetric Eigenvalue Problem*, SIAM (1998), chapter 8, <https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9781611971163>, for the shift's convergence. Written in our own words from the books (chapter 29.4).

modules.cost: a matrix of r × c entries is one allocation of r · c doubles; access is constant time.
modules.does: [`Matrix`] is a dense matrix stored by rows, every entry a finite `f64`, made only by fallible constructors (an allocation that cannot be made is [`LinalgError::OutOfMemory`], never an abort). [`Work`] is a budget in units of one multiply-add: each factorisation knows its cost from its shape, charges it in full before touching a number, and refuses with [`LinalgError::OutOfWork`] when the budget cannot cover it, so a factorisation either finishes or never starts (chapter 15.6: "budgets in work, not time").
guarantees: **Finite.** Every entry of every [`Matrix`] is finite; a constructor refuses NaN and infinities with [`LinalgError::NotFinite`], and a factorisation whose arithmetic overflows reports it the same way instead of returning infinities.

**Charged before it starts.** A factorisation's cost is a function of its shape alone, stated on each function, and is charged before any arithmetic: the same budget gives the same answer, or the same refusal, on every target.
**No panic, no abort.** Indices are checked; allocations are fallible.
modules.job: Dense matrices of finite doubles, the errors of every factorisation, and the work budget each one charges before it starts.

method.text: row-major dense storage, as LAPACK's column-major storage transposed (E. Anderson et al., *LAPACK Users' Guide*, 3rd ed., SIAM (1999), <https://www.netlib.org/lapack/lug/>), with the work model of G. H. Golub and C. F. Van Loan, *Matrix Computations*, 4th ed., Johns Hopkins (2013), section 1.1.15 (flop counts).

modules.cost: as charged above; one copy of A and a few vectors of length n.
modules.does: [`PivotedQr::factor`] factors an m × n matrix as A·Π = Q·R, Q a product of Householder reflections, R upper triangular with diagonal magnitudes that never increase, Π the column order chosen by largest remaining norm. [`Cod::factor`] decides the rank r from R's diagonal and a relative tolerance, then removes R's trailing columns by reflections from the right, giving A·Π = Q·[T 0; 0 0]·Zᵀ with T r × r upper triangular: the complete orthogonal decomposition. From it, [`Cod::least_squares`] gives the least-squares solution of A·x = b of least norm (chapter 15.6's full step: the limit of the damped steps, never a pivot-order basic solution), and [`Cod::null_space`] an orthonormal basis of the null space. [`canonical_null_space`] turns that basis into chapter 15.8's canonical one: reduced echelon form over the variable order, each vector 1 at its own leading variable and 0 at the others', so the basis is unique.
guarantees: **Deterministic.** Plain scalar loops in a fixed order (chapter 15.6). A pivot column is the one of largest remaining norm, the first on a tie; norms are scaled by the column's largest magnitude, so they never overflow for finite entries.

**Least change, never basic.** In a rank-deficient or under-determined system the solution has the least Euclidean norm among all least-squares solutions; no free variable is set to zero in pivot order.

**Rank decided once, by the caller's tolerance.** A diagonal entry of R at most `tol` times the first ends the rank; the tolerance is the caller's (chapter 15 derives it from the tolerance ladder). Like every column-pivoted QR, it can miss a near rank deficiency that no column norm shows: Kahan's matrix is the classic case (tested).
**Charged first.** A factorisation charges 2·m·n·min(m, n) multiply-adds before it starts, the decomposition r²·n more, a solve 2·m·n, a null space n²·(n − r).
modules.job: Householder QR with column pivoting, the complete orthogonal decomposition, the minimum-norm least-squares solution, and the canonical null space.

method.text: G. H. Golub and C. F. Van Loan, *Matrix Computations*, 4th ed., Johns Hopkins (2013): algorithm 5.1.1 (the Householder vector), 5.4.1 (QR with column pivoting), section 5.4.2 (the complete orthogonal decomposition) and 5.5 (least squares in the rank-deficient case); the column norms downdated as LAPACK's `xLAQP2` does, recomputed when the downdate loses more than √u of its relative accuracy (Z. Drmač and Z. Bujanović, *On the failure of rank-revealing QR factorization software*, ACM TOMS 35 (2008), doi:10.1145/1377612.1377616); the trailing columns removed as LAPACK's `xTZRZF` does (E. Anderson et al., *LAPACK Users' Guide*, 3rd ed., SIAM (1999), <https://www.netlib.org/lapack/lug/>). Written in our own words from the books and papers (chapter 29.4).

modules.cost: constant per call; [`rotate_slices`] is linear in the vectors' length.
modules.does: [`hypot`] gives √(a² + b²) without overflow or underflow; [`givens`] gives the rotation (c, s) and r with c·y + s·z = r and −s·y + c·z = 0, which zeroes z against y; [`rotate`] applies a rotation to a pair of numbers, and [`rotate_slices`] to two vectors element by element.
guarantees: **No spurious overflow or underflow.** [`hypot`] divides both numbers by the larger magnitude before squaring, so the squares lie in [0, 1] and the sum in [1, 2].
**Deterministic.** IEEE 754 operations in the order written and the correctly rounded square root of `geom_num::math`; no fused multiply-add.
**Exact identity when nothing is to be zeroed.** A zero z gives c = 1, s = 0 and r = y, so a rotation that has nothing to do changes no bit.
modules.job: Plane rotations and the norm of two numbers, for the iterative factorisations.

method.text: Givens rotations as Golub and Van Loan compute them (G. H. Golub and C. F. Van Loan, *Matrix Computations*, 4th ed., Johns Hopkins (2013), section 5.1.8 and algorithm 5.1.3), with the norm scaled as LAPACK's `xLAPY2` does (E. Anderson et al., *LAPACK Users' Guide*, 3rd ed., SIAM (1999), <https://www.netlib.org/lapack/lug/>); written in our own words (chapter 29.4).

modules.cost: as charged above; one allocation of n² doubles for LU or Cholesky, n doubles per solve.
modules.does: [`Lu::factor`] factors a square matrix as P·A = L·U by Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting, and [`Lu::solve`] solves A·x = b with it. [`Cholesky::factor`] factors a symmetric positive definite matrix as A = G·Gᵀ, and [`Cholesky::solve`] solves with it. [`solve_lower`] and [`solve_upper`] are forward and back substitution on a triangle, and [`solve_tridiagonal`] solves a tridiagonal system by Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting.
guarantees: **Deterministic.** Plain scalar loops in a fixed order: no SIMD, no fused multiply-add, no threads (chapter 15.6). A pivot is the largest magnitude in its column, the first such row on a tie, so the same matrix gives the same factors, bit for bit, on every target.

**Refused, never guessed.** A zero pivot is [`LinalgError::Singular`], a non-positive Cholesky pivot or an asymmetric matrix [`LinalgError::NotPositiveDefinite`], an overflow [`LinalgError::NotFinite`]: no result holds an infinity or a NaN. Tiny pivots are allowed: conditioning is the caller's to judge (the complete orthogonal decomposition in [`crate::qr`] decides rank).

**Charged first.** Each factorisation charges its cost to the [`Work`] budget before any arithmetic: n³ multiply-adds for LU and Cholesky (an upper bound: n³/3 and n³/6 are the leading terms), n² for a solve with factors, n for a tridiagonal solve.
modules.job: Square systems: LU with partial pivoting, Cholesky, triangular and tridiagonal solves.

method.text: G. H. Golub and C. F. Van Loan, *Matrix Computations*, 4th ed., Johns Hopkins (2013): algorithm 3.4.1 (Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting, outer-product form), 3.1.1 and 3.1.2 (row-oriented forward and back substitution), 4.2.2 (Cholesky, gaxpy form) and section 4.3.6 with LAPACK's `dgtsv` (tridiagonal elimination with partial pivoting, which fills one extra superdiagonal; E. Anderson et al., *LAPACK Users' Guide*, 3rd ed., SIAM (1999), <https://www.netlib.org/lapack/lug/>), written in our own words from the books (chapter 29.4's row for LAPACK, Golub and Van Loan and the Thomas algorithm).

modules.cost: Jacobi charges n²·(5m + 2n) per sweep and converges in a handful of sweeps; Golub–Kahan charges 8·m·n² + 4·n³ for the reduction and the accumulation, then (k + 1)·(4(m + n) + 12) per QR step. Each allocates its working copy, U and V.
modules.does: [`Svd::jacobi`] and [`Svd::golub_kahan`] factor an m × n matrix as A = U·Σ·Vᵀ, with k = min(m, n) singular values in Σ, largest first, U m × k and V n × k with orthonormal columns. A wide matrix is factored through its transpose.
guarantees: **Deterministic.** Fixed sweep order (pairs (p, q), p < q, row by row), fixed deflation and shift rules, IEEE 754 operations in the order written, the correctly rounded square root of `geom_num::math`, no fused multiply-add, and a stable sort with ties broken by column index. The same input gives the same bits on every target.

**Accuracy, checked against exact rationals.** Both are backward stable: the computed factors are those of a matrix A + E with ‖E‖ a small multiple of u·‖A‖ (Golub and Van Loan, 8.6.3), so each singular value is within that of the exact one. Jacobi does better on graded matrices A = B·D with B well conditioned: each singular value to a small multiple of u·κ(B) in relative terms, however small (Demmel and Veselić, theorem 4.4). The tests check both claims with exact rational arithmetic: the residual and the orthogonality of U and V, and each singular value bracketed by exact inertia counts of Aᵀ·A.

**Bounded.** Jacobi stops after [`MAX_SWEEPS`] sweeps and Golub–Kahan after 6·k² QR steps with [`LinalgError::NoConvergence`]; neither has ever needed it in the tests. Each sweep or step charges its work before it runs; the reductions charge theirs first.
**Typed failures.** Columns whose norms differ by more than the doubles can hold (a rotation angle that is not finite) are [`LinalgError::NotFinite`], never a silently wrong factor.
modules.job: The singular value decomposition, two ways: one-sided Jacobi, accurate to the last bits of tiny singular values of graded matrices, and Golub–Kahan, the fast general method.

method.text: M. R. Hestenes, "Inversion of matrices by biorthogonalization and related results", *Journal of the SIAM* 6(1) (1958), 51–90, <https://doi.org/10.1137/0106005>. J. Demmel and K. Veselić, "Jacobi's method is more accurate than QR", *SIAM Journal on Matrix Analysis and Applications* 13(4) (1992), 1204–1245, <https://doi.org/10.1137/0613074>. G. Golub and W. Kahan, "Calculating the singular values and pseudo-inverse of a matrix", *Journal of the SIAM, Series B* 2(2) (1965), 205–224, <https://doi.org/10.1137/0702016>. G. H. Golub and C. F. Van Loan, *Matrix Computations*, 4th ed., Johns Hopkins (2013), algorithms 5.4.2 (bidiagonalisation), 8.6.1 and 8.6.2 (the Golub–Kahan SVD step and algorithm) and section 8.6.3 (accuracy).

errors.doc: Why an operation of this crate could not produce a result.

kinds.doc: A numeric error from the numbers layer: a value out of range, not finite, degenerate, a step conversion in the wrong direction, or a step that a bit budget rules out ([`NumError::BudgetExceeded`], a defect).
kinds.name: Num

kinds.doc: The transform's linear part is singular, or so close to singular that its orientation cannot be certified, so it has no inverse.
kinds.name: Singular

kinds.doc: Two frames cannot be related by an exact integer shift.
kinds.name: FrameMismatch

kinds.doc: Geometry does not fit the frame it belongs to: a coordinate would lie beyond ±(2^40 − 1) steps of that frame's origin (chapters 17.1 and 22).
kinds.name: FrameRangeExceeded

kinds.doc: A 2D point, vector or box was given a transform that does not act in the plane: it changes some point's z, so it does not map the plane z = 0 of a 2D frame onto itself (chapter 14.10's 2D transforms leave z unchanged). It is refused, never projected.
kinds.name: NotInPlane

errors.name: MathError

invariants: **Exact where it decides.** Grid vectors, grid and rational transforms and grid boxes use integers only, and every product's bit budget is derived in its doc comment. Arithmetic that could leave its range is checked and returns [`NumError::OutOfRange`](geom_num::NumError) instead of wrapping.

**The same result in every build profile; defects reported, never answered.** As in the numbers layer, every integer addition, subtraction, multiplication, division and negation in this crate's code is a checked method, never a native operator, and no cast loses a value silently (each cast's bound is written beside it), so nothing depends on overflow checks being on. A step that its bit budget proves fits can fail only through a defect, and is then reported as [`NumError::BudgetExceeded`](geom_num::NumError), never replaced by a guessed value: that is why exact products and classifications return a `Result`. For valid inputs every such result is `Ok`. Clippy enforces this (`arithmetic_side_effects` and the lossy-cast lints are denied); tests and the benchmark may use native arithmetic.

**Certified elsewhere.** Floating-point boxes round outward; transform classifications and orientations are decided with interval arithmetic, never with a guessed tolerance (the only tolerance used is the ladder's angular bound); conversions to the grid round exactly once and say whether they were exact.
**Never NaN, never infinite.** Every floating-point value this crate makes is finite; an operation whose result would not be returns an error.

**Deterministic.** Only IEEE 754 basic operations (which Rust never fuses into a fused multiply-add), integer arithmetic and the maths of `geom_num::math`. No hash maps, no randomness, no platform maths, no recursion; every loop is bounded, by a fixed or proven count or by the length of the caller's own input (`from_points`, [`FrameRecord::home_of`]).
**Safe.** No `unsafe`, no panics, no unchecked indexing.
crates.job: points, vectors, exact and general transforms, boxes and frames, the small vocabulary every geometry crate above the numbers layer shares.

modules.cost: constant time and no allocation for every operation except `from_points`, which is one union per point. Grid boxes compare integers (at most six comparisons for a union, an intersection or a containment test); moving one by a [`GridTransform`] moves its two corners. [`FBox3::transformed`] is 18 interval operations, a product and a sum for each entry of the linear part (an interval sum is two IEEE additions, a product four multiplications and six comparisons, each followed by a one-step widening of both bounds); [`FBox3::to_grid_outward`] is six roundings and six range checks; [`FBox2`]'s operations are the same on two axes (its transform, eight interval operations).
guarantees: **Never empty, always ordered.** Every box has `min ≤ max` (`lo ≤ hi`) on every axis; constructors refuse anything else with [`NumError::EmptyInterval`], and an intersection that would be empty is `None`.
**Closed.** Boxes contain their boundary: two boxes that share only a face, an edge or a corner overlap.
**Finite.** `FBox2` and `FBox3` bounds are finite, with zero stored as +0; operations that would overflow return [`NumError::NotFinite`].
**2D in the plane only.** A 2D box is moved only by a transform that leaves z unchanged; any other is refused with [`MathError::NotInPlane`], never projected.
modules.job: Axis-aligned boxes: exact boxes on the grid, and floating-point boxes that round outward.

method.text: closed intervals per axis, so a box is the product of three intervals and every operation is per-axis interval logic; outward-rounded interval arithmetic as in R. E. Moore, R. B. Kearfott and M. J. Cloud, *Introduction to Interval Analysis*, SIAM (2009), <https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898717716>.

modules.cost: constant time, no loops, no allocation; each operation is a fixed sequence of IEEE operations on `two_sum` and `two_prod`. [`DD::add`] is four `two_sum`s and two additions; [`DD::add_f64`] two `two_sum`s and one addition; [`DD::mul_f64`] one `two_prod`, two `two_sum`s and two more operations; [`DD::mul`] one `two_prod`, one `two_sum` and four more operations; [`DD::div`] three divisions, two [`DD::mul_f64`]s, two [`DD::sub`]s, one `two_sum` and one [`DD::add_f64`]; [`DD::sqrt`] one correctly rounded `geom_num::math::sqrt`, one `two_prod`, one [`DD::sub`], one division and one `two_sum`. Operands outside `two_prod`'s range, and every division and square root, add a power-of-two scaling of each part going in and of the result coming out (`scale_b`: a bit decomposition and one or two multiplications). [`DD::round_shifted`] is two roundings to integers, one `two_sum` and a few `i128` additions and comparisons.
guarantees: relative error bounds on the exact result of the operation applied to the exact values of the operands (u = 2^−53). The middle column is proven on each method below, in full, with every higher-order term kept; it is the bound the kernel relies on. The last column is the tighter bound Joldes, Muller and Popescu prove for the same algorithm, as the authors state it (see the sources; their journal text was not available to us).
modules.job: Double-double arithmetic: a real number held as the unevaluated sum of two doubles.

method.text: the papers below, whose algorithms each operation follows. T. J. Dekker, "A floating-point technique for extending the available precision", *Numerische Mathematik* 18 (1971), 224–242, <https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01397083>: the double-length representation and the addition and multiplication. Y. Hida, X. S. Li and D. H. Bailey, "Algorithms for quad-double precision floating point arithmetic", *15th IEEE Symposium on Computer Arithmetic* (2001), 155–162, <https://doi.org/10.1109/ARITH.2001.930115>: the QD library's forms, including its accurate division and its square root. M. Joldes, J.-M. Muller and V. Popescu, "Tight and rigorous error bounds for basic building blocks of double-word arithmetic", *ACM Transactions on Mathematical Software* 44(2) (2017), <https://doi.org/10.1145/3121432>: the algorithm names, and the tighter bounds in the table as the authors state them in their JNCF 2017 slides, <https://jncf2017.lip6.fr/files/slides/popescu.pdf>, slide 17 (read 2026-10-21), with the `AccurateDWPlusDW` bound as 3u²/(1 − 4u) in J.-M. Muller's NAC 2024 talk, <https://webusers.imj-prg.fr/~jean-claude.bajard/NAC2024/Supports/NAC2024_JMM.pdf> (read 2026-10-21). That talk also reports the Coq formalisation of these proofs by Muller and Rideau, *ACM TOMS* 48(1) (2022), <https://doi.org/10.1145/3484514>, which found and repaired flaws in some published proofs; the kernel therefore relies only on the bounds proven here.

modules.cost: constructing, copying and comparing an error is constant time; `Display` writes one short sentence and allocates nothing.
guarantees: **Plain values.** Every error is `Copy`, compares with `==` and holds only enums and integers, so it can be returned from `no_std` code, matched exhaustively and compared in tests.

**Says what went wrong.** `Display` writes one fixed sentence per variant, with the offending coordinate for `FrameRangeExceeded` and the numbers layer's own sentence for `Num`. (The numbers layer's sentence for `BudgetExceeded` names `geom-num`; reported by this crate, the defect is in `geom-math`.)
modules.job: Errors from this crate that the numbers layer has no word for.

method.text: the kernel's error model, chapter 22 of the architecture: each variant says what was wrong in plain words and carries the value that caused it (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/22-errors-queries-ai.md`).

modules.cost: no allocation. [`pow2`], [`exponent`], [`dyadic`] and [`scale_b`] are a few bit operations and at most two floating-point multiplications. [`pow2_big`], [`shl_into`] and [`round_scaled`] are linear in the number of 64-bit limbs (20 for [`Big`], at most 40 anywhere in the crate). [`sign_minus_sqrt`] is three schoolbook multiplications of L-limb integers (at most L² limb products each) and one subtraction. [`rational_to_f64`] is one 128-bit division and at most 181 shift-and-subtract steps. [`gcd_u128`] takes at most 257 remainder steps (the remainder at least halves every two steps). [`divrem_u128`] takes exactly 64·L shift-and-subtract steps.
guarantees: **Exact, or it says so.** Every integer result is exact, and one that does not fit its type is `None`, never a wrapped value. Every rounded result is rounded once, to nearest, ties to even: [`round_scaled`] and [`rational_to_f64`] also say whether they were exact, and [`scale_b`], like IEEE 754's scaleB, returns ±∞ when the exact result overflows.

**The same result in every build profile.** Every integer addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a variable and negation is a checked method that returns `None` instead of wrapping, or `abs_diff`, which is exact for every input; the only native integer operations are shifts by amounts below the width and division and remainder by the constant 64, none of which can overflow. So nothing depends on overflow checks being on. A `None` that the bounds written here rule out is passed on, and the caller reports it as [`NumError::BudgetExceeded`](geom_num::NumError), never as an answer.

**No panics.** Every shift amount is below the width it shifts (each says why), every limb access is checked, and every loop has a fixed or proven bound (below). The only casts are of values whose bound is written beside them.
modules.job: Exact helpers shared by the crate: doubles as exact dyadic numbers, exact scaling of doubles by powers of two, wide integers built from shifted products, exact rounding of a wide integer divided by a power of two, the exact sign of a − b·√n, the correctly rounded double nearest a quotient of integers, and long division of a wide integer by a 128-bit one.

method.text: A double is exactly m·2^k with integer m (IEEE 754-2019, section 3.3); scaling by a power of two is IEEE's scaleB (section 5.3.3), rounded once. The quotient of two integers is rounded to the nearest double, ties to even (roundTiesToEven, section 4.3.1), by binary long division that produces the 53 bits of the significand, one more bit, and a sticky bit for whether anything nonzero remains (D. E. Knuth, *The Art of Computer Programming*, vol. 2, section 4.3.1); IEEE 754-2019, <https://doi.org/10.1109/IEEESTD.2019.8766229>. The sign of a − b·√n is decided by comparing a² with b²·n when a and b have the same sign: exact geometric computation with algebraic numbers of degree two, evaluated in exact integers instead of rounded square roots (C. K. Yap, "Towards exact geometric computation", *Computational Geometry* 7 (1997), 3–23, <https://doi.org/10.1016/0925-7721(95)00040-2>). Greatest common divisors by Euclid's algorithm, and long division of a wide integer one bit at a time (Knuth, *The Art of Computer Programming*, vol. 2, sections 4.5.2 and 4.3.1, <https://www-cs-faculty.stanford.edu/~knuth/taocp.html>).

modules.cost: constant time, no loops beyond the two or three components, no allocation. Arithmetic, dot and cross products are at most nine IEEE operations plus a finiteness check per result; `length` and `normalized` add a pass over the components for the largest, one exact power-of-two scaling per component (`scale_b`), the squared sum and one correctly rounded square root, then one more scaling (`length`) or one division per component (`normalized`).
guarantees: **Finite.** Every component is finite: made only by constructors that check, and by operations that check their results and return [`NumError::NotFinite`] when a result would overflow. No value here is ever NaN or infinite (chapter 21: NaN's bits are not deterministic).

**Deterministic.** Only IEEE 754 addition, subtraction, multiplication and division, each correctly rounded to nearest on every target, evaluated in the fixed order written in each function. Rust never contracts `a * b + c` into a fused multiply-add on its own, and nothing here asks for one. Square roots come from [`geom_num::math::sqrt`], correctly rounded. No `f64::max`, `f64::min` or platform maths.
**Exact conversions from the grid.** A grid point or grid vector has components below 2^42 in magnitude, so it converts to `f64` with no rounding.

**Lengths without spurious overflow or underflow.** `length` and `normalized` first scale the vector by the power of two that brings its largest component into [1, 2) (exact, except that a component more than 2^1022 times smaller than the largest may round, which changes nothing visible), so the squares neither overflow nor underflow. Where the plain formula would not overflow or underflow, the result has the same bits as the plain formula, because scaling by a power of two commutes with every rounding in the normal range. With u = 2^−53, the squared length has a relative error below 2u + u² for [`F2`] (two squares, one sum) and 3u + 3u² for [`F3`]; the square root halves it and adds its own rounding, so the length is within a relative 2.01u ([`F2`]) or 2.51u ([`F3`]) of the exact length, plus 2^−1070 relative for components that round when scaled. Only the zero vector cannot be normalized.

**Defects reported, never answered.** The one integer step of the scaling (an exponent's negation) is checked, and the maths functions' errors are passed on. None of them can occur for finite components; one that did would be [`NumError::BudgetExceeded`] or the maths function's own error, never a guessed length.
modules.job: Floating-point points and vectors, finite by construction, with deterministic arithmetic.

method.text: IEEE 754-2019 binary64 basic operations, round to nearest, ties to even, and its scaleB (<https://doi.org/10.1109/IEEESTD.2019.8766229>), under Rust's floating-point semantics, which guarantee those results on every supported target and forbid implicit contraction (Rust RFC 3514, <https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3514-float-semantics.html>); the scaling before squaring is the classic remedy for overflow and underflow in Euclidean norms (J. L. Blue, "A portable Fortran program to find the Euclidean norm of a vector", *ACM Transactions on Mathematical Software* 4(1) (1978), 15–23, <https://doi.org/10.1145/355769.355771>), here with an exact power-of-two scale.

modules.cost: no allocation, and constant time for every operation except [`FrameRecord::home_of`], which is linear in the number of operands.
guarantees: Map to frame rounds once, to the nearest step, ties to even, and says whether it was exact, for every frame; coordinates beyond ±(2^40 − 1) steps are refused with [`NumError::OutOfRange`].
Frame to map gives the nearest doubles to the exact map coordinates, ties to even, with whether they are exact, for every frame.
Frames are never mixed without an exact shift: anything else is refused with [`FrameMismatch`].
No conversion returns a value it could not certify, and no exact sign that fails is replaced by a guess: a defect is reported as [`NumError::BudgetExceeded`].
modules.job: Frames: the record that ties a model's flat grid to a map projection, conversion between map coordinates and the grid, exact shifts between frames on a shared lattice, and the regional lattice of frames for long networks.

method.text: the frame record and conversion rules of chapter 17.1 (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/17-survey-terrain-civil.md`), with EPSG:2193 as given in PROJ's copy of the EPSG data (<https://github.com/OSGeo/PROJ/blob/5fa31c29f0a806568ed7bc76c1a557604db4a804/data/sql/projected_crs.sql#L375>); double-double arithmetic as in [`crate::dd`]; the exact settling as the filter-then-exact pattern of the kernel's predicates (chapter 6.2; J. R. Shewchuk, *Discrete & Computational Geometry* 18 (1997), <https://doi.org/10.1007/PL00009321>), with exact values of doubles read as dyadic rationals (IEEE 754-2019, <https://doi.org/10.1109/IEEESTD.2019.8766229>) and numbers a + b√n compared exactly by their squares (C. K. Yap, *Computational Geometry* 7 (1997), <https://doi.org/10.1016/0925-7721(95)00040-2>).

provenance.name: PROJ (its copy of the EPSG dataset, whose own terms of use cover the data)
provenance.purpose: for the defining parameters of EPSG:2193, NZTM2000. No code copied.

modules.cost: constant time, no allocation. Applying is, per axis, one pick, an optional negation, one addition and one range check; composing and inverting rebuild three rows (composing checks three translations); the determinant counts at most three inversions and three negations.
guarantees: **Exact.** Applying, composing and inverting use integer arithmetic only. Composition and inversion of signed permutations are again signed permutations, so nothing ever rounds.

**Range-checked.** Applying to a point checks that the result stays within the frame's ±(2^40 − 1) steps and returns [`NumError::OutOfRange`] otherwise. Translations are kept within [`TRANSLATION_MAX`] = 2(2^40 − 1) steps per axis, the largest that can map some grid point to another; a composition whose translation would exceed it returns `OutOfRange` too.

**Orientation known exactly.** The determinant is ±1, computed from the permutation's parity and the signs; [`GridTransform::reverses_orientation`] says whether a mirror is involved, which reverses arcs, face normals and winding numbers.

**2D is the plane z = 0, with the same transforms.** The kernel has one family of transforms for 2D and 3D (principle 8). A transform that leaves every z unchanged ([`GridTransform::acts_in_plane`]) maps a 2D frame's plane onto itself, and [`GridTransform::apply_2d`] and [`GridTransform::apply_vector_2d`] give exactly what [`GridTransform::apply`] gives at z = 0; its orientation in the plane is its orientation in 3D. Any other transform is refused for 2D input ([`MathError::NotInPlane`]), never projected. Chapter 14.10's exact 2D transforms are all of this kind: translations in x and y, quarter turns about z, and mirrors about axis-aligned and 45-degree lines ([`GridTransform::mirror_diagonal`]), each composed with a translation for a line off the origin.

**The same result in every build profile.** Every integer step (a negation, a sum) is a checked method, never a native operator, so nothing depends on overflow checks being on. The bit budget below proves each fits; one that did not would be reported as [`NumError::BudgetExceeded`], never answered.
modules.job: Exact transforms of the grid: whole-step translations, quarter turns about the axes, mirrors.

method.text: the hyperoctahedral group B₃ (the symmetry group of the cube) represented as signed permutations, composed by composing the permutations and multiplying the signs, with the inverse given by the transpose, as in A. Björner and F. Brenti, *Combinatorics of Coxeter Groups*, Graduate Texts in Mathematics 231, Springer (2005), section 8.1 (the group `B_n` of signed permutations), <https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-27596-7>; chapter 7 of the architecture names which transforms stay exact (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/07-geometry-types.md`).

modules.cost: constant time, no allocation. [`RationalTransform::apply`] is nine `i128` products and three Euclidean divisions. [`RationalTransform::compose`] is 40 `i128` products and a reduction. [`RationalTransform::inverse`] is 36 `i128` products (determinant, adjugate and scaling), nine 256-bit products, twelve greatest common divisors and six long divisions of a 256-bit integer by their result (256 shift-and-subtract steps each), and a reduction. [`RationalTransform::classify`] is at most 28 `i128` products. A reduction folds 13 values into their greatest common divisor, then divides each by it. Every greatest common divisor is Euclid's algorithm on `u128`, at most 257 remainder steps.
guarantees: a [`RationalTransform`] is exact. Its image of a grid point is computed in exact integer arithmetic and rounded once, half to even, with whether it was already on the grid; it composes and inverts exactly; its classification is decided exactly, with no tolerance; equal transforms have equal fields; and a step its budget proves fits that fails all the same is reported as [`NumError::BudgetExceeded`], never answered.
modules.job: Rational affine transforms: `p ↦ (M·p + t)/d` with an integer matrix M, an integer vector t and a positive integer d.

method.text: exact rational arithmetic on a common denominator, reduced by Euclid's algorithm (D. E. Knuth, *The Art of Computer Programming*, vol. 2, section 4.5.2, <https://www-cs-faculty.stanford.edu/~knuth/taocp.html>), the inverse by the adjugate (Cramer's rule), and the classification by the Gram matrix as in [`crate::transform`] (R. Hartley and A. Zisserman, *Multiple View Geometry in Computer Vision*, 2nd ed. (2004), section 2.4, <https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511811685>), here exactly.

modules.cost: constant time, no allocation. Applying is ten `i128` products for M(q) and nine for the image, and three Euclidean divisions; composing is sixteen products and a reduction (four greatest common divisors); a 2D search is about twenty interval operations, at most 200 steps of the simplest-rational loop and one certificate (about 60 interval operations); a 3D search is at most 36 roundings and certificates.

modules.cost: constant time, no allocation. [`Transform::apply_point`] is 18 IEEE operations and [`Transform::compose`] 63. [`Transform::classify`] is fewer than 100 interval operations (the determinant enclosure, then one or two Gram matrices and their row sums), each a few IEEE operations with a one-step widening. [`Transform::inverse`] is a classification, 60 IEEE operations and 18 power-of-two scalings. [`Transform::apply_grid`] decides each coordinate by the cheapest stage that can: about twenty IEEE operations in plain doubles; if those cannot decide, three exact products and three double-double additions; only then the exact sum of four shifted terms in an integer of 128 bits up to 2176 bits (34 limbs, chosen by how far apart the exponents are) and one exact rounding, each linear in the limbs. A coordinate outside the frame always takes that exact stage, which finds the rounded coordinate its error reports.
guarantees: **Finite.** Every entry is finite; operations whose results would overflow return [`NumError::NotFinite`]. Zero entries are stored as +0, so equal transforms have equal bits.
**Deterministic.** Each entry of a product is evaluated as `(a₀b₀ + a₁b₁) + a₂b₂`, in that order, with IEEE 754 operations only; no fused multiply-add, no platform maths.

**Never a wrong orientation.** [`Classification::mirror`] comes from a certified determinant sign. When the sign is not certain the transform is `Degenerate`, and [`Transform::inverse`] refuses it with [`MathError::Singular`].

**Grid points round once.** [`Transform::apply_grid`] gives the exact image of a grid point under the exact entries, rounded to the nearest grid point, ties to even, with whether it was already on the grid. An image outside the frame is refused with its exact rounded coordinate (saturated at the ends of `i128`, as [`NumError::OutOfRange`] documents), never an estimate.

**Defects reported, never answered.** The integer steps (the exponents of the row scalings and of the exact rounding) are checked methods, and the maths functions' errors are passed on. For finite entries none can fail; one that did is reported as [`NumError::BudgetExceeded`] (or the maths function's own error), never turned into a classification or a coordinate. Where a stage of [`Transform::apply_grid`] can decline (the two filters), such a failure only makes it decline, and the exact stage decides.

guarantees: **Exact.** Integer arithmetic only. A dot or cross product is the exact integer, never a rounded one; its sign is an exact predicate.

**No overflow, no panic, the same result in every build profile.** Every integer step is a checked method (`checked_add`, `checked_sub`, `checked_mul`, `checked_neg`), never a native operator, so nothing depends on overflow checks being on. Products are proved to fit `i128` (|v| < 2^127) with room to spare, and a step the bit budget proves fits can only fail through a defect in this crate: it is then reported as [`NumError::BudgetExceeded`], never answered, so a defect can never pass for an exact result. For grid vectors every such result is `Ok`. Sums and differences of vectors, which can leave the vector range, return [`NumError::OutOfRange`].
**Deterministic.** The same integers on every target.

errors.name: RngError

invariants: Every grid coordinate is a whole number of grid steps with magnitude at most [`grid::COORD_MAX`] (2^40 − 1). Every exact predicate's bit budget assumes this, and its module carries the written derivation (for the explicit-point predicates, in [`predicate`]'s header), whose arithmetic is asserted when the crate compiles.

Every predicate returns a [`sign::Sign`], never a number, and is exact: no rounding decides a sign. A computation that cannot complete is reported as [`NumError::BudgetExceeded`], never answered; no input can cause one, only a defect in this crate.
A [`plane::Plane`] and a [`plane::Tpi`] check their bit budgets when they are made, so every computation on them fits its type.

Committing a three-plane point to the grid ([`plane::Tpi::to_grid`]) rounds each coordinate to the nearest step, ties to even, moving it by at most half a step ([`ladder::COMMIT_PER_AXIS`]), and says whether it moved.

Integer arithmetic on fixed-width values in kernel code is a checked method (`checked_*`, or in [`wide`] and [`wide32`] the `overflowing_*` limb steps, whose carry or borrow is kept), so nothing depends on overflow checks being on: a result that does not fit is `None` or an error, never a silently wrapped value. Three kinds of step compute modulo a power of two on purpose, and each cites what defines it so. In [`rng`], Philox's multiplications and key schedule, modulo 2^32 (its 32 × 32-bit product is formed modulo 2^64, as its reference does, and never reaches 2^64), and Lemire's threshold, a negation modulo 2^64. In the large accumulator inside [`exact_sum::ExactSum::add_slice`] and [`exact_sum::ExactSum::add_iter`], the sum of a double's whole bit pattern modulo 2^64, as Neal's method specifies, from which the exact sum of the significands is recovered. In those two a `wrapping_*` method is the specified operation, not a result that failed to fit. And in the CORE-MATH ports of [`math`], a `wrapping_*` method where the C source computes modulo 2^64 or 2^128 on purpose, each with a comment saying why the C does it (a two's complement negation, a sum of which only the low bits are read, or a limb sum whose carry is kept by comparison as [`wide`] keeps its own), so a wrap there is the computation the proof describes, never a lost value. Every other integer step in the ports is checked too: its `None`, which each step proves cannot come, ends the computation with the canonical NaN, which the public functions report as `NotFinite`. Only the compiler's evaluation of constants uses native operators, where an overflow stops the build. Counts of steps never saturate: a saturated bound would understate the truth.

No floating-point value produced here from finite inputs is NaN. [`math`] returns a [`real::Real`] or an error; an [`interval::Interval`] has finite bounds or is refused as `NotFinite`; [`eft`] reports a pair that is not exact with an infinite second part; a [`dd::DD`] is finite by construction; [`exact_sum::ExactSum`] gives a `Real` or `NotFinite`; [`rng`] draws its doubles as `Real`s in [0, 1); [`brent`]'s searches and [`quadrature`]'s integrals return `Real`s, and stop at a caller's cap with an error, never a best guess. Inside [`math`], where the ports compute on raw doubles, any NaN is the canonical `0x7ff8_0000_0000_0000`, and no public function returns one.

Every interval operation encloses the exact result of its operation on any reals in its operands, and an enclosure that needs a maths function without a proven error is refused ([`NumError::UnprovenMaths`]).
A bound carries its grid step, and bounds add exactly in the finer step ([`exactness::Exactness`]).

Every double-double operation ([`dd::DD`]) is within its stated error bound of the exact result: the published, machine-checked bound of its algorithm (the theorem is named on each operation), plus, from the range of binary64, 2^−398 relative for products, quotients and roots and 2^−1074 absolute for products and quotients. A `DD` is never NaN or infinite: an overflow is [`NumError::NotFinite`].

A sum of doubles taken with [`exact_sum::ExactSum`] is exact until it is rounded once, to nearest with ties to even, so its bits depend only on the terms, never on their order, on how they were split into chunks, or on the order of merges.

No `unsafe`, no panics outside tests, no platform maths: every maths function comes from [`math`]. `sinpi`, `cospi`, `exp`, `ln` and `atan2` are correctly rounded CORE-MATH ports with proven error bounds, so their bits are fixed by their specification. Everything else comes from the pure-Rust `libm` crate, the same code on every target; where `libm` uses a processor instruction instead (the square root, and the fused multiply-add where the processor has one), it is one IEEE 754 defines exactly, so results are identical on every target. The `libm` functions without a proven bound are kept apart in [`math::unproven`], and nothing in this crate uses them.
crates.job: numbers: where coordinates live, how "which side is this on" is answered exactly, how curved computations carry proven bounds, where maths functions come from, where a randomised method's random numbers come from (a counter-based generator keyed by explicit seeds), and the tolerance ladder.

modules.cost: each step is a few dozen floating-point operations and one evaluation of `f`; the number of steps is at most about (log₂((b − a)/δ))² for [`zero`] and of the order of log((b − a)/δ)/log(1/0.618) golden-section steps for [`minimum`] (δ the tolerance), and in any case at most `cap`. No allocation, no recursion.
modules.does: [`zero`] narrows a bracket `[a, b]` across which `f` changes sign, by bisection, the secant step and inverse quadratic interpolation, taking an interpolated step only while it stays well inside the bracket and keeps shrinking it fast enough, so it converges as surely as bisection and usually much faster. [`minimum`] narrows an interval holding a minimum of `f` by golden-section steps and successive parabolic interpolation, under the same safeguards. Chapter 12.4 asks for exactly this in one unknown ("bracketing in the manner of Brent (1973)"); a caller that has a derivative takes a Newton step only inside the bracket this returns.
guarantees: **The bracket is kept.** [`zero`] returns `x` with `f(x) = 0` exactly, or `x` and `other` with `f(x)` and `f(other)` of opposite signs and |x − other| at most 4u|x| + `tol` (u = 2^−53): a sign change of `f` as computed lies between them, whatever the rounding inside `f`.

**The interval is kept.** [`minimum`] evaluates `f` only inside `(a, b)`, never closer than its tolerance to either end, and returns the point with the least value it evaluated; on a function unimodal on `[a, b]` that point is within 2(√u|x| + `tol`/3) of the minimum.

**A cap, never a guess.** Each call evaluates `f` at most `cap` times; reaching the cap is [`BrentError::CapReached`], never the best point so far. A function error is returned as it is ([`BrentError::Num`]).

**Never NaN, deterministic.** Every value is a finite [`Real`]; the steps use only IEEE 754 basic operations in a fixed order, so every target computes the same points. An interpolation whose arithmetic would overflow is replaced by the bisection or golden-section step, as an unacceptable interpolation is.
modules.job: Brent's methods for one unknown: a zero of a function in a bracket, and a minimum of a function on an interval, with function values only.

method.text: R. P. Brent, *Algorithms for Minimization without Derivatives*, Prentice-Hall (1973), chapter 4 (procedure `zero`) and chapter 5 (procedure `localmin`), <https://maths-people.anu.edu.au/~brent/pub/pub011.html>, written in our own words from the algorithms as G. E. Forsythe, M. A. Malcolm and C. B. Moler give them in *Computer Methods for Mathematical Computations*, Prentice-Hall (1977), routines `zeroin` and `fmin`. Netlib's copies of those two routines carry no licence file, so they were read only as a description of the method, as chapter 29.4's "Brent 1973" row allows for such sources, for the order of Brent's tests and his stopping rules; no code was taken.

modules.cost: constant time and no allocation: a few `i128` products for the weight and the numerators, two products in [`I256`] for a side, and one restoring long division per coordinate to commit, as in [`crate::plane`].
guarantees: Every result is exact, or an error. A [`Sign`] is decided by integer arithmetic alone, never by a rounded crossing point, so an arrangement built on these answers is consistent.

Nothing overflows silently. Every step is a checked operation in `i128` or a fixed-width [`Wide`] integer, and a step that did not fit would be reported as [`NumError::BudgetExceeded`], never answered; for grid points no step can fail (the budgets on [`Ssi::homogeneous`] and [`Ssi::orient2d`]).
Deterministic: integers only, except the generated `f64` filters, whose answers are proven to be the exact sign or no answer (chapter 6.2); no platform maths and no allocation.

**Bounded proofs, and what is only tested** (chapter 28.7; piece G41 collects them here). Verus proves that the generated exact paths of `ssi_weight` and `ssi_side`, which every answer here rests on, compute their values exactly and never overflow for every input in their declared ranges (piece G39: the twins in `verus/generated/`, token for token the shipped modules), on [`Wide`] arithmetic that is itself proven exact (G37). The routing between filter and exact path, the homogeneous coordinates' budgets and the rounding to the grid are tested against exact oracles, not proven (`tests/attack_g29.rs`, `tests/verification.rs` and this module's tests), and the filters' error bounds are checked against exact arithmetic until G40 certifies them.
modules.job: Where two lines cross in the plane, exact: the implicit point where the line through two grid points crosses the line through two others, which side of a third line it lies on, and committing it to the grid.

method.text: the crossing point of two lines in homogeneous integer coordinates, classified against a line by multiplying by the sign of the weight so that nothing is divided, the plane-based method of [`crate::plane`] in two dimensions (Campen and Kobbelt 2010, <https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8659.2009.01609.x>; Attene 2020's indirect predicates, <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cad.2020.102856>, method only, re-derived here). Each sign goes through its generated filter first and its generated exact path when the filter cannot decide (`ssi_weight` and `ssi_side`, chapter 6.2), then through the hand-written path.

modules.cost: constant time, no allocation, and no loops other than at most three power-of-two steps per scaling. Counting `two_sum` as 6 floating-point operations, a fused multiply-add as one call to [`crate::math::fma`] (one instruction where the processor has one, through `libm`'s runtime dispatch on x86-64; a correctly rounded integer routine on WebAssembly), and the final `two_sum` that restores the invariant: [`DD::add`] is 26 operations and [`DD::add_f64`] 13; [`DD::mul_f64`] 2 fused multiply-adds and 13 operations, [`DD::mul`] 3 and 15, [`DD::div_f64`] 1 and 18, [`DD::div`] 6 and 44, [`DD::sqrt`] one square root, one fused multiply-add and 15. The multiplicative ones add the scaling: for each operand a read of its exponent bits and two power-of-two scalings (one to three multiplications each), and two scalings of the result; [`DD::mul`] also compares its two scaled operands to order them.
guarantees: with u = 2^−53 (the unit roundoff of binary64), each operation returns the exact result of the operation on the exact values of its operands, `r`, within `|result − r| ≤ B·|r| + A`:
modules.job: Double-double arithmetic: a real number held as the unevaluated sum of two doubles, with a proven error bound on every operation.

method.text: the algorithms are those whose bounds are proven and machine-checked (Joldes, Muller and Popescu 2017, <https://doi.org/10.1145/3121432>, and the other references below): addition, `AccurateDWPlusDW` (JMP Algorithm 6, the QD library's "IEEE addition" of Li et al.) and `DWPlusFP` (JMP Algorithm 4, QD's); multiplication by a double, `DWTimesFP3` (JMP Algorithm 9), and of two `DD`s, `DWTimesDW3` (JMP Algorithm 12), the ones JMP recommend when a fused multiply-add is available; division by a double, `DWDivFP3` (JMP Algorithm 15), and of two `DD`s, `DWDivDW3` (JMP Algorithm 18, the more accurate of their two divisions); the square root, `SQRTDWtoDW` (LLMPR Algorithm 8); `TwoProduct` as Kahan's `Fast2Mult` with a fused multiply-add ([`two_prod_fma`], JMP Algorithm 3), and `TwoSum` as Knuth's ([`crate::eft::two_sum`]).

modules.cost: constant time and no allocation. Each function is a fixed sequence of floating-point operations, comparisons and bit reads; outside Dekker's direct range `split` also scales by 2^64 and back, and `two_prod` scales by powers of two (`scale`), each scaling at most two steps.
guarantees: **Exact or reported, never silently wrong.** For finite inputs the pair is exact whenever an exact pair exists, and then both parts are finite. When none exists, the second part is an infinity with the sign of the exact error, so one check, `e.is_finite()`, tells a caller whether the pair is exact. No exact pair exists only when the rounded sum or product overflows, when the high half of a split would be ±2^1024, or when the exact error of a product is finer than the smallest subnormal 2^−1074 (possible only for |a · b| < 2^−969). The tests check every case against exact rationals (`num-rational`) on random and adversarial inputs.

**Never NaN from finite inputs.** The second part is NaN only when the first part is NaN: a NaN input, or an IEEE operation on infinities that is itself NaN (∞ − ∞, 0 · ∞). Any other non-finite input gives an infinite second part. So the crate's "never NaN" invariant (`lib.rs`) holds here for every finite input; for infinite inputs it holds except where IEEE 754 itself makes the rounded sum or product NaN.

**The rounded part is the IEEE 754 result.** `s` is `a + b` and `p` is `a * b` as Rust computes them (round to nearest, ties to even). An exact error is at most half a unit in the last place of that result, so the pair does not overlap: `s + e` rounds back to `s`.

**One zero.** A second part that is zero is +0, never −0: the exact error of a sum or a product, and the low half of a split, whatever the signs of the inputs and however Veltkamp's split falls. So the second part depends on the exact pair alone, as an exact zero does in IEEE arithmetic (a zero sum of operands of opposite signs is +0 under round to nearest, IEEE 754-2019, section 6.3) and as it does for a two-product by fused multiply-add. Hence [`fast_two_sum`] and [`two_sum`] agree bit for bit (a NaN aside, whose bits Rust does not fix), and `two_prod(−a, b)` is `(−p, −e)` for a nonzero `e` and `(−p, +0)` for a zero one. Where the last step of an algorithm can give −0, the function adds +0, which turns −0 into +0 and leaves every other value as it is (the proof is on the crate's one helper for it, `zero_to_plus` in `real.rs`, which [`crate::interval`] uses too); each function's documentation shows where that is needed and why it is needed nowhere else.

**Deterministic.** Only `+`, `−`, `×` and `÷` on `f64` (`÷` only by a power of two), comparisons, and reads and writes of a double's bits. Rust computes these to IEEE 754 binary64, each rounded once, on every target the kernel builds for (RFC 3514). The RFC names the exception itself: on 32-bit x86 without SSE2 (the i586 targets) the x87 unit computes with a different precision and so can round twice, which would break these algorithms; the kernel does not support those targets. The RFC also rules out fusing `a * b + c` into one fused multiply-add, which would break them too, and none is used on purpose either: `two_prod` follows Dekker's splitting instead of `mul_add`, which `core` lacks and which is a slow software call on wasm32 (evidence note 05, section 1).

**No integer overflow.** The only integer steps that run are on the 11-bit exponent fields: bit masks, shifts by 52 places that keep the field inside 64 bits, `abs_diff`, which is exact for every input, and `checked_sub`, whose `None` ends a loop. There is no other integer arithmetic at run time (the compiler alone evaluates the checks on the constants, where an overflow would stop the build) and no cast, so nothing here depends on overflow checks being on.

**Bounded proofs, and what is only tested.** Kani proves (piece G41, chapter 28.7) that `split` adds back exactly or reports, for every finite double; that `two_sum` and `fast_two_sum` agree and give the rounded sum and its error for every finite operand against five others, in either order (against the largest double, for operands below 2^969, where no step overflows; the overflow fallback is only tested, because its NaN intermediate trips Kani's NaN check; over every pair of operands at once the solver ran past CI's hour); and that `two_prod` gives the rounded product and its error for every finite first factor against 3, the splitter, 2^996 and the smallest subnormal, and for every first factor whose significand has at most 14 bits (every sign and exponent) against −0.1 and the largest double: one factor for each of its paths. The proofs module has one harness per value, with kissat as the SAT solver; the `two_prod` harnesses unwind `scale`'s loop at most three times (its callers pass at most 1074, so it steps at most twice), and Kani checks that bound is enough. In WSL (2026-10-28, sharing the machine) the full-width harnesses took 4 to 54 minutes and the 14-bit ones up to 26; with all 53 bits free, −0.1 and the largest double ran past four hours. Every other pair, and everything through the fused multiply-add, is tested against exact rationals.
modules.job: Error-free transformations: a rounded sum or product of two doubles and its exact error.

method.text: Dekker 1971 (`fast_two_sum`, Veltkamp's `split`, `two_prod`) and Knuth (`two_sum`), in the form and with the proofs of Shewchuk 1997: Theorem 6 (fast two-sum), Theorem 7 (two-sum), Theorem 17 (split) and Theorem 18 (two-product). Shewchuk's proofs assume an unbounded exponent (his section 2.1 leaves overflow and underflow aside); each function below derives the conditions under which they hold in binary64 and says what it does outside them. `fast_two_sum` puts its operands in the order Dekker's method needs. `two_sum` runs Knuth's six operations and, in the one case where an intermediate overflows, returns `fast_two_sum`'s pair instead. `split` and `two_prod` run Veltkamp's and Dekker's operations unchanged where the conditions hold, and otherwise first move their inputs into that range by exact powers of two, then check that the way back is exact. T. J. Dekker, "A floating-point technique for extending the available precision", *Numerische Mathematik* 18 (1971), 224–242, <https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01397083>. J. R. Shewchuk, "Adaptive precision floating-point arithmetic and fast robust geometric predicates", *Discrete & Computational Geometry* 18 (1997), 305–363, <https://doi.org/10.1007/PL00009321>. D. E. Knuth, *The Art of Computer Programming*, volume 2, section 4.2.2. S. Boldo, "Pitfalls of a full floating-point proof: example on the formal proof of the Veltkamp/Dekker algorithms", *Automated Reasoning* (IJCAR 2006), Lecture Notes in Computer Science 4130: Veltkamp's high half is the input rounded to nearest. IEEE 754-2019, *IEEE Standard for Floating-Point Arithmetic*, section 6.3 (the sign of an exact zero), <https://doi.org/10.1109/IEEESTD.2019.8766229>. RFC 3514, "Float semantics": <https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3514-float-semantics.html>.

modules.cost: [`ExactSum::add`]: about twenty integer operations, two of them checked additions into chunks, plus a propagation (about 67 steps) every 2047 terms. [`ExactSum::add_slice`] from [`LARGE_SLICE`] terms up: about eight per term (a shift, two loads, a checked decrement, the unmasked addition and two stores), plus zeroing 41 KB once per call, one transfer (about twenty steps) per 4096 terms with the same sign and exponent, and a final transfer of each chunk used. [`ExactSum::add_iter`]: the same per term, after at most [`LARGE_SLICE`] terms one by one when the stream's length is not known. Neal measures exact summation of large arrays this way in under twice the time of plain ordered summation; `tests/exact_sum_bench.rs` holds `add_slice` and `add_iter` to that on 10^6 terms, including the inputs hardest for the large accumulator (a few chunks hit in random order). Measured there in release on an Intel i7-10750H with the machine otherwise quiet (2026-10-22), against a plain ordered sum of the same terms: `add_slice` and `add_iter` 0.9 to 1.4 times on uniform, spread, coordinate and one-binade terms, 1.7 times on the hardest case (subnormals of random signs); [`ExactSum::add`] one term at a time 3 to 6 times. So the board's bar is met by the large accumulator's paths, which kernel code with many terms uses; [`ExactSum::add`] is for a few terms at a time. (Under load from other processes the large accumulator's loop, bound by loads and stores, slows more than the plain sum, bound by the latency of one addition, so the ratio is only meaningful on a quiet machine.) [`ExactSum::merge`]: two propagations and 67 checked additions. [`ExactSum::round`]: a copy of the 67 chunks, at most two propagations and a scan.
guarantees: **Exact, then correctly rounded.** [`ExactSum::round`] returns the exact sum of every finite term added (directly, by [`ExactSum::add_slice`] or [`ExactSum::add_iter`], or through merges) rounded to the nearest double, ties to even, as a [`Real`]. An exact zero is +0, whatever the signs of the zero terms (as in Neal's code). The tests hold it bit for bit to an exact oracle (`dashu`).

**Order-free.** The result depends on the multiset of terms only: not on their order, on how they were split into slices or accumulators, on the order or shape of the merges, or on which of the two internal paths (below) took them. The state's value is the exact sum, the special flags are an OR and a maximum, and the rounding is a function of the value.

**Special values as Neal specifies.** A NaN or an infinity among the terms does not disturb the finite sum; [`ExactSum::round_ieee`] then returns, in this order of precedence: a NaN, the one with the largest payload (its 52 fraction bits read as an integer) with its sign cleared, if any term was a NaN; a NaN if both +∞ and −∞ were added; the infinity if only one sign was; otherwise the rounded finite sum, which is ±∞ when its magnitude is at least 2^1024 − 2^970 (an overflow, possible even when every term is finite). [`ExactSum::round`] reports all of these as [`NumError::NotFinite`], so the kernel never sees a NaN or an infinity from it.

**No silent overflow.** Integer arithmetic is checked, except the one addition Neal's method defines modulo 2^64 (the large accumulator's chunks, below), where wrapping is the specification. The accumulator holds magnitudes below 2^1100, so it cannot overflow before 2^64 terms have been added (a term at most Ω < 2^1024, counted once for every accumulator it reaches through merges); should an internal step ever fail, the sum is marked lost and [`ExactSum::round_ieee`] gives Neal's report for it, a NaN with every payload bit set.

**Bounded proofs, and what is only tested.** Kani proves (piece G41, chapter 28.7) that adding one term never panics, that a finite term rounds back to itself and a non-finite one is reported, and that a finite term and its negation cancel to +0, for every sign and every fraction at the exponent fields 0, 1, 31, 32, 1023 and 2046 (and 2047, the non-finite terms): the subnormals, the smallest binade, the two binades either side of the first chunk boundary, one's binade and the largest, one harness per field with kissat as the SAT solver. Each unwinds every loop at most 68 times (the 67 chunks, and one more for the loop's exit), and Kani checks that bound is enough; without it the slices whose length depends on the term unwind without end. Every other exponent field, and every sum of more than one term, is tested bit for bit against the exact oracle.
modules.job: `ExactSum`: the exact sum of any number of doubles, rounded once, to nearest, at the end.

method.text: R. M. Neal, "Fast exact summation using small and large superaccumulators", arXiv 1505.05571 (2015), <https://arxiv.org/abs/1505.05571>, and his C code `xsum` (MIT licence, copyright 2015–2024 Radford M. Neal), <https://github.com/radfordneal/xsum>, read at commit `b766b3e104cdbd6769c8df033fb430700fce32dd` (2024-11-13, `stable-version-3`). Both of Neal's superaccumulators are used, rebuilt to this crate's rules: **The small superaccumulator**, the value an [`ExactSum`] holds: 67 signed 64-bit chunks, chunk i weighing 2^(32i − 1075), so consecutive chunks overlap by 32 bits and carries can wait. A double with exponent field E (1 for subnormals) and 53-bit significand M (52 bits for subnormals) is `M·2^(E − 1075)`; with `E = 32j + k`, it adds or subtracts `M·2^k mod 2^32` to chunk j and `⌊M·2^k / 2^32⌋ < 2^52` to chunk j + 1. A carry propagation (each chunk keeps its low 32 bits, the rest goes to the next) puts every chunk but the top one in [0, 2^32); 2047 additions can follow before the next, since 2^32 + 2047·2^52 < 2^63. Neal, section 3. **The large superaccumulator**, used by [`ExactSum::add_slice`] for long slices and by [`ExactSum::add_iter`] (with [`Extend`] and [`FromIterator`]) for long streams: 4096 unsigned 64-bit chunks, one for each sign-and-exponent pattern, each with a count. A term is added to its chunk as a whole 64-bit pattern, with no masking; after n additions the chunk holds `n·(index·2^52) + Σ fractions` modulo 2^64, so at most 4096 additions per chunk keep `Σ fractions < 2^64` recoverable exactly: `chunk − n·index·2^52`, modulo 2^64. That chunk is then moved into the small accumulator (fractions plus `n·2^52` implicit bits, as three 32-bit parts), when its count runs out and at the end. Neal, section 4.

modules.cost: constant and no allocation: combining two bounds is two checked refinements (a division, a remainder and a multiplication each) and one checked addition.
guarantees: a bound is a count of grid steps together with its step, because a count alone means nothing: 64 steps of `Q0` are 10 µm, 64 steps of `Q1` are 0.4 µm. Combining two bounds first converts both to the finer of their steps (25 per rung, exactly; chapter 6.1), then adds the counts, so a body certified to 64 steps of `Q0` with one certified to 64 steps of `Q1` is certified to 64 · 25 + 64 = 1,664 steps of `Q1`, never to 128 of anything. Every step of that is checked: a sum that does not fit is `None`, never saturated, because a saturated sum is smaller than the true one and so would no longer be a bound.

**The exact path is exact.** `value` returns the exact value for every input in the domain: the certificate bounds every intermediate within its type, and a step that did not fit would give `None`, never a wrapped value, since every step is a checked method. Nothing depends on overflow checks being on.

**Proven, or checked and labelled so** (chapter 28.6). The bounds are derived exactly by the written proof below and re-derived by an independent checker in geom-gen's tests (its own parser, big integers and analysis), which also reads this committed code, this module's helpers included; the filters are tested against the exact paths on millions of random and near-degenerate inputs at the grid's extremes and on inputs placed just inside and just outside each bound. On top of that, each module's guarantees say whether its filter's bound is machine-checked: proven where Gappa's proofs, checked by Rocq, cover every input (`kernel-certificates.yml`, pieces G35 and G40), and "checked, not proven" with its open issue otherwise.

**Deterministic.** `f64` addition, subtraction and multiplication are correctly rounded on every target and Rust never fuses them (RFC 3514); the conversion of a rounded input rounds to nearest, ties to even, on every target; the maxima use comparisons only. The same inputs give the same answer on every target, and the answer is the exact sign whenever it is given, so the filter can never change a result.

**No overflow, no underflow, no NaN, no panic, no allocation.** Every value the filter computes is a whole number below 2^1000 in magnitude (checked by the generator), so none is subnormal or infinite.

method.text: Meyer and Pion's almost-static filters, which chapter 6.2 calls semi-static (*FPG: A code generator for fast and certified geometric predicates*, Real Numbers and Computers 2008, <https://inria.hal.science/inria-00344297>): a forward error analysis at unit input bounds, with groups of variables and translated inputs, gives a constant that the run-time maxima of the groups scale. The groups here are the axes; Geogram's orient2d groups each row of its determinant instead (`max1` over `a11` and `a12`), equally sound, so its maxima are not the same quantities as these. Geogram's PCK generates its filters with FPG from one description per predicate (Lévy 2016, <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cad.2015.10.004>; BSD-3-Clause, read for method at commit 16843b4804de35f14ef54667950ab4c8acdd0062). Here the analysis is exact (whole polynomials in u, no upward rounding), the translations are exact because grid differences are below 2^53, which halves FPG's orient2d constant, rounded inputs (`f64` copies of wider integers) carry their rounding into the bound (chapter 23.2), and FPG's under- and overflow guards are unnecessary because every value is a whole number far from the ends of the `f64` range. The exact path replaces Geogram's expansion arithmetic with fixed-width integers chosen per step from the certificate (Fortune and Van Wyk 1996, <https://doi.org/10.1145/231731.231735>; chapter 23.3).

method.text: the grid ladder of chapter 6.1 (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/06-numbers.md`): exact scaling by 25 per rung, and coarsening by Euclidean division rounded to the nearest step (R. T. Boute, "The Euclidean definition of the functions div and mod", ACM Transactions on Programming Languages and Systems 14(2), 1992, <https://doi.org/10.1145/128861.128862>), as [`coarsen`] derives.

modules.cost: constant time and no allocation per operation; [`Interval::norm`] is linear in its number of components.
guarantees: **Inclusion**, as above, for `add`, `sub`, `mul`, `div`, `mul_add`, `square`, `sqrt`, `norm` and `neg`. These are built from the operations IEEE 754 rounds correctly, so one step outward is a proven enclosure. The same holds for `sinpi`, `cospi`, `exp` and `ln`, built from the correctly rounded functions of [`crate::math`] in `math/enclose.rs`, which carries their proofs. An enclosure that needs a function whose error is not proven (the radian `sin` and `cos`, which only `libm` supplies) or whose interval version is not built yet (`atan2`) is refused with [`NumError::UnprovenMaths`].

**Finite, ordered, never NaN.** Both bounds are finite and `lo ≤ hi`. An operation whose widened bound would leave the finite doubles (a rounded bound that reaches ±(2 − 2^−52) · 2^1023 or overflows) returns [`NumError::NotFinite`] instead.

**Tight.** Each computed bound is the first or second double beyond the exact bound of the operation over its operands, never farther: the rounding lands on the exact bound or on one of the two doubles either side of it, and the widening moves one double outward. So the lower bound is at least the double below the largest double at or below the exact lower bound, and the upper bound at most the double above the smallest double at or above the exact upper bound. A bound that is exact by construction is not widened, so it is the exact bound itself: both bounds of `neg`, the lower bound 0 of `square` over an interval holding zero, a zero bound of `sqrt`, and the exact values and peaks of `sinpi`, `cospi`, `exp` and `ln` (`math/enclose.rs`). `norm` chains several operations, so each of its steps is tight in this sense but the whole is not. Counted in steps, where the step at a value is the spacing of the doubles in its binade, a computed bound is at most 2.5 steps of the exact bound outside it, at most 2 steps of the computed bound, less than 2 steps of the larger of the two, and at most 1.5 steps when the two steps are equal. The first two maxima are reached at ties next to a power of two, where the spacing halves: 1 + (−2^−54) = 1 − 2^−54 is a tie that rounds to the even 1 and is widened to 1 + 2^−52, which is 2.5 steps of 2^−53 (the spacing just below 1) above the exact value; and 1 + 2^−53 is a tie that also rounds to 1 and is widened to 1 − 2^−53, exactly 2 steps of 2^−53 (the spacing at that bound) below the exact value.

**Deterministic.** Only IEEE 754 basic operations and comparisons, which Rust computes to IEEE 754 binary64 on every target the kernel builds for (RFC 3514, whose own exception, 32-bit x86 without SSE2, is not one of them); `next_up` and `next_down`, which are integer operations on the bits; the correctly rounded `sinpi`, `cospi`, `exp` and `ln` of [`crate::math`], fixed bit for bit by their specification; and the square root and fused multiply-add of [`crate::math`]. The fused multiply-add is `libm` 0.2.16's `fma`, correctly rounded as IEEE 754 requires whether `libm` uses the processor's instruction or its own routine. That root is not Rust's but `libm` 0.2.16's `sqrt`, which is the processor's IEEE 754 square root on x86-64 (`sqrtsd`, with SSE2) and on aarch64 (`fsqrt`, with NEON), and on wasm32 libm's portable integer routine (`src/math/generic/sqrt.rs`: Goldschmidt iterations, then musl's decision of the last bit), because libm uses WebAssembly's square root instruction only with its `unstable-intrinsics` feature, which is off. IEEE 754 requires the square root to be correctly rounded, and the portable routine is written to the same result, so every route gives the same bits. Inclusion for the roots needs only a faithful root; equality across targets needs the correctly rounded one, which on wasm32 rests on libm's routine rather than on hardware, and libm's own comments rest that routine's last bit on testing, not on a proof. So `tests/attack2_interval.rs` holds `math::sqrt` bit for bit to an exact oracle (roots within a tiny fraction of a unit of a midpoint, subnormal operands, exact roots), and CI runs it on wasm32-wasip1 too (`.github/workflows/kernel.yml`). Minimum and maximum are written as comparisons, not with `f64::min` and `f64::max`, which may return either zero when given −0 and +0. A zero bound is always stored as +0, so equal intervals have equal bits whatever their history.
modules.job: Intervals of doubles that certainly contain an exact real result, in round-to-nearest arithmetic.

method.text: interval arithmetic in round-to-nearest with outward widening, as in Geogram's `intervalRN` (after Harris) and in CGAL's widening with `nextafter` when it cannot change the rounding mode. Harris widens each bound by the relative factor 1 ± 2^−52, a second rounded operation; this module moves each bound by exactly one step, which is tighter and needs no further rounding. The square is the interval power of Moore, Kearfott and Cloud, which is IEEE Std 1788-2015's `sqr`: over an interval holding zero x² is smallest at zero, otherwise at the bound nearer zero, and largest at the bound farther from zero. The roots follow IEEE Std 1788-2015's `sqrt`, whose domain is [0, +∞): `sqrt` refuses an operand that reaches outside the domain, and the private root inside `norm` is the standard's set-based evaluation over the part of the operand inside it. The length is the natural interval extension of √(c₁² + … + cₙ²) (Moore, Kearfott and Cloud), built from those operations. The fused multiply-add is the natural extension of x · y + z over the box of operands, with IEEE 754's correctly rounded `fusedMultiplyAdd` (IEEE 754-2019, section 5.4.1) at the corners. R. Harris, "Why interval arithmetic won't cure your floating point blues", *Overload* 19(103), June 2011, <https://accu.org/journals/overload/19/103/harris_1974/>. Geogram `interval_nt.h` (BSD-3-Clause), the round-to-nearest `intervalRN` class: <https://github.com/BrunoLevy/geogram/blob/40d72165ceeeb0a61977d6fdf74d929bfdd77b7b/src/lib/geogram/numerics/interval_nt.h#L455-L462>. CGAL `FPU.h`, widening with `nextafter`: <https://github.com/CGAL/cgal/blob/cbc3b81d4607c6f3a9d1f3a47d8709a2be3e6bfa/Number_types/include/CGAL/FPU.h#L347-L358>. R. E. Moore, R. B. Kearfott and M. J. Cloud, *Introduction to Interval Analysis*, SIAM, 2009: the integer power of an interval and the natural interval extension of an expression. IEEE Std 1788-2015, *IEEE Standard for Interval Arithmetic*: the required elementary functions `sqr` and `sqrt`, the set-based flavour, and the decoration `trv` that reports a cut domain. `libm` 0.2.16 (MIT), `src/math/sqrt.rs`, `src/math/arch/` and `src/math/generic/sqrt.rs`: <https://github.com/rust-lang/compiler-builtins/tree/dfd2203a4d6110820ad7bb65cafe1bf331a03a3d/libm/src/math>.
