modules.cost: constant per call and no allocation: each function checks its argument, then runs its port's fast path, and the accurate path only when the fast path's rounding test cannot decide; each module states its own cost. Speed against `libm` is measured as above.
guarantees: **A finite result or an error, never NaN or an infinity.** Each function returns a [`Real`], or: - [`NumError::NotFinite`] when an argument is NaN or infinite (checked first), or the result would be infinite: an overflow, such as `exp(1000)`, or a pole, such as `ln(0)`; - [`NumError::OutsideDomain`] when the function has no real value there: the square root or a logarithm of a negative number, the arcsine or arccosine of a number beyond ±1, or a negative number to a power that is not a whole number. The domain is checked before the function is evaluated, so no function is evaluated where its value would be NaN.
**Accuracy**, as the table below says: proven for the functions here, documented but not proven for those in [`unproven`].
**Deterministic.** The same bits on every target, thread count and build: the correctly rounded results by their specification, the others because they are the same pure-Rust code everywhere.

**Bounded proofs, and what is only tested.** Every function here returns its value through [`Real::new`], which Kani proves refuses exactly NaN and the infinities (`real`'s proofs), so none returns a NaN or an infinity, whatever its argument. Kani also proves (piece G41, chapter 28.7) that [`abs`], [`floor`], [`ceil`] and [`round_ties_even`] are exact for every finite double: a whole number (or the magnitude) at the right place, ties to even, and `NotFinite` for exactly the non-finite arguments. The correctly rounded functions rest on CORE-MATH's proofs and on IEEE 754 (for [`sqrt`] and [`fma`]), and are tested bit for bit against a big-number oracle (`tests/math_reference.rs`); their code (argument reduction, tables, polynomials) is beyond a bounded proof.

guarantees: correctly rounded, with one qualification below. The result is the binary64 number nearest the exact angle of the point `(x, y)` from the positive x-axis, in `[−π, π]` (ties to even), so the error is at most half an ulp. Domain: every pair of doubles, with C99 Annex F's special values (`atan2(±0, +0) = ±0`, `atan2(±0, −0) = ±π`, `atan2(±∞, ±∞) = ±π/4` or `±3π/4`, and so on); a NaN in either argument gives the canonical NaN (`0x7ff8_0000_0000_0000`). The proof is at the end of this documentation.

modules.cost: constant time and no allocation: the point function at each of the two ends (one or two calls of the correctly rounded `sinpi`, `cospi`, `exp` or `ln`), two widening steps, and for the periodic two a fixed number of exact integer comparisons for the peak tests.
guarantees: **Inclusion.** The result contains `f(t)` for every real `t` in the interval, not only for the doubles in it. *Proof.* `exp` and `ln` are increasing, so their image is `[f(lo), f(hi)]`. `sin(πt)` is monotone between consecutive half-integers, where its derivative `π·cos(πt)` vanishes; its maxima (value 1) are at `t ≡ ½` and its minima (−1) at `t ≡ −½ (mod 2)`. So its image is the hull of the two ends' values and of ±1 for every maximum or minimum inside; `cos(πt) = sin(π(t + ½))` likewise, with maxima at even and minima at odd integers. A correctly rounded result `r` of an exact value `v` satisfies `next_down(r) ≤ v ≤ next_up(r)` (round to nearest is faithful), so the widened ends enclose the exact ends. Where an end is exact (a multiple of ½ for `sinpi` and `cospi`, whose value is then exactly 0 or ±1; `exp(0)`; `ln(1)`), it is used without widening. Values of `sinpi` and `cospi` are clamped to `[−1, 1]`, and the lower bound of `exp` to `+0`, which the exact functions never leave.

**Exact peak tests.** Whether the interval contains a maximum or a minimum is decided exactly, with no rounding, by [`Arc`]: the peaks of periodic fields fall at exact half-integers of their phase (chapter 16.2), and the test never misses one or invents one.
**Tight.** Each bound is at most two floating-point steps outside the exact bound: the correctly rounded value plus one widening step.

**Never NaN.** The results are [`Interval`]s, finite and ordered, with a zero bound stored as +0 ([`Interval::new`]); a function outside its domain returns an error, never a NaN (chapter 21), with the errors of the point functions: `exp` fails with [`NumError::NotFinite`] when its upper bound overflows; `ln` fails with [`NumError::OutsideDomain`] when the interval holds a negative number, where the logarithm is not a real number, and with [`NumError::NotFinite`] when its lower bound is zero, where the logarithm is `−∞`.

**Deterministic.** Only the correctly rounded functions of [`crate::math`] (their ports, on the finite bounds of an interval, which the public functions would accept unchanged), IEEE 754 basic operations, comparisons, `rint` (exact), `next_up` and `next_down`.

modules.cost: none at run time, since every literal is read by the compiler; reading one is linear in its length.
guarantees: **Evaluated by the compiler, always.** `hf!("…")` expands to an inline `const` block, `const { parse("…") }`, so every literal is read during compilation, whatever the context: a `const` item, a table, or an expression in a function body. No string is ever parsed at run time, and the kernel's machine code holds only the resulting constants.

**Exact or it does not compile.** The literal's value must be a binary64 number exactly: a significand that needs more than 53 bits (or more than the subnormal range allows), or a value outside the finite range, fails an assertion in [`parse`] or a function it calls. Because [`parse`] runs inside a `const` block, that assertion is evaluated by the compiler: a bad literal is a build error, never a run-time panic. Kernel code reaches [`parse`] only through the macro; only the unit tests below call it directly.
**No rounding at all.** The significand is accumulated as an integer, then placed in the bit pattern; no floating-point operation is involved.

**Checked arithmetic.** Every integer step is a checked method, as in the rest of the crate (`lib.rs`); the assertions before each step keep it in range, and a step that failed anyway would fail the assertion in [`step`], again a build error. Signed and unsigned values meet only through `abs_diff`, `unsigned_abs` and lossless widening, so no conversion loses a value.

modules.cost: on the exact path, the predicate itself. Only on an exact tie, a walk over the masks of the N·(N − 1) perturbed entries (6 for orient2d, 12 for orient3d and incircle, 20 for insphere) until a coefficient is not zero, each candidate an exact N × N determinant by cofactors (at most 120 products in [`I256`]); for points in general position but for the tie, the first few masks decide, and even five coincident points with distinct keys are decided within 2^16 masks.
guarantees: Never zero, never a guess: every answer is `Positive` or `Negative`, decided by exact integer arithmetic, or an error. Points that share a key cannot be told apart by any perturbation, so they are refused with [`NumError::Degenerate`].
The exact sign wins: where [`crate::predicate`]'s predicate is not zero, the perturbed one returns its sign unchanged.

Consistent: the answers are the signs of one perturbed configuration of points, so every predicate agrees with every other on the same keyed points; swapping two arguments flips the sign, and every permutation multiplies it by its parity, as for the exact predicates.

Keys, never addresses: the order is the keys' order alone, so the answers are the same on every run and every target, whatever the points' places in memory (Geogram's default, ordering by address, is exactly what chapter 6.2 rules out).
Deterministic: integers only, no floating point, no allocation, no recursion.

Bounded proofs, and what is only tested: Kani proves (piece G41, chapter 28.7) that `distinct` refuses exactly the keys that repeat, for every two to five `u64` keys; that the lift |p|² of every frame point, in 2D and 3D, fits an `i128` (no step overflows); and that `bit_of` gives the bit for every index below 32 and refuses the rest. The cascade over the masks (up to 2^20 of them, each an exact determinant in [`I256`]) is beyond a bounded proof: its steps are [`I256`]'s, whose arithmetic Kani and Verus prove (`wide`), its bit budget is derived below, and it is tested against exact rationals on every tie class.
modules.job: Symbolic perturbation, ordered by persistent keys: orient2d, orient3d, incircle and insphere with no zero answer, for the algorithms that need every sign to be non-zero (Delaunay and constrained triangulations, ray parity; chapter 6.2).

method.text: Simulation of Simplicity (Edelsbrunner and Mücke 1990, <https://doi.org/10.1145/77635.77639>), entry j of point i moved by ε^(2^e) with e increasing along a global order of the points, with the lifted coordinate perturbed as an entry of its own (as Devillers and Teillaud perturb the lift for Delaunay, <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.comgeo.2010.09.010>), so the lifted predicates always reach a non-zero term. The perturbed determinant is a polynomial in ε. By multilinearity in the rows, each term chooses, in each row, either the row itself or one of its perturbed entries, so it belongs to a set S of perturbed entries in distinct rows and distinct columns, with degree Σ 2^e over S and coefficient the determinant with the rows of S replaced by the unit vectors of their columns. Degrees are sums of distinct powers of two, so they order the sets S exactly as the sets' bit masks order them: the first non-zero coefficient, walking the masks upwards from 1, decides the sign as ε goes to 0. Mask 0 is the unperturbed determinant. Consulted for the cascade's shape: Geogram's `_SOS` predicates (BSD-3-Clause), no code copied.

modules.cost: constant time and no allocation. Every function is a fixed number of products and sums in `i128` and fixed-width integers: [`Plane::side_of_tpi`] is four products in [`I384`] after the point's homogeneous coordinates, repeated in [`I512`] only on the total path; [`Tpi::to_grid`] is one restoring long division per coordinate, 40 steps when the point lies within the frame's range and at most 127 otherwise, each step a few operations on six or eight 64-bit limbs.
guarantees: Every result is exact, or an error. A [`Sign`] is decided by integer arithmetic alone; no rounding ever decides it. Only [`Tpi::to_grid`] rounds: it rounds the exact rational point to the nearest grid point (ties to even) and says whether it rounded, moving each coordinate by at most [`COMMIT_PER_AXIS`](crate::ladder::COMMIT_PER_AXIS), half a step.

Nothing overflows, and nothing could wrap silently if it did. A [`Plane`] can only be made by [`Plane::through`] from grid points (within 2^40 − 1 steps of the origin), which checks the plane's budget below at construction (chapter 6.2); a [`Tpi`] can only be made by [`Tpi::new`], which checks that its homogeneous coordinates fit their types. Every intermediate fits its type by the derivation written on each function; the arithmetic of every derivation, and every figure in the table below, is asserted when the crate compiles (the budget exponents in the source, from `GRID_DIFFERENCE_BITS` on); and every operation, on `i128` and on wide integers alike, is checked, so none of this depends on a build with overflow checks. In summary, with B = 40 and every coordinate below 2^B in magnitude: | Quantity | Bound | Type | | --- | --- | --- | | Plane normal n | 2^(2B+3) = 2^83 | `i128` | | Plane offset d | 2^(3B+5) = 2^125 | `i128` | | Grid point against a plane, n · p + d | 2^126 | `i128` | | Three-plane denominator w | 2^(6B+12) = 2^252 | [`I256`] | | Three-plane numerators X | 2^(7B+14) = 2^294 | [`I320`] | | Three-plane point against a plane, n · X + d · w | 2^(9B+19) = 2^379 | [`I384`] | At B = 26 the same formulas give 9B + 19 = 253 bits, within the 256 bits EMBER uses for its 26-bit inputs (evidence note 05, section 4). The bounds are safe rather than tight: they bound every factor separately, and a triangle inside the frame cannot make every product maximal at once. With M = 2^40 − 1, what grid points can reach is |`n_i`| ≤ 4M² and |d| ≤ 4M³ (82 and 122 bits; derivations on [`Plane::through`]), |n · p + d| ≤ 16M³ (124 bits, on [`Plane::side`]), and from the plane bounds, because each of w, `X_i` and n · X + d · w is a determinant whose largest magnitude over a box of entries lies at a corner of the box, |w| ≤ 256M^6, |`X_i`| ≤ 256M^7 and |n · X + d · w| ≤ 4096M^9 (248, 288 and 372 bits; derivations on [`Tpi::homogeneous`] and [`Plane::side_of_tpi`]). Planes and three-plane points built from the corners of the frame's cube reach every one of these exactly (tested).
Deterministic: integers only, no floating point, no platform maths, no allocation.

**Bounded proofs, and what is only tested** (chapter 28.7; piece G41 collects them here). Verus proves that the generated exact paths of `plane_side`, `tpi_weight`, `tpi_side`, `lpi_weight` and `lpi_side`, which every answer here rests on, compute their values exactly and never overflow for every input in their declared ranges (piece G39: the twins in `verus/generated/`, token for token the shipped modules), on [`crate::wide`] arithmetic that is itself proven exact (G37). The budgets in the table above are asserted when the crate compiles; the constructors' checks, the routing between filter and exact path and the rounding to the grid are tested against exact oracles, not proven (`tests/plane.rs`, `tests/attack_plane.rs`), and the filters' error bounds are checked until G40 certifies them.

method.text: plane-based geometry with vertices as three-plane intersections in homogeneous integer coordinates, as in Campen and Kobbelt 2010 ([doi:10.1111/j.1467-8659.2009.01609.x](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8659.2009.01609.x)), Nehring-Wirxel, Trettner and Kobbelt 2021 ([doi:10.1016/j.cad.2021.103015](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cad.2021.103015)) and EMBER 2022 (Trettner, Nehring-Wirxel and Kobbelt, [doi:10.1145/3528223.3530181](https://doi.org/10.1145/3528223.3530181)). Classifying a homogeneous point by multiplying by the sign of w, so that nothing is divided, follows Attene 2020's indirect predicates ([doi:10.1016/j.cad.2020.102856](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cad.2020.102856); method only, re-derived here). The rounding division is restoring binary long division (Knuth, *The Art of Computer Programming*, volume 2, section 4.3.1). The reach of the bounds uses Hadamard's determinant inequality (J. Hadamard, 1893, *Bulletin des Sciences Mathématiques* 17).

modules.cost: per call, the generated filter's few dozen `f64` operations where the routing runs it, and the exact path only when the filter cannot decide (or first, where the filter does not pay): a fixed number of checked integer operations, each module's header gives the counts. No allocation and no recursion.
guarantees: **Exact for every input.** No rounding ever decides a sign, and `Zero` means exactly degenerate. Each predicate documents its degenerate cases, including which sign a degenerate but non-zero answer has.

**The same answer in every build profile; no overflow, no panic.** Outside its tests this module uses no native `+`, `-` or `*` on a fixed-width integer, and no cast: every operation is a checked method (`checked_sub`, `checked_mul`, `checked_add`, `checked_neg`) that returns `None` instead of wrapping. So nothing here depends on overflow checks being on, which they are not in a default release build. `tests/attack_predicate.rs` scans this file's code to keep it that way.
**Deterministic.** The same answer on every target: the integer paths are exact, and the filter's `f64` operations are correctly rounded everywhere and give a sign only when it is the exact sign.

**Bounded proofs, and what is only tested** (chapter 28.7; piece G41 collects them here). Verus proves that the generated exact paths of [`orient2d`], [`orient3d`], [`incircle`] and [`insphere`] compute their determinants exactly and never overflow, for every grid input (pieces G36 and G38: the twins in `verus/generated/`, token for token the shipped modules), and that the [`crate::wide`] arithmetic they run on is exact (G37). Kani proves that [`orient2d`] answers with the exact sign, nothing panicking or overflowing on the way, filter and routing included, for every coordinate within one step of 0 or of an edge of the frame (piece G14: geom-fuzz's `orient2d_proof`). The filters' error bounds are checked against exact arithmetic, not proven, until pieces G35 and G40 certify them; the routing and every other input are tested against exact oracles (`tests/attack_predicate.rs`, the verification suite).
modules.job: Exact geometric predicates on grid points: orientation in 2D and 3D, in-circle and in-sphere.

method.text: the determinant forms of Shewchuk, *Adaptive Precision Floating-Point Arithmetic and Fast Robust Geometric Predicates*, Discrete & Computational Geometry 18 (1997) (<https://doi.org/10.1007/PL00009321>; reference code <https://www.cs.cmu.edu/afs/cs/project/quake/public/code/predicates.c>): orientation is the determinant of the edge vectors, and in-circle and in-sphere are the orientation of the points lifted onto the paraboloid z = |p|², written relative to the query point so every entry is a small difference. Shewchuk evaluates these in floating point with adaptive expansions; on the grid the inputs are integers below 2^40, so the same determinants evaluate exactly in fixed-width integers. The filter and the exact path in front of the hand-written ones are generated (module [`crate::generated`], whose header states their method, proof and cost). The total path's bounds follow the static bit-length analysis of Fortune and Van Wyk, *Static Analysis Yields Efficient Exact Integer Arithmetic for Computational Geometry*, ACM Transactions on Graphics 15(3) (1996), carried in Rust's type system so that the compiler checks them.

modules.cost: [`gauss_legendre`] is n evaluations of f and an exact sum; [`integrate`] is 2n + 1 evaluations per panel, at most `cap` + 1 panels, and a search of at most [`MAX_PANELS`] panels per bisection. No allocation (the panels live in a fixed array on the stack, 40 bytes each), no recursion.
modules.does: [`gauss_legendre`] applies an n-point Gauss–Legendre rule (n from 1 to 20) on `[a, b]`. [`integrate`] estimates ∫ₐᵇ f by one of the six Gauss–Kronrod rules ([`crate::quadrature_rules::GAUSS_KRONROD`]), splitting the panel with the largest error estimate in two until the summed estimate meets the tolerance: QUADPACK's QAG strategy. The rules are generated by geom-gen, every node and weight correctly rounded (`quadrature_rules`'s header). Chapter 12's transcendental enclosures (the Fresnel integrals of clothoids) integrate with the Gauss–Legendre rules and bound the remainder themselves; [`integrate`]'s estimate is for measures that need no proof (an arc length to report, a mass property).
guarantees: **Exact to the rules' degrees.** The n-point Gauss rule integrates every polynomial of degree at most 2n − 1, and a Kronrod rule of 2n + 1 points every one of degree at most 3n + 1, up to the rounding of the rule's entries and of the sum (`tests/quadrature.rs` checks every rule against exact rational integrals).

**An estimate, labelled as one.** [`Integral::error`] is the sum over panels of |Kronrod − Gauss|, Kronrod's classic estimate of the Gauss result's error, which for smooth functions far exceeds the Kronrod result's. It is not a bound: a caller that needs a proven bound encloses the remainder from a derivative bound instead (chapter 12.10).
**A cap, never a guess.** At most `cap` bisections, and at most [`MAX_PANELS`] panels; reaching either without meeting the tolerance is [`QuadError::CapReached`], never the best value so far.

**Deterministic and order-free.** Panels are evaluated and split in a fixed order (the first panel with the largest estimate is split, left half in its place, right half last), every sum is taken exactly with [`ExactSum`] and rounded once, and the result is a finite [`Real`]; the same bits on every target.
modules.job: Numerical integration in one variable: fixed Gauss–Legendre rules, and an adaptive integrator on Gauss–Kronrod rules with an error estimate.

method.text: the Gauss–Kronrod pair and the adaptive bisection of R. Piessens, E. de Doncker-Kapenga, C. W. Überhuber and D. K. Kahaner, *QUADPACK: A Subroutine Package for Automatic Integration*, Springer (1983), doi:10.1007/978-3-642-61786-7, routines QK and QAG; the error estimate |K − G| is Kronrod's (A. S. Kronrod, *Nodes and Weights of Quadrature Formulas*, Consultants Bureau (1965)), without QUADPACK's empirical rescaling.

guarantees: every node and weight is the `f64` nearest to its exact value, ties to even, decided by geom-gen from an exact rational enclosure; nodes are ascending and symmetric about 0; in a Kronrod rule the Gauss nodes are the odd positions, the same bits as the Gauss rule's own. The n-point Gauss rule integrates every polynomial of degree at most 2n − 1 exactly, and a Kronrod rule every one of degree at most 3n + 1 (n even) or 3n + 2 (n odd), up to the rounding of its entries (`tests/quadrature.rs`).

method.text: Golub and Welsch's eigenvalue method for the Gauss rules, with Sturm-count bisection (G. H. Golub and J. H. Welsch, Mathematics of Computation 23 (1969), doi:10.1090/S0025-5718-69-99647-1), and Kronrod's extension from its definition, the zeros of the Stieltjes polynomial with interpolatory weights (A. S. Kronrod 1965; G. Szegő 1935, doi:10.1007/BF01448041); the generator's header gives the details.

guarantees: Every `Real` is finite: [`Real::new`] is the only way to make one, and it refuses NaN and the infinities.
Equality and order are both IEEE 754's `totalOrder`, so they agree, and −0 and +0 are different values, on every target.

[`Real::total_max`] and [`Real::total_min`] have named tie rules: they pick by `totalOrder`, so −0 is below +0, and on a tie, which under `totalOrder` is always the same bits, they return the first argument.
modules.job: `Real`: a floating-point number that is never NaN and never infinite.

method.text: IEEE 754-2019's `totalOrder` predicate (section 5.10, <https://doi.org/10.1109/IEEESTD.2019.8766229>), through `f64::total_cmp`; never producing NaN follows Rust RFC 3514 (<https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3514-float-semantics.html>).

modules.cost: a block is ten rounds, each two 32 × 32 → 64-bit multiplies and four exclusive ors, with nine two-word key additions between them, and gives four 32-bit words. [`Stream::next_u32`] computes a block on every fourth call, and [`Stream::next_u64`] and [`Stream::next_f64`] on every second call. [`Stream::below`] draws on average 2^64 / (2^64 − (2^64 mod n)) words of 64 bits, fewer than two for every n and fewer than 1 + 2^−32 for n below 2^32. It computes the 64-bit remainder 2^64 mod n at most once per call, the first time a word's low half is below n, which happens for each word with probability exactly n / 2^64 (for odd n the low half is uniform; for even n = 2^k · m it is a multiple of 2^k, each from 2^k words). A [`StreamRange`] operation is a few integer operations. A [`Stream`] is a few dozen bytes and allocates nothing. Speed is measured once the benchmark harness exists (piece G18); no figure is claimed here.
guarantees: **Specified, and checked against the reference.** [`philox4x32_10`] is Philox4x32-10 as its authors specify it (Method, below). The tests reproduce Random123's published known answers (`tests/rng_kat.rs`), and golden hashes pin every draw function's output on every CI target, WebAssembly included (`tests/rng_determinism.rs`).
**Explicit inputs only.** A [`Seed`] and a [`StreamId`] are plain integers the caller writes. There is deliberately no `Default`, no constructor from entropy and no global or thread-local generator.

**Integers, and no step that wraps or drops a bit unseen.** Every operation is on integers. Wrapping happens only where the method is defined modulo a power of two: the specification's 32 × 32-bit product, formed modulo 2^64 as its reference forms it (it never reaches 2^64), and its key schedule, modulo 2^32; and Lemire's threshold, a negation modulo 2^64. Every other step is a checked method, or exact by construction (words split and joined through their bytes, widening casts, bit masks and shifts by constants with their ranges written beside them, and `abs_diff` where the invariants make it the difference), and each place says why. A checked step's failure either has a meaning, which is then the answer (a stream id past 2^64 − 1 lies past every range's end), or is ruled out by a proof written beside it and reported as [`RngError::Defect`] should it happen all the same, never answered. The floating-point steps, in [`Stream::next_f64`], are exact. So results are the same bits on every target, in debug and release, with overflow checks on or off, and no lint on arithmetic or casts is allowed outside the tests.

**Exactly uniform, given uniform words.** [`Stream::below`] and [`Stream::range_inclusive`] give every value of the range from exactly the same number of 64-bit words (Lemire's rejection method, so there is no modulo bias), and [`Stream::next_f64`] gives each of the 2^53 values k · 2^−53 in [0, 1) from exactly 2^11 words. That Philox's words are themselves indistinguishable from uniform and independent is the authors' claim, from the `TestU01` library's Crush batteries: seven rounds of Philox4x32 pass, and ten keep three rounds as a safety margin. This module relies on that claim; it does not prove it.

**Streams never overlap and never wrap.** For one key, Philox is a bijection on counters (each round can be undone; `tests/rng_properties.rs` inverts it), so no two (stream, block) pairs share a block. A stream is 2^64 blocks of four words; moving to the next block carries from counter word 0 into word 1, never into the stream's words. Drawing past the end returns [`RngError::Exhausted`].

**Ranges handed out never overlap.** Chunks of one size cut from one [`StreamRange`] are disjoint and lie inside it, with checked integer arithmetic; a range too small for a request returns [`RngError::TooFewStreams`] (`tests/rng_ranges.rs` checks both against a model in arbitrary-precision integers).
**All or nothing.** A draw that fails leaves its stream exactly as it was.

**No panics, no `unsafe`, no allocation, no `std`.** The block function, every draw and every range operation are `const fn`s, so a table of random numbers can be computed at compile time, with the same bits.
modules.job: Counter-based random numbers from explicit seeds (Philox4x32-10): the one generator every randomised kernel method draws from.

method.text: the published methods below. **Philox4x32-10**: J. K. Salmon, M. A. Moraes, R. O. Dror and D. E. Shaw, "Parallel random numbers: as easy as 1, 2, 3", SC '11, section 4.3, <https://doi.org/10.1145/2063384.2063405>. Each round is the paper's generalised Feistel S-box on two pairs of words, with the two multipliers its search found for Philox-4x32; the key steps through a Weyl sequence between rounds. The word order, the multiplier for each word and the order of key steps and rounds follow the authors' reference implementation, Random123's `philox.h` (BSD-3-Clause, D. E. Shaw Research), at <https://github.com/DEShawResearch/random123/blob/9545ff6413f258be2f04c1d319d99aaef7521150/include/Random123/philox.h>. The code here is written from the specification; none of Random123's code is copied. The tests quote its known-answer vectors, which are facts. **Integers in a range**: D. Lemire, "Fast random integer generation in an interval", *ACM Transactions on Modeling and Computer Simulation* 29(1), 2019, <https://doi.org/10.1145/3230636> (arXiv:1805.10941). Multiply the word by the bound, keep the high half, and reject the few words whose low half is below 2^64 mod n. As in the paper's nearly divisionless method, that remainder is computed at most once per call, and only once a word's low half is below n. **Doubles**: the top 53 bits of a 64-bit word times 2^−53, as S. Vigna recommends in "Generating uniform doubles in the unit interval", <https://prng.di.unimi.it/>. **Stream ranges**: consecutive, equal, disjoint blocks of stream ids, cut with checked 64-bit arithmetic, in which a step past 2^64 − 1 is past the range's last id. A counter-based generator reaches any stream directly from its id (Salmon and others, above), so handing each consumer its own ids is all that independent streams need.

modules.cost: constant: every function is one comparison or one `match`.
guarantees: predicates return a sign, never a number, so no caller can compare a rounded value against a threshold by accident. `Zero` means "exactly on it", decided exactly.
modules.job: The result of every exact predicate: negative, zero or positive.

method.text: the sign of an exactly computed quantity, as chapter 6.2's exact predicates return it (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/06-numbers.md`): a comparison with zero, and the sign rules of negation and multiplication of the reals.

modules.cost: for `L` limbs, addition, subtraction, negation, comparison and resizing are O(L) limb operations and multiplication O(L²), on the stack with no allocation; the kernel's widths are 4 to 8 limbs.
guarantees: every arithmetic operation is checked: it returns `None` when the true result does not fit, and never wraps silently. The kernel proves that its predicates never overflow; these checks turn a wrong proof into a detectable failure instead of a wrong sign.
modules.job: Fixed-width signed integers for exact predicates.

method.text: schoolbook addition, subtraction and multiplication on magnitudes with 128-bit intermediates (Knuth, *The Art of Computer Programming*, volume 2, section 4.3.1, <https://www-cs-faculty.stanford.edu/~knuth/taocp.html>). There is no division: predicates never need it.

modules.cost: for `L` limbs, addition, subtraction, negation, comparison and conversion are O(L) limb operations; a product of an `A`-limb and a `B`-limb value is A · B limb products, each one 32 × 32 → 64-bit multiply, on the stack with no allocation.
guarantees: **Checked.** Every arithmetic operation and conversion returns `None` when the true result does not fit, and never wraps silently: a certificate that was wrong shows as `None`, never as a wrong sign.

**Checked inside too.** A limb sum or difference uses `overflowing_add` or `overflowing_sub`, which return the full result as the low 32 bits and the carry or borrow; only the carry out of the top limb is dropped, as two's complement defines, before the sign test that decides overflow. A limb product uses `checked_mul` and `checked_add` on `u64`, which cannot fail ((2^32 − 1)² + 2 (2^32 − 1) = 2^64 − 1, written beside each), split into its 32-bit halves through its bytes, with no cast and no shift. Nothing depends on overflow checks being on.
**The same values as `Wide`.** Each operation gives the value [`crate::wide::Wide`]'s gives on the same integers (tested against it and against big integers below and in `tests/attack_g42.rs`).
modules.job: Fixed-width signed integers in 32-bit limbs, for the width-aware limb variant of the exact paths.

method.text: schoolbook addition, subtraction and multiplication on magnitudes with 64-bit intermediates (Knuth, *The Art of Computer Programming*, volume 2, section 4.3.1, <https://www-cs-faculty.stanford.edu/~knuth/taocp.html>), as [`crate::wide::Wide`] with 32-bit limbs; the products of operands of different widths follow the same algorithm with the operands' own limb counts. There is no division: predicates never need it.

errors.name: NurbsError

invariants: Every algorithm's doc comment names its source: a NURBS Book algorithm number or a paper's DOI (7).
Bounds are conservative, from Bernstein and interval arithmetic rounded outward, never from sampling (principle 2, 12.3).
Sums run in a fixed written order (basis sums, Horner steps); no platform maths (21, 23.4).
Well-formedness is checked at construction: knots non-decreasing, multiplicities at most degree plus one, weights positive (24.7).
A fit states its certified error and is never accepted when it misses its bound; its least-squares solves go through `geom-linalg` (13.21, 15.6).
crates.job: NURBS algorithms: basis, evaluation, knot operations, degree change, fitting, Bernstein bounds, Bezier extraction, symbolic products, skinning, Gordon and Coons combination.

modules.cost: each removal pass tries O(n) knots, each try O(n·D) to remove and re-insert and O(m·p) to check the data; each least-squares step O(m·n²); each projection O(p²·D) a step. All of it is charged to the meter as it goes.
modules.does: [`Curve::approximate`] interpolates the data at a low degree, then repeats: remove every knot it can while each data point stays within the tolerance (algorithm A9.8), raise the degree of the knot vector by one, fit by least squares on it, and move each data point's parameter to the nearest point of the new curve. When the degree asked for is reached it removes knots once more and stops. If a step fails (the least-squares system is not determined, or a point ends up beyond the tolerance), it starts again from an interpolant one degree higher, as `NLib`'s `N_FitCrvApprox` does.
guarantees: **Within the tolerance, certified.** Each data point carries a certified upper bound on its distance from the current curve at its parameter. Interpolation and least squares set it by interval evaluation (`crate::enclose`); a knot removal adds the certified change of the curve at that parameter, which re-inserting the knot in interval arithmetic bounds control point by control point: the change at u is Σ `N_l`(u)·(`P̃_l` − `P_l`), at most Σ `N_l`(u)·|`P̃_l` − `P_l`| with each `N_l`(u) bounded above by an interval enclosure. A removal is kept only if every bound stays within the tolerance, so the result is within it at every data point; its `error` is the smaller of that bound and a fresh interval evaluation, point by point. `NLib` bounds a removal's change by the same sum in floating point, with the removal's error at one control point from the book's formula.

**Never a best-so-far curve.** If even the interpolant of the degree asked for is not within the tolerance, the result is [`NurbsError::OutsideTolerance`]; `NLib` returns whatever its last attempt left.

**Parameters improve or stay.** A parameter moves by Newton's method on (C(u) − Q)·C′(u) only while each step brings the curve point nearer the data point, inside the domain; the ends stay at the ends.
**Deterministic.** Knots are tried smallest bound first, the first on a tie; every loop runs in a fixed order; Newton's method stops after at most [`NEWTON_STEPS`] steps.
modules.job: Curve approximation to a stated error (The NURBS Book, section 9.4.4): the curve of a given degree that passes within a tolerance of every data point, with as few control points as knot removal can leave.

method.text: W. Tiller's knot removal (*Computer-Aided Design* 24(8) (1992), 445–453, <https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-4485(92)90012-Y>) used for approximation as Piegl and Tiller's section 9.4.4 and algorithm A9.8 give it, with least squares at each degree (section 9.4.1) and point inversion by Newton's method (section 6.1) (The NURBS Book, 2nd ed., Springer (1997), <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-59223-2>), in the order of steps `NLib` takes.

modules.cost: constant per operation; nothing allocates.
modules.does: each knot operation (insertion, refinement, Bezier extraction, removal, degree change) is written once, generic over [`Num`], and run once in `f64` and once in `geom-num`'s [`Interval`]. The two runs make the same operations in the same order on the same data. Every interval operation rounds to nearest and widens by one step, so it contains the exact result of the operation for any operands in its inputs; rounding to nearest is monotone, so it also contains the double the `f64` run computes from operands inside those inputs. By induction over the run, each interval contains both the exact value and the double, and its width bounds their distance. [`Hom`] is a homogeneous control point, w·P with its weight w, combined as `NLib`'s `N_Combine2CPts` combines them.
guarantees: **Enclosure.** For a computation written once over [`Num`], each value of the interval run contains the exact value and the value of the `f64` run (the argument above; geom-num's `interval` module proves the inclusion of each operation).
**The same doubles as a plain computation.** The `f64` implementation is IEEE 754's correctly rounded operation, nothing else: no fused multiply-add, no reordering.

**Typed failures.** An interval bound that leaves the finite doubles, or a divisor interval that contains zero, is [`NurbsError::NotFinite`]; the `f64` run is checked for finite results where the operations collect them.
modules.job: The arithmetic the knot operations run in twice: doubles for the result, and intervals for a certified bound on that result's rounding.

method.text: interval arithmetic with outward rounding by one step (R. E. Moore, R. B. Kearfott and M. J. Cloud, *Introduction to Interval Analysis*, SIAM (2009), <https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898717716>) as `geom-num` implements it, used as a running error bound for a floating-point computation that makes the same operations (N. J. Higham, *Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms*, 2nd ed., SIAM (2002), section 3.3, <https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898718027>).

modules.cost: n·`lower`·(`upper` + `width`) multiply-adds to eliminate and n·(`upper` + 1)·`width` to substitute, charged to the meter first; one allocation of n·(`lower` + `upper` + 1) doubles.
modules.does: a [`Band`] holds a square matrix whose row i has its nonzero entries in columns i − `lower` to i + `upper`; [`Band::solve`] solves A·X = B for a block B of `width` columns, eliminating below the diagonal in order and substituting back, all inside the band.
guarantees: **Stable without pivoting, for the matrices it is given.** The B-spline collocation matrix at increasing parameters is totally positive (C. de Boor, "Total positivity of the spline collocation matrix", *Indiana University Mathematics Journal* 25(6) (1976), 541–551, <https://doi.org/10.1512/iumj.1976.25.25043>), and Gaussian elimination without pivoting on a totally positive matrix is backward stable, its computed factors staying nonnegative (C. de Boor and A. Pinkus, "Backward error analysis for totally positive linear systems", *Numerische Mathematik* 27 (1977), 485–490, <https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01399609>). The end derivative rows of section 9.2.2 come first and last and only fix their control points, so the rest is a submatrix of such a matrix, which is totally positive too.

**Refused, never guessed.** A pivot that is not positive (the Schoenberg–Whitney condition fails, or rounding has met a nearly singular matrix) is [`NurbsError::Undetermined`]; a result that is not finite is [`NurbsError::NotFinite`].
**Deterministic.** Rows eliminated in order, columns in order, no fused multiply-add.
modules.job: Banded linear systems solved by Gaussian elimination without pivoting, for the collocation matrices of interpolation.

method.text: Gaussian elimination without pivoting on a totally positive band matrix, as de Boor and Pinkus analyse it (<https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01399609>), in the band storage and with the band triangular solves of G. H. Golub and C. F. Van Loan, *Matrix Computations*, 4th ed., Johns Hopkins (2013), section 4.3; the right-hand sides are carried through the elimination.

modules.cost: [`Basis::new`] is linear in the number of knots and keeps them (one allocation). [`Basis::span`] is a binary search, O(log m). [`Basis::eval`] and [`Basis::eval_one`] take O(p²) operations, [`Basis::eval_derivs`] O(p² + n·p) for n derivatives, and [`Basis::eval_one_derivs`] O(p² + n²); none of them allocates, and their scratch arrays, sized for [`MAX_DEGREE`], take at most about 14 KiB of stack.
modules.does: [`Basis::new`] checks chapter 24.7's rules for a knot vector and keeps it. [`Basis::span`] finds the knot span of a parameter (A2.1); [`Basis::eval`] gives the p + 1 functions that do not vanish there (A2.2) and [`Basis::eval_derivs`] their derivatives (A2.3); [`Basis::eval_one`] and [`Basis::eval_one_derivs`] give one function and its derivatives (A2.4, A2.5). At a knot of reduced continuity a function's derivatives differ from the left and from the right, so every evaluation takes a [`Limit`]; at an end of the domain only the side inside it exists, and that side is used whatever the limit asks.
guarantees: **Well formed or refused.** A basis has a degree from 1 to [`MAX_DEGREE`], at least 2p + 2 knots, every knot finite and none smaller than the one before, no value repeated more than p + 1 times, a finite difference between the last knot and the first, and a domain [`u_p`, `u_(m−p)`] that is more than one value (chapter 24.7). Unclamped knot vectors are accepted, so periodic curves can be stored as they are (chapter 7).

**Parameters inside the domain only.** A parameter that is NaN, infinite or outside the domain is [`NurbsError::ParameterOutside`]; `NLib` clamps it to the nearest span in silence. A domain end is in the last (or first) span with more than one value, found exactly, where `NLib` steps over equal knots within 10^−12.

**Basis values, near exact.** The values of [`Basis::eval`] and [`Basis::eval_one`] lie in [0, 1], and each is within `γ_(6p)` · N of the exact value N for the knots and parameter given: every step of the scheme adds or multiplies quantities that are not negative, and the knot difference that divides each step is at least the term it divides, so each level adds at most six roundings, all relative. On a clamped knot vector the values at the ends of the domain are exactly 1 and 0. [`Basis::eval_derivs`] gives the same bits for the values as [`Basis::eval`].

**Derivatives, bounded by their magnitudes.** Each derivative of order k ≥ 1 is within `γ_(6p+2)` · M of the exact derivative, where M is the same scheme run on magnitudes: every difference of two terms replaced by the sum of their absolute values, with the exact knots and parameter. Each level of the derivative scheme adds at most four roundings to the terms it combines and the sums and the final factor p!/(p − k)! at most 2k more, so 6p + 2 covers every order (the tests check this bound against exact rationals). A derivative that overflows, which a span far shorter than its neighbours can cause, is [`NurbsError::NotFinite`]; the functions never return a value that is not finite.
**Deterministic.** Only IEEE 754 addition, subtraction, multiplication and division in the fixed order written here; no fused multiply-add, no platform maths.
modules.job: B-spline bases: a degree and a knot vector, checked once, and the basis functions and their derivatives at a parameter (The NURBS Book, algorithms A2.1 to A2.5).

method.text: the triangular schemes of de Boor and Cox for the basis functions, and Piegl and Tiller's algorithms A2.1 to A2.5 for spans, values and derivatives, as `NLib` implements them, with `NLib`'s division order: each quotient of a knot difference by the sum it belongs to is taken before it multiplies a basis value, so no quotient exceeds 1. C. de Boor, "On calculating with B-splines", *Journal of Approximation Theory* 6 (1972), 50–62, <https://doi.org/10.1016/0021-9045(72)90080-9>. M. G. Cox, "The numerical evaluation of B-splines", *IMA Journal of Applied Mathematics* 10 (1972), 134–149, <https://doi.org/10.1093/imamat/10.2.134>. L. Piegl and W. Tiller, *The NURBS Book*, 2nd ed., Springer (1997), sections 2.2 to 2.5, <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-59223-2>. N. J. Higham, *Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms*, 2nd ed., SIAM (2002), lemma 3.1 and section 3.4, <https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898718027>.

provenance.purpose: translated to safe `no_std` Rust from `N_BasisFindSpan`, `N_BasisEval`, `N_BasisDerivs`, `N_BasisIEval` and `N_BasisIDerivs`; a parameter outside the domain is an error instead of being clamped, and the domain's ends find their span exactly instead of stepping over knots within 10^−12; the span search stops by its loop invariant, without `NLib`'s guard against a repeated midpoint; the end shortcuts of `N_BasisEval` are dropped, because its scheme gives the same exact values there, and those of `N_BasisIEval` apply only to a clamped end, where they are exact; the zero-divisor guard (10^−24) is dropped, because a valid basis never divides by a difference that is not positive; the factor p!/(p − k)! is a double rather than an integer, which overflowed past degree 12; the checks of `N_KnotVectorIsValid` are those of chapter 24.7, which also accept unclamped knots and interior knots repeated p + 1 times; every result that could overflow is checked.

modules.cost: extraction O(s·p²·D) in intervals for s spans (O(`s_u`·`s_v`·(p + q)·p·q·D) for a surface); a box, slab or hodograph is linear in the coefficients; a clip O(p²); each result one allocation, charged first.
modules.does: [`Curve::bernstein`] and [`Surface::bernstein`] run Bezier extraction (A5.6, A5.7) in `geom-num`'s interval arithmetic, so each piece's coefficients enclose the exact Bernstein coefficients of the exact curve or surface the stored doubles define. On a piece, [`BernsteinCurve::bound`] and [`BernsteinPatch::bound`] give a box holding every point of it; [`BernsteinCurve::hodograph`] and [`BernsteinPatch::partial`] give the derivative as a Bernstein form of one degree less (nonrational); [`BernsteinCurve::derivative_bound`] and [`BernsteinPatch::derivative_bound`] bound the derivative of a rational piece too, through the quotient rule's numerator and the weights' range. [`BernsteinCurve::slab`] and [`BernsteinPatch::slab`] bound the signed distance n·(x − o) over a piece, for any direction n; [`BernsteinCurve::fat_line`] (in the plane) and [`BernsteinPatch::fat_plane`] choose n from the piece's end points or corners, as Sederberg and Nishita's fat line does. [`BernsteinCurve::clip`] is a Bezier clipping step: the part of a curve's domain where it can meet a slab.
guarantees: **Enclosures of the exact.** Every coefficient is an interval holding the exact Bernstein coefficient: extraction makes the same operations as in doubles, each rounded outward (`crate::arith`). Every bound below is computed from these intervals with outward rounding, so it holds for the exact curve or surface, not only for its doubles.

**The convex hull property.** A Bezier piece lies in the convex hull of its control points (for a rational piece, of its Euclidean points, since the weights are positive), so a box, a slab or any linear function's range over the coefficients bounds the piece (The NURBS Book, properties P3.4 and P4.4; Farouki and Rajan, *Computer Aided Geometric Design* 5(1) (1988), 1–26). A derivative is bounded from the hodograph, the derivative's own Bernstein form; a rational derivative C′ = (A′·W − A·W′)/W² from its numerator's coefficients and the smallest and largest weights, W lying between them.

**Clipping keeps every meeting.** [`BernsteinCurve::clip`] returns a parameter range outside which the exact curve is outside the slab, or `None` when the whole curve is: the hull of the control polygon of the distance to each side of the slab, computed with each coefficient at its upper bound and every crossing rounded outward.

**Typed refusals.** A piece needs a domain of more than one value, coefficients that are finite, and positive weights ([`NurbsError::Weight`]); hodographs and products of rational pieces are [`NurbsError::Rational`] (bound their numerators instead); a fat line or plane of a piece whose end points or corners give no direction is [`NurbsError::Degenerate`].
**Deterministic.** Fixed loops in index order; no fused multiply-add.
modules.job: Bernstein forms: the Bezier pieces of curves and surfaces as interval enclosures of their exact Bernstein coefficients, and the bounds the convex hull property gives them: boxes, derivative boxes from hodographs, slabs, fat lines and fat planes, and the parameter range a Bezier clipping step keeps.

method.text: Bezier extraction (The NURBS Book, 2nd ed., algorithms A5.6 and A5.7, <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-59223-2>) in interval arithmetic, the convex hull property and hodographs (sections 1.4 and 3.3), and Bezier clipping with fat lines (T. W. Sederberg and T. Nishita, "Curve intersection using Bézier clipping", *Computer-Aided Design* 22(9) (1990), 538–549, <https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-4485(90)90039-F>), its hull taken over every pair of control points so it needs no convex hull routine.

modules.cost: O(s·p²) operations for s spans, each twice; one allocation per piece and its enclosure.
modules.does: [`Curve::to_bezier`] walks the knot vector from left to right. At the end of each span it inserts the end knot until it is repeated p times, which leaves the span's p + 1 control points as the Bezier points of that piece, and carries the points it shares with the next span forward (`NLib`'s `N_CrvDecomposeBez`, the book's A5.6). Each piece is returned as a curve of degree p on the knots [a, …, a, b, …, b], rational if the input is. The kernel is generic over `crate::arith`'s numbers and runs in doubles and in intervals (`crate::ops`).
guarantees: **The same curve, piece by piece, within the reported deviation.** Piece i equals the input on its span in real arithmetic; the reported deviation bounds, with certainty, how far rounding moved any piece. A priori, each homogeneous coordinate is within `γ_(10t)` · M of its exact value, with t the number of insertions made (at most p − 1 per interior knot) and M the largest absolute value of that coordinate over the input's control points: every new point is a convex combination, as in `crate::insert`.

**Clamped input only.** Extraction starts from a clamped end, as A5.6 and `NLib` assume; an unclamped curve is [`NurbsError::NotClamped`]. Interior knots repeated p + 1 times (a discontinuous curve) are allowed: the pieces then do not share an end point.
**Budgeted.** The pieces and the interval run are charged to the meter first.
modules.job: Bezier extraction of NURBS curves (The NURBS Book, algorithm A5.6): a clamped curve as one Bezier curve per knot span.

method.text: Piegl and Tiller's algorithm A5.6 (The NURBS Book, 2nd ed., section 5.4, <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-59223-2>), knot insertion until every knot has multiplicity p (Boehm 1980, <https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-4485(80)90154-2>), as `NLib` implements it.

provenance.purpose: translated to safe `no_std` Rust from `N_CrvDecomposeBez`, generic over the number type so the same steps give the pieces and their interval enclosure; an unclamped curve is refused instead of `NLib`'s skipping of extra end knots as bad data; pieces are returned as curves with their own knots.

modules.cost: constant per charge; [`vec_for`] makes one allocation.
modules.does: an operation that builds a curve or surface (knot insertion and refinement, Bezier extraction, knot removal, degree change, derivative curves) knows the size of its result before it computes it. [`charge`] charges one work unit per control point and per knot of the result, and reserves their logical bytes: 8 bytes per coordinate and per weight, and 8 per knot. [`vec_for`] then reserves the real memory fallibly, so a refusal is the meter's `OutOfMemory`, never an abort.
guarantees: **The same charge on every machine.** The charges are counts of the result's control points and knots and fixed sizes per kind, never pointer widths or allocator sizes, so a budget failure is the same everywhere (chapter 23.10).
**Charged before the work.** Each operation charges before it allocates or computes, so an operation over its budget does no work.
modules.job: What a NURBS operation that builds new control points charges to the work meter, and how it reserves the memory for them (chapter 23.10).

method.text: the work units and logical bytes of chapter 23.10 (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/23-performance.md`), through `geom-run`'s [`WorkMeter`]; fallible reservation with `Vec::try_reserve_exact` (<https://doc.rust-lang.org/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html#method.try_reserve_exact>).

modules.cost: construction is linear in the control points and makes one allocation (two if rational). [`Curve::point`] takes O(p²) operations and [`Curve::derivs`] O(p² + k·p·D + k²·D) for k derivatives; neither allocates. [`Curve::derivative_curve`] takes O(k·n·D) operations and one allocation for the points and one for the knots, charged to the meter first.
modules.does: a [`Curve`] holds a [`Basis`] and n + 1 control points of dimension D, with weights if it is rational. A rational curve stores its points in homogeneous form, w·P, as the algorithms of The NURBS Book use them, so a curve built from homogeneous points keeps them exactly and knot operations never divide by a weight. [`Curve::point`] sums the basis functions that do not vanish times their control points (A3.1), and for a rational curve divides by the summed weights (A4.1). [`Curve::derivs`] sums the basis derivatives against the points (A3.2); for a rational curve it applies Leibniz's rule to w·C = A (A4.2). [`Curve::derivative_curve`] builds the k-th derivative of a nonrational curve as a curve of degree p − k by differencing the control points (A3.3).
guarantees: **Well formed or refused.** A curve has exactly as many control points (and weights) as its basis has functions, every coordinate finite, every weight positive and finite, and every weighted coordinate w·P finite.

**Points.** A nonrational point is within `γ_(7p+1)` · Σ `N_j`·|`P_j`| of the exact point: the basis values carry `γ_(6p)` each, and one product and p sums add p + 1 roundings. A rational point is within `γ_(14p+3)` · (Σ `N_j`·|`w_j`·`P_j`|) / (Σ `N_j`·`w_j`): the sums carry `γ_(7p+1)`, the weight sum relative to itself because every term is positive, and the division one more. On a clamped curve the ends are the end control points exactly (for a rational curve, the quotient w·P / w, rounded once).

**Derivatives.** A nonrational derivative of order k ≥ 1 is within `γ_(7p+3)` · Σ `M_j`·|`P_j`|. A rational derivative of order k is within `γ_e` · `MC_k`, e = (k + 1)(14p + 8 + k), where `MC_k` = (Σ `M_(k,j)`·|`w_j`·`P_j`| + `Σ_(i=1..k)` C(k, i) · (Σ `M_(i,j)`·`w_j`) · `MC_(k−i)`) / Σ `N_j`·`w_j` is Leibniz's recurrence run on magnitudes: each step adds the error of the sums, two products, k subtractions and the division to the error of the lower orders. The value of order 0 has the same bits as [`Curve::point`].

**Derivative curves.** The k-th derivative curve's control points are each within `γ_(4k)` of the same differences run on magnitudes (each difference of two points replaced by the sum of their absolute values); each level adds a rounded knot difference, a quotient, two products and a sum. Its value at a parameter is the k-th derivative of the curve.

**Typed failures.** A result that overflows is [`NurbsError::NotFinite`]; a derivative curve across a knot where a lower derivative jumps is [`NurbsError::Discontinuous`], where `NLib` reports a numerical error; derivative curves of rational curves are [`NurbsError::Rational`] (their symbolic form needs products of B-splines, piece G59).
**Deterministic.** Fixed summation order (by increasing control point index), no fused multiply-add, no platform maths.
modules.job: NURBS curves in two and three dimensions: construction under chapter 24.7's rules, points and derivatives (The NURBS Book, algorithms A3.1, A3.2, A4.1 and A4.2), and the control points of derivative curves (A3.3).

method.text: Piegl and Tiller's algorithms A3.1 to A3.3, A4.1 and A4.2 (The NURBS Book, 2nd ed., sections 3.2, 3.3 and 4.2 to 4.3, <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-59223-2>), as `NLib` implements the points and derivative curves; the error bounds follow Higham's rounding-error analysis (*Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms*, 2nd ed., SIAM (2002), chapter 3, <https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898718027>).

provenance.purpose: translated to safe `no_std` Rust from `N_CrvEval`, `N_CrvDerivs` and `N_CrvNonRatGetDerivCrvsAll`, for any dimension D instead of `NLib`'s homogeneous 4D points with its "no z" and "no w" markers; rational derivatives by the book's A4.2 on the stored homogeneous points, where `N_CrvDerivs` forms rational basis derivatives against points divided by their weights; a parameter outside the domain and a derivative order above the maximum are typed errors; derivative curves keep the knots `u_k` to `u_(m−k)`, so unclamped curves work too, where `NLib` rebuilds clamped ends; each overflow is checked.

modules.cost: O(p²·D) operations; nothing allocates.
modules.does: [`Curve::point_by_corner_cutting`] takes the p + 1 homogeneous control points of the span that holds the parameter and replaces them p times by convex combinations of neighbours, α·Q + (1 − α)·R with α = (u − `u_i`) / (`u_(i+p+1−r)` − `u_i`) at level r; the one point left is C(u) in homogeneous form, divided by its weight for a rational curve. It computes the same point as [`Curve::point`] by a different route, every step a convex combination, which makes it the reference evaluation that knot insertion and subdivision rest on.
guarantees: **Convex steps.** For a parameter in the span [`u_k`, `u_(k+1)`], every α lies in [0, 1]: `u_i` ≤ `u_k` ≤ u ≤ `u_(k+1)` ≤ `u_(i+p+1−r)` for every i and r the algorithm visits, and the rounded differences keep that order, so no step extrapolates.

**Near exact.** Each homogeneous coordinate of the point is within `γ_(10p)` · M of its exact value, M the largest absolute value of that coordinate over the p + 1 points used, by the argument of `crate::insert` with one insertion pass per level; a rational point then adds the division by the weight, which is computed the same way.
**Typed failures.** A parameter outside the domain is [`NurbsError::ParameterOutside`]; a point that overflows, [`NurbsError::NotFinite`].
modules.job: Points of NURBS curves by corner cutting (The NURBS Book, algorithm A5.2): de Boor's algorithm, which inserts the parameter until it is repeated p times and takes the point that leaves.

method.text: de Boor's algorithm (C. de Boor, "On calculating with B-splines", *Journal of Approximation Theory* 6 (1972), 50–62, <https://doi.org/10.1016/0021-9045(72)90080-9>), as the corner cutting of Piegl and Tiller's algorithm A5.2 (The NURBS Book, 2nd ed., section 5.2, <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-59223-2>), written from the recurrence; the span is found by [`crate::basis`], so the domain's ends are evaluated inside it.

modules.cost: O(s·(p + t)·p) operations for s spans, each twice, and O((p + t)·p) for the matrix; the result and its enclosure are allocated once.
modules.does: [`Curve::elevate`] walks the knot vector as Bezier extraction does (A5.6), raises each Bezier piece from degree p to p + t with the coefficients C(p, j)·C(t, i − j) / C(p + t, i) (`NLib`'s elevation matrix, filled for the first half of the rows and mirrored), and removes the knots the extraction added, so each distinct knot ends repeated t times more than before (`NLib`'s `N_CrvElevateDegree`, the book's A5.9). The kernel is generic over `crate::arith`'s numbers and runs in doubles and in intervals (`crate::ops`).
guarantees: **The same curve, within the reported deviation.** Elevation does not change the curve in real arithmetic; the reported deviation bounds, with certainty, how far rounding moved it. The removal steps divide by knot differences that can be small, so no a priori bound is stated; the interval run measures the rounding of each case.

**Exact coefficients.** Every binomial coefficient comes from Pascal's triangle, exact for degrees up to [`MAX_DEGREE`] (`crate::basis`), so only the reciprocal 1 / C(p + t, i) and two products round.

**Where it applies.** The curve must be clamped ([`NurbsError::NotClamped`]) with no interior knot repeated more than p times ([`NurbsError::Discontinuous`]), as `NLib`'s check requires, and p + t must not exceed [`MAX_DEGREE`] ([`NurbsError::Degree`]). t = 0 returns the curve unchanged.
**Budgeted.** The result and the interval run are charged to the meter first.
modules.job: Degree elevation of NURBS curves (The NURBS Book, algorithm A5.9): the same curve with degree p + t.

method.text: Piegl and Tiller's algorithm A5.9 (The NURBS Book, 2nd ed., section 5.5, <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-59223-2>; L. Piegl and W. Tiller, "Software-engineering approach to degree elevation of B-spline curves", *Computer-Aided Design* 26(1) (1994), 17–28, <https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-4485(94)90004-3>), as `NLib` implements it.

provenance.purpose: translated to safe `no_std` Rust from `N_CrvElevateDegree`, `N_BezGetDegreeElevationMatrix` and `N_BezElevateDegree`, generic over the number type so the same steps give the result and its interval enclosure; Pascal's triangle is computed rather than read from `NLib`'s table of 18 rows; a new curve is returned instead of edited in place; the degree limit is [`MAX_DEGREE`].

modules.cost: O(p² + k·p·D) interval operations for a curve's derivative of order k, O(p² + q² + p·q·D) for a surface point; nothing allocates but the lists of errors, charged first.
modules.does: [`curve_derivative`] encloses C^(k)(u) and [`surface_point`] S(u, v), for the exact curve or surface that the stored doubles define, evaluated at the exact parameter given. [`distance_bound`] turns an enclosure and a data point into an upper bound on their distance. [`curve_errors`] and [`surface_error`] apply them to every data point of a fit.
guarantees: **Enclosure.** Every value is computed in `geom-num`'s interval arithmetic, each operation rounded outward (`crate::arith`), from the exact knots, parameter and control points, so it holds the exact value; the distance bound is the upper end of an enclosure of the Euclidean norm, so it is at least the exact distance.

**The book's schemes.** The basis functions come from the triangular scheme of de Boor and Cox (A2.2), a derivative from the differenced control points of the derivative curve (A3.3, equation 3.8) and that curve's basis, of degree p − k on the same knots; the same operations as the double-precision code, in intervals.

**Typed failures.** A rational curve or surface is [`NurbsError::Rational`] (fits make only nonrational ones); a parameter outside the domain is [`NurbsError::ParameterOutside`]; an enclosure that leaves the finite doubles is [`NurbsError::NotFinite`].
modules.job: Certified evaluation: interval enclosures of the exact point and derivatives of a nonrational curve, and the exact point of a nonrational surface, at a parameter; and from them certified distances to data, the errors every fit reports.

method.text: interval arithmetic (R. E. Moore, R. B. Kearfott and M. J. Cloud, *Introduction to Interval Analysis*, SIAM (2009), <https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898717716>) on Piegl and Tiller's algorithms A2.2 and A3.3 (The NURBS Book, 2nd ed., sections 2.2 and 3.3, <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-59223-2>).

modules.cost: a few machine words; nothing allocates.
modules.does: [`NurbsError`] names the failure and, where one exists, the index of the knot, control point or weight at fault, so a caller can report it or repair the input (chapter 22's errors that say what to do). A construction checks the rules of chapter 24.7 ("NURBS well formed") and returns the first rule broken, in the order the constructor's documentation gives.
guarantees: **Typed, never silent.** Each of `NLib`'s silent fallbacks (a parameter clamped into the domain, a degenerate span stepped over, a best-so-far result returned beside an error flag) is a variant here instead (chapter 29.7).
**Comparable and stable.** Every variant holds integers only, so errors compare with `==` and print the same on every target.
modules.job: The one error type of the NURBS algorithms: every way an input can be malformed, a parameter can fall outside a domain, a result can fail to be finite, or a budget can stop an operation.

method.none: an error enum and its `Display` and `Error` implementations.

modules.cost: linear in the control points for a plane; O(p²·q²) wide multiplications for a normal patch; one allocation per result, charged first.
modules.does: a Bezier piece whose control points are grid points (chapter 6.1) has integer Bernstein coefficients. [`plane_coefficients`] gives the coefficients of n·x + d over it, for a plane of `geom-num`'s exact [`Plane`] type: they are n·`P_k` + d, by affine invariance, so the signs of [`Signs`] decide exactly whether the piece can meet the plane (chapter 12.3's exact path: "all of its signs, zeros included, are then exact"). [`normal_patch`] gives the normal patch of a nonrational grid Bezier patch in scaled form, its coefficient (a, b) being C(2p − 1, a)·C(2q − 1, b)·`n_ab` times a positive constant, so each has the direction and sign of the Bernstein coefficient `n_ab` of `S_u` × `S_v`; a boundary edge whose control points are one grid point is divided out exactly.
guarantees: **Plane coefficients within 2^126.** [`Plane`] holds |`n_i`| < 2^83 and |d| < 2^125 (checked at construction). Each |`n_i`·`x_i`| < 2^83·2^40 = 2^123, the sum of three below 3·2^123 < 2^125, and with d below 2^126: in `i128` (limit 2^127), every step checked.

**Normal coefficients within 2^193.** In scaled form the partial derivatives' coefficients are C(p − 1, i)·C(q, j)·(`P_(i+1,j)` − `P_ij`) and C(p, i)·C(q − 1, j)·(`P_(i,j+1)` − `P_ij`), differences of at most 2M < 2^41. Products of scaled forms are plain convolutions (the binomials are already inside), and a cross product's component is a difference of two products, so coefficient (a, b) is at most 2·(2M)²·Σ C(p − 1, i1)·C(p, i2)·C(q, j1)·C(q − 1, j2) = 2·(2M)²·C(2p − 1, a)·C(2q − 1, b) < 2^83·2^(2p−1)·2^(2q−1) = 2^(81+2p+2q) ≤ 2^193 for p, q ≤ 28 ([`crate::MAX_DEGREE`]), and every partial sum below the same bound: in `geom-num`'s [`I256`] (limit 2^255), every step checked. A check that fails would be a defect in this derivation, reported as [`NurbsError::Defect`], never a wrong sign.

**Collapsed edges, exactly.** An edge counts only when its grid points are equal; then the normal patch's row along it is zero (checked), and in scaled form dividing by the factor that vanishes there is dropping that row: f = Σ `c_k`·t^k·(1 − t)^(n−k) with `c_0` = 0 is t·Σ `c_(k+1)`·t^k·(1 − t)^(n−1−k), and with `c_n` = 0 it is (1 − t)·Σ `c_k`·t^k·(1 − t)^(n−1−k).
**Deterministic.** Integer arithmetic only.
modules.job: Exact integer paths for Bernstein forms on the grid: the Bernstein coefficients of a plane's equation over a grid Bezier piece, and the normal patch of a grid Bezier patch, with every sign (zeros included) exact, each within a written bit budget.

method.text: exact integer evaluation with bit budgets derived before the code, as chapter 6.2 requires, on the Bernstein form's affine invariance and products in the scaled basis t^k·(1 − t)^(n−k) (R. T. Farouki and V. T. Rajan, *Computer Aided Geometric Design* 5(1) (1988), 1–26; the normal patch as in `crate::product`, after Sederberg and Meyers 1988, <https://doi.org/10.1016/0167-8396(88)90029-5>).

modules.cost: linear in the number of data points (times D for the distances), plus p additions per averaged knot; each result is one allocation, charged to the meter first.
modules.does: a fit takes data points `Q_k` and returns a [`CurveFit`] or a [`SurfaceFit`]: the nonrational curve or surface, the parameter of each data point, and `error`, a certified upper bound on `max_k` |`Q_k` − C(`u_k`)| at those parameters (so also on the distance from every data point to the curve). [`parameters`] gives a polygon's parameters by the uniform, chord-length or centripetal rule, and [`grid_parameters`] a grid's, averaged over its rows and columns. [`averaged_knots`] builds the knot vector of an interpolation, each interior knot the average of p consecutive parameters, and [`least_squares_knots`] that of a least-squares fit with fewer control points than data points, placed so every knot span holds a parameter. Every fit takes a [`FitVersion`]: the operation log records it, and a change to any fit's result is a new version while every old one keeps its behaviour (chapter 26.2).
guarantees: **Certified errors.** Every fit's `error` is computed after the fit, by evaluating the curve or surface at each data parameter in interval arithmetic (`crate::enclose`), so it bounds the exact distance from each data point to the exact curve the returned doubles define. A fit never reports a smaller error than it has, and a fit to a stated error that cannot meet it is [`NurbsError::OutsideTolerance`], never a best-so-far curve (chapter 13.21).

**Parameters on [0, 1], strictly increasing.** The first parameter is exactly 0 and the last exactly 1. Two neighbouring points whose parameters would be equal (they coincide, or round to one value) are [`NurbsError::CoincidentData`]; `NLib` divides by a zero total in silence or leaves equal parameters that make its systems singular.

**Knots for the data.** [`averaged_knots`] gives the knots under which interpolation at the parameters is well posed (Schoenberg–Whitney's condition holds); [`least_squares_knots`] gives knots under which every span holds at least one parameter, so the least-squares system has full rank. Both are clamped on [0, 1].
**Deterministic.** Sums in index order; distances by a scaled sum of squares and `geom-num`'s correctly rounded square root; no fused multiply-add.
modules.job: Fitting NURBS to data (The NURBS Book, chapter 9): what every fit shares, the parameters of the data points, and the knot vectors built from them.

method.text: The NURBS Book, 2nd ed., section 9.2.1: the uniform rule, chord length (equations 9.4 and 9.5) and the centripetal rule (equation 9.6, after E. T. Y. Lee, "Choosing nodes in parametric curve interpolation", *Computer-Aided Design* 21(6) (1989), 363–370, <https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-4485(89)90003-1>); knots by averaging (equation 9.8); a grid's parameters averaged over its rows and columns (algorithm A9.3); and section 9.4.1's knot placement for least squares (equations 9.68 and 9.69). L. Piegl and W. Tiller, *The NURBS Book*, 2nd ed., Springer (1997), <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-59223-2>, as `NLib` implements them and as `geomdl` (MIT) numbers them.

modules.cost: one comparison per call; nothing allocates.
modules.does: the algorithms of The NURBS Book index knots, basis functions and control points by sums and differences of the degree, the span and loop counters. The kernel's lints forbid unchecked indexing and unchecked integer arithmetic (principle 13), so every such index goes through these helpers, which return [`NurbsError::Defect`] instead of panicking.
guarantees: **No panic, no wrong element.** A read or write out of bounds, or an index sum or difference that would overflow, is `Err(Defect)`; every other call reads or writes exactly the element named.
**Unreachable for valid inputs.** Each algorithm's indices are bounded by sizes its input checks have established, so `Defect` marks a bug in this crate and the tests treat it as one.
modules.job: Checked reads, writes and index arithmetic for the NURBS algorithms' arrays.

method.text: Rust's checked slice access (`get`, `get_mut`) and checked integer arithmetic (<https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.usize.html#method.checked_add>).

modules.cost: insertion takes O(n + r·p) operations and refinement O(n + (n + k)·p) for k new knots, each twice; each allocates the result's points and knots and its enclosure.
modules.does: [`Curve::insert_knot`] inserts one parameter value r times (Boehm's algorithm, A5.1); [`Curve::refine`] inserts a non-decreasing list of values at once (A5.4). Each new control point is a convex combination of two older ones, α·Q + (1 − α)·R with α = (u − `u_i`) / (`u_(i+p)` − `u_i`) in [0, 1], in homogeneous coordinates for a rational curve. The kernels are generic over `crate::arith`'s numbers and run twice, in doubles for the result and in intervals for its certified rounding (`crate::ops`). Surfaces use the same kernels on each row or column of their nets (`crate::net`).
guarantees: **The same curve, within the reported deviation.** In real arithmetic insertion does not change the curve; the reported deviation bounds, with certainty, how far rounding moved it. An a priori bound also holds: each new homogeneous coordinate is within `γ_(10t)` · M of its exact value, with t the number of knots inserted and M the largest absolute value of that coordinate over the input's control points, because each pass of one insertion turns every error ε into at most (1 + `γ_10`)·ε + `γ_10`·M (the quotient α carries three roundings, 1 − α four, and the two products and the sum three more).

**Interior knots only, multiplicity at most p.** A value outside the open domain is [`NurbsError::KnotOutside`], as `NLib` refuses an end parameter; a list that is not finite and non-decreasing is [`NurbsError::KnotOutside`]; a value that would be repeated more than p times is [`NurbsError::TooManyKnots`] (`NLib` checks this for single insertion only).
**Budgeted.** The result's points and knots, and the interval run, are charged to the meter before anything is computed.
modules.job: Knot insertion and refinement of NURBS curves (The NURBS Book, algorithms A5.1 and A5.4): more knots and control points, the same curve.

method.text: Boehm's knot insertion and the Oslo-style refinement of Piegl and Tiller, algorithms A5.1 and A5.4 (The NURBS Book, 2nd ed., section 5.2, <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-59223-2>; W. Boehm, "Inserting new knots into B-spline curves", *Computer-Aided Design* 12(4) (1980), 199–201, <https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-4485(80)90154-2>), as `NLib` implements them.

modules.cost: O(n·p²·D) to solve a curve and O(n·p²) to certify it; a surface of r × s points costs O(r·s·(p² + q²)·D); charged to the meter first.
modules.does: [`Curve::interpolate`] chooses parameters by the rule asked for, knots by averaging, and solves the collocation system Σ `N_i`(`u_k`)·`P_i` = `Q_k` for the control points (A9.1). [`Curve::interpolate_at`] does the same at parameters and on a basis the caller gives. [`Curve::interpolate_with_ends`] adds two control points so the curve also has given first derivatives at its ends. [`Surface::interpolate`] interpolates a grid row by row and then column by column through the intermediate points, one system per direction for all of them (A9.4). Each returns its certified error (`crate::fit`).
guarantees: **Interpolates, certified.** The error returned bounds the distance of every data point from the exact curve or surface of the returned doubles at its parameter; it is rounding, not approximation. With end derivatives, `constraint_error` bounds |C′(0) − `D_0`| and |C′(1) − `D_m`| the same way.

**Well posed or refused.** Parameters that do not increase, or that leave a basis function with no parameter in its support (the Schoenberg–Whitney condition), are refused as [`NurbsError::ParameterOrder`] or [`NurbsError::Undetermined`]; `NLib` solves on and returns whatever the elimination gives.
**Stable.** The systems are solved inside their band without pivoting (`crate::band`), which is backward stable for these totally positive matrices.
**Deterministic.** Fixed orders throughout; the same data give the same bits on every target.
modules.job: Global interpolation of curves and surfaces (The NURBS Book, sections 9.2.1, 9.2.2 and 9.2.5): the curve through every data point, optionally with given end derivatives, and the surface through a grid.

method.text: Piegl and Tiller's algorithms A9.1 and A9.4 and section 9.2.2 (The NURBS Book, 2nd ed., Springer (1997), <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-59223-2>), as `NLib` implements them; the end derivatives enter as P₁ − P₀ = (`u_(p+1)` − `u_1`)/p · `D_0` and `P_n` − `P_(n−1)` = (`u_(n+p)` − `u_n`)/p · `D_m`, the first and last derivative control points of A3.3.
