provenance.purpose: translated to safe `no_std` Rust from `N_FitCrvInterp`, `N_FitCrvInterpGivenParams` and `N_FitCrvDerivs`, for any dimension; solved by our own band elimination instead of `NLib`'s banded LU; missing end derivatives are an error where `N_FitCrvDerivs` estimates them from a cubic through four points; the end-derivative factors use the knots at both ends, where `NLib` assumes a domain of [0, 1]; every fit returns its certified error.

modules.cost: a fit with m + 1 data points and n + 1 control points takes O(m·n²) for the decomposition and O(m·n) per coordinate, charged to the meter first; a surface takes one decomposition per direction and one solve per row or column and coordinate.
modules.does: [`Curve::least_squares`] fits a curve of n + 1 control points to m + 1 data points: parameters by the rule asked for, knots by equations 9.68 and 9.69, the end points interpolated and the interior control points minimising Σ |`Q_k` − C(`u_k`)|². [`Curve::least_squares_at`] is algorithm A9.6's general form: weighted data at the caller's parameters on the caller's basis, with points and derivatives anywhere met exactly ([`Constraint`]). [`Surface::least_squares`] fits a grid (A9.7): least squares through each column of the grid, then through each row of the result, the corners interpolated. Each returns its certified error (`crate::fit`).
guarantees: **By QR, never normal equations.** Every system goes through `geom-linalg`'s complete orthogonal decomposition (Householder QR with column pivoting), as chapter 15.6 asks: the book and `NLib` form Nᵀ·N, which squares the condition number. Constraints are met by the null-space method: a particular solution of the constraints and a basis of their null space from one decomposition, then least squares in that space.

**Determined or refused.** A system whose numerical rank is below its number of unknowns (some span with no data, the Schoenberg–Whitney condition broken) is [`NurbsError::Undetermined`], decided by a rank tolerance of max(rows, columns)·u relative to the largest pivot, `NumPy`'s default for `lstsq` (<https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.linalg.lstsq.html>); constraints that repeat or contradict each other are [`NurbsError::Constraints`]. `NLib` solves on with whatever its LU gives.

**Certified.** `error` bounds the distance of every data point from the returned curve at its parameter, and `constraint_error` how far each constraint is missed, both by interval evaluation (`crate::enclose`); the least-squares optimum is only as good as rounding allows, but the bounds are always true.
**Deterministic.** `geom-linalg`'s fixed pivot and loop order; sums in index order.
modules.job: Least-squares approximation of curves and surfaces (The NURBS Book, sections 9.4.1 to 9.4.3): fewer control points than data points, the curve or surface nearest the data in the least-squares sense, with ends or other constraints met exactly.

method.text: Piegl and Tiller's least-squares curve and surface approximation, section 9.4.1 (equations 9.63 to 9.67), algorithm A9.6 (weighted and constrained) and A9.7 (surfaces) (The NURBS Book, 2nd ed., Springer (1997), <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-59223-2>), solved by the complete orthogonal decomposition and the null-space method for equality-constrained least squares (G. H. Golub and C. F. Van Loan, *Matrix Computations*, 4th ed., Johns Hopkins (2013), sections 5.4.2, 5.5 and 6.2) in place of the book's normal equations and Lagrange multipliers.

modules.cost: the curve operation's cost times the number of lines, each twice; the new net and its enclosure are allocated once, and each line's result once.
modules.does: each surface algorithm of the book is its curve algorithm applied to every column of the net (direction u) or every row (direction v), with the same coefficients, because the coefficients depend only on the knots of that direction. So [`Surface::insert_knot`], [`Surface::refine`], [`Surface::to_bezier`] and [`Surface::elevate`] run the curve kernels of `crate::insert`, `crate::bezier` and `crate::elevate` on each line of the net, in doubles for the result and in intervals for its certified rounding (`crate::ops`).
guarantees: **The same surface, within the reported deviation.** In real arithmetic these operations do not change the surface; the reported deviation bounds, with certainty, how far rounding moved it, by the partition of unity of the tensor-product basis.
**The curve operations' conditions, in the direction asked for.** Each refusal is the curve operation's, for the basis of that direction.
**Line by line, as the book.** Every line gets exactly the operations its curve would, in the same order, so a surface's line equals the curve operation on that line, bit for bit.
modules.job: Knot insertion, refinement, Bezier extraction and degree elevation of NURBS surfaces (The NURBS Book, algorithms A5.3, A5.5, A5.7 and A5.10).

method.text: Piegl and Tiller's algorithms A5.3, A5.5, A5.7 and A5.10 (The NURBS Book, 2nd ed., sections 5.2 to 5.5, <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-59223-2>), which apply the curve algorithms A5.1, A5.4, A5.6 and A5.9 to the rows or columns of the net, as `NLib`'s surface tools do with its curve routines.

provenance.purpose: `NLib`'s surface insertion, refinement, Bezier extraction and elevation are rebuilt on the ported curve kernels applied line by line, in place of its separate surface loops, with the curve kernels' changes; every result carries its certified deviation.

modules.cost: linear in the number of control points; [`homs`] and [`split`] make one allocation each.
modules.does: a knot operation returns a [`Changed`] value: the new curve, curves or surface, and `deviation`, an upper bound on the distance between the new shape and the old one at every parameter of the domain. For an operation that is exact in real arithmetic (insertion, refinement, Bezier extraction, degree elevation) the deviation is only the rounding of the new control points; for an approximation (knot removal, degree reduction) it also holds the approximation's own error. [`rounding`] turns the interval run of an operation (`crate::arith`) into the rounding part: chapter 7's rule that a conversion "returns the NURBS, whether it is exact, and its maximum error".
guarantees: **Certified.** For a nonrational result with control points Q̂ whose exact counterparts are Q, the shapes differ by Σ `N_i`·(`Q̂_i` − `Q_i`), at most `max_i` |`Q̂_i` − `Q_i`| because the basis functions are not negative and sum to 1; the interval run bounds each |`Q̂_i` − `Q_i`| by the Euclidean norm of its interval's widths, rounded up. For a rational result, S = A / W and Ŝ − S = ((Â − A) − S·(Ŵ − W)) / Ŵ, so |Ŝ − S| ≤ (max |Δ(w·Q)| + `P_max`·max |Δw|) / min ŵ, where `P_max` bounds |S| (the largest distance of an input control point from the origin, by the convex hull property) and min ŵ is the smallest weight of the result, which bounds Ŵ below. Every step is computed in interval arithmetic and its upper bound taken.
**Refused, never weak.** A result with a weight that is not positive is [`NurbsError::Weight`]; a bound that is not finite is [`NurbsError::NotFinite`].
modules.job: What every knot operation returns, and the certified bound on how far its result lies from the curve or surface it was given.

method.text: the partition of unity and the convex hull property of B-splines (The NURBS Book, 2nd ed., Springer (1997), properties P2.4, P3.4 and P4.4, <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-59223-2>), with interval arithmetic for every bound (`crate::arith`).

modules.cost: constant; nothing allocates.
modules.does: one algorithm serves 2D and 3D (chapter 7: "One curve family serves 2D and 3D"). Curves and surfaces are generic over the dimension D and store coordinates as `[f64; D]`; [`Point`] converts `geom-math`'s [`F2`] and [`F3`], and arrays, to and from those coordinates.
guarantees: **Exact both ways.** `coords` copies the components, and `from_coords` builds the point from them unchanged.
**Finite.** `from_coords` refuses a coordinate that is NaN or infinite with [`NurbsError::NotFinite`], as `geom-math`'s constructors do.
modules.job: The control points the NURBS algorithms accept and return: `geom-math`'s finite points in two and three dimensions, and plain coordinate arrays.

method.none: a trait and its implementations, which only copy components.

modules.cost: a product of degrees (p1, q1) and (p2, q2) takes O((p1 + 1)(p2 + 1)(q1 + 1)(q2 + 1)·D) interval operations; a rational normal patch three products of degree (3p − 1, 3q − 1); one allocation per result, charged first.
modules.does: the product of two polynomials in Bernstein form is a polynomial of the summed degree in Bernstein form, coefficient k being Σ C(p, i)·C(q, k − i)/C(p + q, k) · `a_i`·`b_(k−i)` (and the same in each direction of a patch). On that rule, [`BernsteinCurve::scaled_by`], [`BernsteinCurve::dot`] and [`BernsteinCurve::cross`] multiply curves exactly, as polynomials, and [`BernsteinPatch::scaled_by`], [`BernsteinPatch::dot`] and [`BernsteinPatch::cross`] patches. [`BernsteinPatch::normal`] builds the normal patch: `S_u` × `S_v` for a nonrational patch, and for a rational one S = A / W the polynomial N = W·(`A_u` × `A_v`) − `W_v`·(`A_u` × A) − `W_u`·(A × `A_v`) = W³·(`S_u` × `S_v`), a positive multiple of the normal. [`Surface::normal_patches`] gives the normal patch of every Bezier patch of a surface, and where a boundary edge of the surface is collapsed to one point (a pole, an apex) divides the factor that vanishes along it out of the patches on that edge, so the bound keeps the normals' directions instead of containing zero.
guarantees: **Exact products, enclosed.** Each coefficient of a product is computed in interval arithmetic from enclosures of its factors' exact coefficients and of the binomial ratios, so it encloses the exact coefficient of the exact product. The binomials come from Pascal's rule in intervals, exact while they stay below 2^53.

**The normal patch's sign and direction.** For a nonrational patch the normal patch's value at (u, v) is `S_u` × `S_v`; for a rational one W³ times it, W > 0. Either way the hull of its coefficients bounds the normals' directions (the Gauss map).

**Collapsed edges divided exactly.** An edge counts as collapsed only when the surface's stored control points along it are one point exactly: identical doubles, or for a rational surface identical quotients w·P / w, compared through exact products (`geom-num`'s `two_prod`). Then S along the edge is a constant, the partial derivative along it vanishes there, and so does N, exactly: N = v·T (edge v = v0), and T's coefficients are N's with the vanishing row dropped and row j scaled by q/(j + 1) (q/(q − j) for v = v1; likewise in u). Chapter 12.9 names this derivation as ours, to be proven in its build piece: the proof is these lines and `tests/bernstein.rs`.
**Typed refusals.** Products of rational forms are [`NurbsError::Rational`] (multiply their numerators and weight functions); factors on different domains are [`NurbsError::Domains`].
**Deterministic.** Sums in index order; no fused multiply-add.
modules.job: Symbolic products of Bernstein forms, and the normal patch of a surface with its collapsed edges divided out: the Gauss-map bound of chapter 12.6.

method.text: products of polynomials in Bernstein form (R. T. Farouki and V. T. Rajan, "Algorithms for polynomials in Bernstein form", *Computer Aided Geometric Design* 5(1) (1988), 1–26) as Piegl and Tiller use them for symbolic operators on NURBS (L. Piegl and W. Tiller, "Symbolic operators for NURBS", *Computer-Aided Design* 29(5) (1997), 361–368, <https://doi.org/10.1016/S0010-4485(96)00074-7>) and `NLib` implements them; the normal patch for Gauss-map bounds (T. W. Sederberg and R. J. Meyers, "Loop detection in surface patch intersections", *Computer Aided Geometric Design* 5(2) (1988), 161–171, <https://doi.org/10.1016/0167-8396(88)90029-5>).

provenance.purpose: translated to safe `no_std` Rust from `N_BezFuncMultiplyBezCrvMatrix`, `N_BezFuncMultiplyBezFunc`, `N_BezSrfFuncMultiply`, `N_BezCrossProduct`, `N_BezSrfCrossProduct` and `N_BezSrfDotProduct`, in interval arithmetic so every coefficient is certified; the binomial ratios from Pascal's rule in intervals instead of `NLib`'s table of 18 rows; the normal patch of rational patches and the division of collapsed edges are ours.

modules.cost: O(s·p²) operations for s spans to reduce, and an elevation and a refinement of the result in intervals to certify, O(s·p²) more; the candidate and the enclosures are allocated once each.
modules.does: [`Curve::reduce_degree`] walks the knot vector as Bezier extraction does (A5.6), reduces each Bezier piece from degree p to p − 1 (the book's equations 5.41 to 5.44: points solved from both ends, the middle one averaged for odd degree), and removes one copy of each knot again, averaging the two estimates where the removal sweeps cross with `NLib`'s weight λ = α / (α + β) (`NLib`'s `N_CrvReduceDegreeOnce`). Every distinct knot loses one copy, so knots of multiplicity 1 disappear. Whether the result is kept is not decided by `NLib`'s error estimate but certified: the candidate is raised back to degree p (A5.9) and the knots it lost are inserted (A5.4), both exact operations run in interval arithmetic, which gives the input's knots and an enclosure of the control points the candidate has on the input's basis; their largest distance from the input's points bounds the distance between the curves (`crate::remove`'s difference bound, with the rational form of `crate::ops`).
guarantees: **Within the tolerance, certified.** A returned curve differs from the input by at most the returned deviation everywhere in the domain, and the deviation is at most `tol`; the bound includes the rounding of every returned control point. Otherwise the result is [`NurbsError::OutsideTolerance`], also when a weight of the candidate is not positive.

**Where it applies.** The curve has degree 2 or more ([`NurbsError::Degree`]), is clamped ([`NurbsError::NotClamped`]) and has no interior knot repeated p + 1 times ([`NurbsError::Discontinuous`]), as A5.11 and `NLib` assume; the tolerance is finite and not negative ([`NurbsError::Tolerance`]).
**Budgeted.** The candidate and its certification are charged to the meter first.
modules.job: Degree reduction of NURBS curves (The NURBS Book, algorithm A5.11), certified: the curve of degree p − 1 is returned only when it provably lies within the tolerance of the input.

method.text: Piegl and Tiller's algorithm A5.11 with Bezier degree reduction by equations 5.41 to 5.44 (The NURBS Book, 2nd ed., section 5.6, <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-59223-2>; L. Piegl and W. Tiller, "Algorithm for degree reduction of B-spline curves", *Computer-Aided Design* 27(2) (1995), 101–110, <https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-4485(95)92147-K>), as `NLib` implements it, certified by exact elevation and refinement in interval arithmetic (`crate::elevate`, `crate::insert`, `crate::arith`).

provenance.purpose: translated to safe `no_std` Rust from `N_CrvReduceDegreeOnce`, `N_BezDegreeReduceCoefs` and `N_BezReduceDegree`; `NLib`'s error estimate (Bezier error terms and basis maxima from a numerical search) and its weight range are replaced by the certified bound above, so the square root of its odd-degree estimate is not needed; a new curve is returned with its deviation instead of a flag.

modules.cost: each removal takes O(n·D) operations to copy the points, O(p·D) to solve, and O(n + p²) in intervals to certify; at most min(times, multiplicity) removals are tried.
modules.does: [`Curve::remove_knot`] removes the knot u up to `times` times. Each removal solves for the new control points from both ends of the affected run, as A5.8 and `NLib`'s `N_CrvRemoveKnot` do (`P_i` = `α_i`·`Q_i` + (1 − `α_i`)·`Q_(i−1)` solved for Q), and where the two sweeps cross it averages their two estimates with `NLib`'s weight λ = α / (α + β). Whether a removal is kept is not decided from those formulas: the candidate curve is re-inserted (u put back as many times as it was removed, Boehm's algorithm) in interval arithmetic, which gives the input's knots and an enclosure of the control points the candidate has in the input's basis; the two curves differ by Σ `N_l`·(`P̃_l` − `P_l`) on that basis, so the largest enclosed |`P̃_l` − `P_l`| bounds their distance (with the rational form of `crate::ops`). A removal is kept only while that certified bound stays within the tolerance; the bound of the last removal kept is the deviation returned.
guarantees: **Within the tolerance, certified.** The returned curve differs from the input by at most the returned deviation everywhere in the domain, and the deviation is at most `tol`. The bound covers the removal's own change and the rounding of every new control point, because it is measured on the doubles returned.

**Never worse than asked.** Where `NLib`'s test can pass a knot whose true change exceeds the tolerance (its basis maxima come from a numerical search, and its rational test uses the input's weights), this one cannot; it may remove fewer knots than an uncertified test.

**Typed refusals.** A tolerance that is negative or not finite is [`NurbsError::Tolerance`]; u not an interior knot is [`NurbsError::KnotOutside`]; u repeated p + 1 times (where the curve may jump) is [`NurbsError::Discontinuous`]. A removal that would make a weight not positive is not kept.
**Budgeted.** Each attempt is charged to the meter before it is computed.
modules.job: Knot removal of NURBS curves (The NURBS Book, algorithm A5.8), certified: a knot is removed only while the curve provably stays within the tolerance asked for.

method.text: Tiller's knot removal (W. Tiller, "Knot-removal algorithms for NURBS curves and surfaces", *Computer-Aided Design* 24(8) (1992), 445–453, <https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-4485(92)90012-Y>) as Piegl and Tiller's algorithm A5.8 gives it (The NURBS Book, 2nd ed., section 5.4, <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-59223-2>) and `NLib` implements it, with the change bounded through re-insertion and the partition of unity (properties P2.4 and P4.4 of the book) in interval arithmetic (`crate::arith`).

provenance.purpose: translated to safe `no_std` Rust from `N_CrvRemoveKnot`, one removal at a time; the decision to keep a removal uses a certified bound from re-insertion in interval arithmetic in place of `NLib`'s distance test with basis maxima from a numerical search, its rescaled tolerance for rational curves and its weight range; a new curve is returned with the deviation instead of being edited in place.

modules.cost: O(p²·D) interval operations per subdivision; a patch O(p·q·(p + q)·D); one allocation per row of coefficients.
modules.does: [`BernsteinCurve::restrict`] gives the Bernstein form of a piece over a sub-span [lo, hi] of its domain, and [`BernsteinPatch::restrict`] of a patch over a sub-box, by de Casteljau subdivision at the sub-span's ends, each a local parameter (t − a)/(b − a) enclosed in an interval. [`BernsteinCurve::value_at`] and [`BernsteinPatch::value_at`] give the homogeneous value and the weight at a parameter, the last point of a subdivision there.
guarantees: **Enclosures of the exact.** Subdivision is linear in the coefficients with weights 1 − s and s; computed with s an interval holding the exact local parameter, and every operation rounded outward, each new coefficient holds the exact coefficient of the exact sub-piece (inclusion monotonicity), so the convex hull bounds of `crate::bernstein` hold for the sub-span.
**Homogeneous.** Rational forms are cut with their weights as a last coordinate, so the weights of the result are the exact weights of the sub-piece's homogeneous form.
**Typed refusals.** A sub-span outside the domain, unordered, or a single value, is [`NurbsError::KnotOutside`]; a parameter outside it [`NurbsError::ParameterOutside`].

modules.cost: construction is linear in the control points and makes one allocation (two if rational). [`Surface::point`] takes O(p² + q² + p·q·D) operations; [`Surface::derivs`] O(p² + q² + du·dv·(p·q·D + du·dv·D)); neither allocates.
modules.does: a [`Surface`] holds two bases, one per parameter direction, and a net of (n + 1) × (m + 1) control points stored row by row (row i follows u, column j follows v), with weights if it is rational, in homogeneous form w·P as for curves. [`Surface::point`] sums, for each row of the p + 1 rows that matter, the q + 1 points against the v basis, then the rows against the u basis (A3.5, as `NLib` does it), and divides by the weights summed the same way for a rational surface (A4.3). [`Surface::derivs`] does the same with basis derivatives (A3.6) and applies Leibniz's rule to w·S = A for a rational surface (A4.4), for every order k ≤ du in u and l ≤ dv in v.
guarantees: **Well formed or refused.** A surface has exactly one control point (and one weight) per pair of basis functions, every coordinate finite, every weight positive and finite, and every weighted coordinate finite.

**Points.** A nonrational point is within `γ_(7p+7q+2)` · `Σ_i` `NU_i` `Σ_j` `NV_j`·|`P_ij`|; a rational one within `γ_(14p+14q+5)` times the same sum over |w·P| divided by Σ `NU_i` `NV_j` `w_ij`. Each inner sum carries `γ_(7q+1)`, and each product with a u basis value and the outer sum add `γ_(6p)` and p + 1 roundings.

**Derivatives.** A nonrational derivative is within `γ_(7p+7q+6)` · `Σ_i` `MU_(k,i)` `Σ_j` `MV_(l,j)`·|`P_ij`|. A rational one is within `γ_e` · `MS_(k,l)`, e = (D + 1)(14p + 14q + 2D + 12), where `MS` is A4.4's recurrence run on magnitudes (every subtraction an addition, with the magnitude sums in place of A and of the weight derivatives); each step of the recurrence adds the error of the sums, two products per term, its sums and subtractions and the division to the largest error of the lower orders, and a chain of steps from order (0, 0) has at most D of them. The value of order (0, 0) has the same bits as [`Surface::point`].

**Typed failures.** A parameter outside its domain is [`NurbsError::ParameterOutside`], a result that overflows [`NurbsError::NotFinite`], an order above [`MAX_DEGREE`] [`NurbsError::DerivativeOrder`].
**Deterministic.** Fixed summation order (v inside u, by increasing index), no fused multiply-add, no platform maths.

invariants: It only runs tasks: it implements `geom-run`'s `Pool` trait, and the fixed chunks, ordered results, ordered errors and order-free combines are the helper's, so every result is the same bits with this pool, on any number of threads, as with no pool at all (23.4, 21).

Every task it is handed runs exactly once, on any thread and in any order, and the pool is re-entrant: a task may call the helper again without blocking a thread, so one pool serves a program's per-element work and an operation's inner work (23.4).
It never panics, except to pass on a task's panic (23.4).
In a browser it starts Web Workers only where shared memory is allowed; elsewhere the kernel runs serially, with the same answer (23.4, 29.4).

It is the one `geom-*` crate that ships and may use `std`, because threads need it (the development crates use it too, and never ship); it still forbids unsafe code and carries `geom-num`'s lint posture (27).

The only published crates it may name are rayon and, for Web Workers, wasm-bindgen-rayon, each by its row of section 29.4. It names rayon, on native targets only ([`native`], piece G33); wasm-bindgen-rayon waits for piece G456, and until then WebAssembly runs serially.

modules.cost: one scope and one spawned job per task, each a small heap allocation inside rayon, and the pool's threads, started once when it is built and stopped when it is dropped.
modules.does: [`Rayon`] owns a `rayon::ThreadPool` of a fixed number of threads and implements [`Pool`]: [`Pool::run_all`] spawns every task into one scope of that pool and returns when all of them have finished. The helper (`geom_run::Exec::with_pool`) decides everything else: the fixed chunks, the order results are read in, the lowest-numbered failure, so every answer is the serial executor's, bit for bit, whatever the pool does (23.4).
guarantees: **Every task runs exactly once**, on some thread of the pool, in any order: each is spawned once into the scope, and the scope returns only after every spawned job has finished.

**Re-entrant.** A task may call the helper again with the same pool. The nested scope runs on the worker thread that opened it, and while it waits that thread runs other jobs of the pool, rayon's work stealing, instead of blocking; so a nested call makes progress on any number of threads, one included.

**No panic of its own.** `run_all` panics only to pass on a task's panic, after every task has finished: rayon's scope catches a job's panic and resumes it when the scope ends. Building a pool reports a failure to start its threads as [`PoolError`], never a panic.

**The thread count is the caller's.** It is fixed when the pool is built and never read by the helper, whose chunks do not depend on it (23.4); rayon's own environment variable (`RAYON_NUM_THREADS`) is not consulted, because the count is set explicitly.

method.text: rayon's scoped spawning, `ThreadPool::in_place_scope` and `Scope::spawn`, whose documented contract is that the scope returns when every job spawned into it, and every job those spawned, has completed, and that a panic in a job is propagated when the scope ends (<https://docs.rs/rayon/1.12.0/rayon/struct.ThreadPool.html#method.in_place_scope>), over its work-stealing scheduler, after Blumofe and Leiserson, "Scheduling Multithreaded Computations by Work Stealing", Journal of the ACM 46(5), 1999 (`doi:10.1145/324133.324234`). rayon's audit is `projects/kit/notes/G33-rayon-audit.md`.

modules.cost: for n items, at most n calls of the function, each with a fresh meter, and one read of the cancellation every [`POLL_EVERY`](crate::POLL_EVERY) items of each chunk. Room for a chunk's results is reserved when the chunk starts, since every item has a result, and the n results are gathered in the order the items run; the items past the crossing that never ran get copies of the one failure. On a pool, at most one wave of chunks past the crossing is run. With a total, add the key sort (`crate::sort`: O(n log n) comparisons, each calling `key` twice, and two buffers of n index–reference pairs, the first kept while the items run), and n slots and the n results again to put the results back in item order.
guarantees: An item's own result is computed from the item alone, under a fresh meter capped at `per_item`; only the batch-total rule looks at other items, and only at the ones before it in key order.
The result has exactly one entry per item, in item order. A broken count is [`Interrupted::Internal`], never a short or misplaced result.

modules.cost: for n items in c chunks, [`map`](Exec::map), [`try_map`](Exec::try_map), [`find_first`](Exec::find_first) and [`filter_ordered`](Exec::filter_ordered) make at most n calls of the function, each with a fresh meter of a few words, and read the cancellation once per [`POLL_EVERY`](crate::POLL_EVERY) items of each chunk; they allocate their result as items run and, on a pool, the bookkeeping of one wave (`crate::pool`). [`map_each`](Exec::map_each) costs the same, with one result per item, plus a sort by key when the batch has a total (`crate::batch`). [`scan_exclusive`](Exec::scan_exclusive) makes 2n + c additions; [`count_then_fill`](Exec::count_then_fill) is two phases and a scan (`crate::scan`); [`sort_stable`](Exec::sort_stable) makes O(n log n) comparisons and holds 2n index–reference pairs (`crate::sort`). guarantees: Every answer is decided by a serial walk over chunk results in index order (`crate::phase`; for a batch's total, in key order, `crate::batch`), so it cannot depend on the pool, the thread count or the order chunks finished in.

Every allocation the helper makes that grows with the input is fallible, so a refused one is [`RunError::OutOfMemory`], never an abort; and a phase whose items may stop early reserves room only as its items run (amortised doubling, so at most about twice what they need), never for the whole input up front.

guarantees: Every chunk holds at least one item; only the last chunk of a problem may hold fewer than the chunk size.
Chunks are contiguous, in index order, and together cover every item exactly once.
No arithmetic here can overflow, whatever the length and size, including `usize::MAX`.
modules.job: Chunk plans: where a problem of a given size is cut into chunks.

method.text: fixed-size static chunking, the boundaries of Rust's own [`slice::chunks`] (<https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/primitive.slice.html#method.chunks>) and of the chunk-size form of OpenMP's worksharing-loop `schedule` clause (OpenMP API 5.2, section 11.5.3, <https://www.openmp.org/spec-html/5.2/openmp.html>). The tests check the boundaries against `slice::chunks` for every size and length they try.

modules.cost: a phase of c chunks runs in at most 7 + ⌈c / `WAVE_MAX`⌉ waves (six doublings from `WAVE_FIRST` reach `WAVE_MAX`). Each wave of w chunks costs two lists of w entries (the tasks and the handles passed to the pool) and one barrier; the slots of the current wave, each a chunk's payload and output, are the only other storage. With no pool there is no list and no barrier: each chunk runs just before it is read.
guarantees: Whatever a pool does, the answer is right. A task run twice writes its slot once (a filled slot is skipped); a task never run is run on the calling thread when its result is read. Only a panic inside the pool escapes, and pools must not panic.
Results are read in index order, never in the order tasks finished.
modules.job: Threads come from the caller: the [`Pool`] trait, and how the helper hands a pool its work.

method.text: the superstep of Valiant's bulk-synchronous parallel model ("A bridging model for parallel computation", Communications of the ACM 33(8), 1990, <https://doi.org/10.1145/79173.79181>): independent work, a barrier, then a serial step that reads the results. No atomic counter, lock or shared mutable state is used; each task writes only its own slot.

modules.cost: for n counts in c chunks, `scan_exclusive` makes n checked additions to sum the chunks, c to turn the sums into bases and n to write the offsets; it reads the cancellation once per chunk in each pass and allocates the n offsets and the c bases. `count_then_fill` adds a count phase and a fill phase (n calls each, as in `crate::phase`) and room for the n counts. Each item's outputs are made in a buffer of exactly its count, with one `U::default()` per output, then moved onto its chunk's outputs and those onto the result.
guarantees: Offsets are exact. A total past `usize::MAX` is [`RunError::OutOfMemory`]: no result of that size can exist on this target, and the limit differs between 32-bit and 64-bit targets, so the failure is never stored.
`count_then_fill` gives each item a slice of exactly the length it counted, so no item can write outside its own range.
modules.job: Exclusive prefix sums of counts, and `count_then_fill`: how new entities get their indices.

method.text: the parallel scan in its blocked form, for fewer processors than elements (sum each block, scan the block sums, then scan within each block from its base), and its use to give each element its output positions, as in Blelloch, "Prefix Sums and Their Applications" (Technical Report CMU-CS-90-190, Carnegie Mellon University, 1990; the 1993 book-chapter version is at <https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~guyb/papers/Ble93.pdf>).

modules.cost: for n items in chunks of s, at most n · (⌈log₂ s⌉ + ⌈log₂ ⌈n / s⌉⌉) comparisons, so O(n log n), each calling `key` twice; two buffers of n (index, reference) pairs and the result of n indices; one read of the cancellation per chunk and per merge.
guarantees: Every merge writes each element of its two runs exactly once into a destination of exactly their combined length, so the result is always a permutation of the indices.
No recursion: every loop is bounded by the number of items.
modules.job: `sort_stable`: the stable sorted order of items by a total key, the same whatever the chunks.

method.text: bottom-up two-way merge sort (Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, volume 3, 2nd edition, 1998, section 5.2.4, "Sorting by merging", straight two-way merging; the book's page is <https://www-cs-faculty.stanford.edu/~knuth/taocp.html>), first within chunks, then across them. Written here rather than taken from `core`'s sorts so that nothing allocates infallibly and no comparison, even of an `Ord` that breaks its contract, can make the helper panic.

As for curves, the laws compare certified objects: enclosures of one exact value must overlap after widening by the stated deviations; the normal bound must keep the sign of every coordinate it decides; doubles must lie in the certified enclosures within a relative 2^−30 (a wrong formula, not rounding).
guarantees: **Sound.** A law reported broken is broken (two certified enclosures of one value that miss each other, a sign the normal bound decides that the exact normal contradicts, or a refusal that did not come).

modules.does: [`ImplicitBound::enclose_box`] gives enclosures of F and of its gradient over a box of points, and whether F is smooth throughout it. `geom-num`'s exact [`Plane`] implements it, F(x) = n·x + d, its first implementor; quadrics and tori come with their kinds (G65) and fields with `geom-field`.
guarantees: **Enclosures.** For every point x of the box, F(x) lies in `value` and ∇F(x) in `gradient`; computed in interval arithmetic rounded outward. A plane's coefficients are integers below 2^126, each held exactly (an integer whose double is not exact is widened by its rounding).
**Smoothness stated.** `smooth` is true only where F is continuously differentiable over the whole box; a kind that cannot tell says false.

modules.cost: a bound or enclosure runs Bezier extraction in intervals, O(`s_u`·`s_v`·(p + q)·p·q) for s spans, plus O(p·q·(p + q)) per patch cut; the normal bound three products per patch; a split O(n·m); a reversal or transform O(n·m).
modules.does: implements [`ParamSurface`] for [`Surface`]. Points and partials are A3.5, A3.6 and A4.4 (`geom-nurbs`). Enclosures and bounds come from the surface's Bernstein patches in interval arithmetic (piece G59): the patch holding (u, v), or each patch meeting the box cut down to it, its box from the convex hull; partials from the patch's partial forms, and for a rational surface `S_d` = (`A_d`·W − A·`W_d`) / W². The normal bound is the hull of the normal patches (`Surface::normal_patches`, collapsed edges divided out) cut down to the box. Conversion to NURBS is the surface itself. A split inserts the parameter until its multiplicity is the degree in that direction and parts the net; a reversal negates and reverses one knot vector; a transform maps the control points with the weights kept.
guarantees: **Certified.** Every enclosure and bound holds the exact value; a split's deviation is the certified rounding of the knot insertion; a transform's the largest certified error of a control point's image (a surface point is a weighted average of its control points).
**Exact where the operation is.** Conversion and reversal change no bit; a grid transform of control points whose images are exact reports 0.
**Refused outside the domain.** Never clamped.

invariants: **Development only.** No kernel crate depends on it except as a development dependency; the [`deps`] check enforces that. It may use `std` (chapter 27 exempts the development crates from `no_std`).

**No randomness of its own.** The kernel has no randomness, and seeds belong to test generators only (28.17). This crate never reads the operating system's random source or a clock: a seed is a test's fixed default, a seed the test fixes, or the value of `SPAREKIT_SEED`, and every one is printed.

**The same data on every target.** Test data comes from integer arithmetic only, and every word drawn from proptest's stream is a whole `u64`, so a seed gives the same inputs on every target, 32-bit and 64-bit, and only the kernel's results can differ. Golden hashes in [`grid`] and [`prop`] check it, and CI runs them natively and under wasm32-wasip1.
**The kernel's lints.** `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`, and no `unwrap`, `expect`, `panic!` or indexing outside tests. A helper fails with a typed error and the test decides.
crates.job: `geom-test` holds the kernel's fixtures, test-data generators, reference implementations, oracle clients and comparisons, and, as binaries, the CI tools: the completeness gate, the golden store, the minimiser and the triage tool
