[`judge`] applies the bars of [`crate::foundation`]: in the foundation set every line run and every branch taken both ways; elsewhere at least 90% of lines. [`check_marks`] checks every `coverage(off)` mark in the kernel's crates against [`crate::quality_ledger::Ledger::coverage_off`].
guarantees: **Test code is not counted.** Lines of items behind `#[cfg(test)]` are left out of both the lines found and the lines run, so tests cannot pad a crate's numbers.

**A line with no code is not counted.** llvm-cov can give a line holding only a comment or an attribute (`#[must_use]` above a `const fn`) a count of 0 though the function runs ([`no_code_lines`]); such a line has nothing to run, so it is left out of both counts.

**Nothing is skipped silently.** A source file that defines a function but has no coverage data was never compiled into the measured tests, and fails; so does a crate with no LCOV file at all, and a foundation crate whose code has `if` or `while` but whose data holds no branch record (the run was made without `--branch`).

**A missing foundation module fails.** A crate of [`crate::foundation::FOUNDATION_MODULES`] with code but no file of its foundation module fails, so moving the module cannot drop it from the foundation bar.

**Every mark cites a checked proof.** A `coverage(off)` mark must have a comment right above it citing `proof: <path>::<name>`, the same proof as its ledger entry, and the cited file must define that function as a Kani harness (`#[kani::proof]`) or a Verus `proof fn`. A ledger entry with no mark is stale and fails.

**Waiting lines are named, and can only go.** A foundation line the tests do not run passes only while the ledger's `awaiting_proof` names it, with the piece that proves it unreachable or tests it ([`excuse_awaiting`]); an entry that matches more or fewer missed lines than it says fails. When every kernel branch outcome of a file with a count of 0 waits so, which of them llvm-cov folded no longer matters, and the file's folding note is not a failure.
**Exact arithmetic.** Percentages are compared as integers: hit × 100 ≥ found × bar.
modules.job: The coverage gate: line and branch coverage of each kernel crate by its own tests, against the bars of section 28.8, and every `coverage(off)` mark against the proof it cites.

method.text: the LCOV tracefile records (`SF`, `DA`, `BRDA`, `BRF`, `end_of_record`) that `llvm-cov export -format=lcov` writes (<https://llvm.org/docs/CommandGuide/llvm-cov.html#llvm-cov-export>), each read by the `lcov` crate 0.8 (MIT OR Apache-2.0, <https://docs.rs/lcov/0.8.2/lcov/>); cargo-llvm-cov 0.9.1 (<https://docs.rs/crate/cargo-llvm-cov/0.9.1>) runs it. Branch coverage is rustc's `-Z coverage-options=branch`, nightly only (<https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustc/instrument-coverage.html>), which cargo-llvm-cov's `--branch` turns on.

modules.cost: O(K × (P + D)) for K kernel crates, P packages in the graph and D dependency entries, declared and resolved, with a logarithmic factor for the ordered maps; plus one `cargo metadata` run, which resolves the workspace from `Cargo.lock`.
modules.does: [`check`] reads the output of `cargo metadata` (which [`cargo_metadata`] runs with every feature of every workspace member on and every platform's dependencies in) and follows every kernel crate's normal and build dependencies through the whole dependency graph, reporting every chain that reaches `geom-test`, `geom-fuzz`, `geom-gen` or `geom-bench`. It also lists every manifest of this repository the answer depends on ([`Report::manifests`]), so CI can check that a change to any of them reruns the rule.
guarantees: **It never passes by accident.** Metadata it cannot read (a missing field, a field of the wrong type, an unknown dependency kind, a resolved edge without its kinds, or no resolved graph, which is what `cargo metadata --no-deps` gives) is an error, not a pass, and so is a workspace with no kernel crate, because a check that checked nothing must not pass.
**Deterministic.** Kernel crates are visited in name order, declared dependencies in manifest order and resolved ones in name order; the report lists violations in that order.
**Every chain is shown** from the kernel crate to the development crate, with the kind of each edge, so the fix is obvious.
**It changes nothing.** [`cargo_metadata`] runs cargo with `--locked`, so it fails rather than write a `Cargo.lock`.
modules.job: The dependency rule: no kernel crate depends, normally or at build time, on a development crate.

method.text: breadth-first search (Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, *Introduction to Algorithms*, 3rd edition, section 22.2) over the union of the declared and resolved graphs from each kernel crate, on the JSON format documented at <https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-metadata.html>. Breadth-first search finds a shortest chain to each development crate. The metadata is read into the typed model of the `cargo_metadata` crate (MIT, <https://docs.rs/cargo_metadata/0.23.1/>), which also builds the `cargo metadata` command: piece G12a put it in place of the field-by-field reading of the JSON that was written here (chapter 29.1). [`check`] takes the JSON itself, not the model, so the tests can seed a violation into real metadata as a manifest would and hand it over.

modules.cost: linear in the length of the path; [`kernel_crates`] reads one directory.
modules.does: [`place`] says, for a path relative to the repository root, which kernel crate it belongs to and whether it is in the foundation set, a development crate, or outside the kernel. [`kernel_crates`] lists the kernel crates in the kernel's folder. The mutation gate ([`crate::mutants`]) and the coverage gate ([`crate::coverage`]) both classify with these, so the two gates can never disagree about what the foundation set is.
guarantees: **One classification for both gates.** The mutation gate and the coverage gate place every path with [`place`], so they cannot disagree about which code is in the foundation set.

**Nothing leaves the foundation bar silently.** A crate of [`FOUNDATION_MODULES`] with code but no file of its module is reported ([`missing_foundation_module`]), and the bars are the integers of 28.8, compared exactly by the gates.
**Development crates are never judged as kernel code**, and a path outside the kernel's crates folder is [`Place::Outside`].
modules.job: The foundation set of section 28.8, the kernel crates the quality gates cover, and their bars.

method.text: chapter 27's rule "one folder per crate, folder name = crate name" (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/27-crates-folders.md`) makes a crate's name its folder's name, so a path classifies by its components alone; the set and the bars are 28.8's (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/28-testing.md`).

modules.cost: as each part's header states.
modules.does: chapter 28.1 puts "the golden store" among `geom-test`'s CI tools, and chapter 28.13 says what it holds and what runs through it. The parts:
guarantees: **One store, one hash.** Every golden digest of the kernel's crates is in the store; [`repo`] fails on a golden digest constant anywhere else, and every one is SHA-256 from [`sha256`].

**Every golden on every leg.** `kernel.yml` runs the store's whole current edition through [`matrix`] on each of its targets and build modes, so a golden added to the store is checked everywhere the day it lands.
**Perturbations change nothing, or the golden fails.** Every golden runs twice on two differently perturbed heaps; order-free cases also run in shuffled orders.

**Edits are visible and approved.** A changed digest without its history record, a removed golden, or any change to a frozen edition is refused; any other edit to an existing golden needs a kernel owner's approval on the pull request's head commit.
modules.job: The golden store and the determinism matrix: every golden digest of the kernel in one store keyed by edition, the one SHA-256 every golden is hashed with, the perturbations every golden must survive, and the runner that checks every golden on every target and build mode.

method.text: golden hashes of canonical outputs per kernel edition and operation version, with perturbations that must change nothing, chapter 28.13 of the kernel architecture (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/28-testing.md`); the determinism matrix of chapter 21 (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/21-determinism.md`), which follows Rapier's and `Box2D`'s determinism tests (`projects/kit/notes/G01-evidence/05-exact-arithmetic-determinism.md`, section 7).

modules.cost: the case's cost twice, plus two perturbations ([`super::perturb`]) and one parse of the store.
modules.does: [`check`] takes a golden's id and its case, a closure that computes the case's canonical output and returns its SHA-256 (and anything else the test wants to look at, such as per-section digests or tallies). It runs the case [`REPEATS`] times, each under [`Heap::shift_and_fragment`] with one of [`PERTURBATION_SEEDS`], then compares the digests with each other and with [`Store::expected`]. It prints one line, `golden <id> (edition <label>): <digest> ...`, which `golden run` reads to know the check really ran, and returns a [`Checked`] holding the first run's value and the verdict, so a test can print its diagnostics before it fails.
guarantees: **Twice, on two heaps.** The case runs exactly [`REPEATS`] times, each run under a different seed's perturbation held for the whole run; a case whose output depends on an address, on leftover state from an earlier run, or on anything else that differs between two runs in one process fails with [`GoldenError::Repeat`], naming both digests. An address-dependent case is caught on every run with glibc's, Windows' and WebAssembly's allocators, and on most runs on macOS ([`super::perturb`] says why).

**The store decides.** The digest must equal the store's for the id in the current edition; otherwise [`GoldenError::Mismatch`] names the edition, the id, both digests and the two things a mismatch can mean (a bug on this target, or a deliberate change that must be recorded in the store and approved by a kernel owner). A golden the store does not hold is [`GoldenError::Store`]. Nothing is ever written to the store from here.
**The repeat is checked before the store**, so a case that is not even repeatable is reported as such, not as a changed golden.
**No panic**: the verdict is returned, and the test decides how to fail.
modules.job: Checking a golden: run its case twice in this process, each time on a differently perturbed heap, require one digest, and require the digest the store holds for it in the current edition.

method.text: golden hashes of canonical outputs with in-process repeats and heap perturbation, chapter 28.13 of the kernel architecture (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/28-testing.md`), the method chapter 21 takes from Rapier's and `Box2D`'s determinism tests (`projects/kit/notes/G01-evidence/05-exact-arithmetic-determinism.md`, section 7).

modules.cost: linear in the two stores' sizes, with a logarithmic factor for the keyed maps; linear in the number of reviews.
modules.does: [`diff`] compares the store at a pull request's base with the store at its head and returns a [`Diff`]: the goldens added, the goldens changed (and how), and every [`Diff::refusals`] entry, a change no approval can make. [`Diff::needs_approval`] says whether a kernel owner's approval is required. [`approved`] decides, from a pull request's reviews, whether that approval has been given. The binary `golden` runs both in `.github/workflows/kernel-golden.yml` on every pull request and every review.
guarantees: **Every difference is seen.** Goldens are matched by edition, id and operation versions; every field is compared; a golden present on one side only is an addition or a removal.
**A refusal is final.** [`Diff::is_acceptable`] is false whenever a refusal exists, whatever the reviews say.
**Approval is per head commit.** A review of an earlier commit does not approve later changes, so an approved store cannot be changed again without a fresh approval.
**Deterministic.** Reports list editions in store order and goldens in key order.
modules.job: The owner-approval rule for edits to the golden store: what a change to the store does, what it may never do, and when a kernel owner must approve it.

method.text: a three-way rule check over the two parsed stores (base, head) in the manner of `cargo-semver-checks`' comparison of a crate's public API across two versions (<https://github.com/obi1kenobi/cargo-semver-checks>): every difference is classified against a written rule; the review rule follows GitHub's documentation of pull request reviews (<https://docs.github.com/en/rest/pulls/reviews>) and author associations (<https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/reference/enums#commentauthorassociation>).

modules.cost: linear in the store and in the output read.
modules.does: [`plan`] groups the current edition's test-checked goldens by crate and test target; [`Group::cargo_args`] gives the `cargo test` arguments that run exactly those test functions (libtest's `--exact` filters) with the leg's own arguments (`--release`, `--target wasm32-wasip1`, ...) and its environment (`RUSTFLAGS` with `-C target-cpu=native` or overflow checks off, `CARGO_TARGET_DIR`), which cargo inherits; [`verify`] reads a run's output and requires that libtest ran exactly the planned functions, all passed, and that every planned golden printed its `golden <id> ... agrees with the store` line ([`super::check`]). The binary `golden run` drives it, and `.github/workflows/kernel.yml` runs it on every target and build mode: debug, release with overflow checks on and as shipped, natively with `-C target-cpu=native`, and on wasm32-wasip1 under wasmtime and Node in debug and release.
guarantees: **Exactly the store's goldens.** One group per crate and test target, in store order, each naming its functions exactly; a golden checked by a file has no test and is checked by `golden check` instead.

**Nothing passes unrun.** [`verify`] fails unless the run has exactly one libtest summary, its verdict is `ok.`, it says exactly the group's number of tests passed, none failed and none was ignored, and every planned id printed its agreeing line: `golden <id> (edition <label>): <64 hexadecimal digits> agrees with the store`, read wherever it starts in an output line. libtest runs tests on one thread on wasm32-wasip1 (no threads) and whenever `RUST_TEST_THREADS=1`, and then prints `test <name> ... ` before the test runs, so the test's own first line follows it on the same output line; with several threads it starts its own.
modules.job: The determinism matrix's runner: every golden of the current edition, run by cargo in whatever configuration a CI leg sets, with proof that each one really ran and agreed.

method.text: libtest's documented output (`test result: ok. N passed; M failed; I ignored; ...`) and command-line filters (<https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustc/tests/index.html>), the golden matrix of chapters 21 and 28.13 (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/21-determinism.md`).

modules.cost: about a thousand allocations (8 to 32 for each of the 52 classes, and up to 16 shift blocks) and half as many frees for one perturbation, at most [`MAX_BYTES`] bytes reserved, linear in that count; nothing is written into the blocks.
modules.does: [`Heap::shift_and_fragment`] drives the program's own global allocator from a [`Seed`] into a layout no other seed gives, and holds it there until the [`Heap`] is dropped:
guarantees: **Seeded.** Every size and choice comes from [`SplitMix64`] keyed by the seed: the requests the allocator sees, in order, are a function of the seed (where they land is the allocator's).

**Bounded.** At most [`MAX_BYTES`] bytes are requested in all, and no block exceeds 64 KiB, so a perturbation never asks for more memory than a small test does and never reaches a size that allocators serve with fresh pages (`mmap`) and return at once, which would perturb nothing.

**Nothing initialised, nothing read.** Blocks are reserved capacity (`Vec::with_capacity`), never written or read, so a perturbation costs allocator calls, not memory traffic; each block passes through `std::hint::black_box` so the optimiser cannot remove an allocation it can see unused.
**Held while the case runs.** The pinned blocks live in the returned [`Heap`] and are freed when it is dropped, after the case.
**No panic; no allocation failure ignored.** A failed allocation aborts the process, as every `Vec` allocation does, never returns a smaller heap silently.
modules.job: The perturbing allocator: a seeded shift and fragmentation of the heap before a golden case runs, so that any result that depends on where memory lands changes from run to run and is caught.

method.text: heap-layout randomisation as in Stabilizer (C. Curtsinger and E. D. Berger, "Stabilizer: Statistically Sound Performance Evaluation", ASPLOS 2013, <https://doi.org/10.1145/2451116.2451141>), whose shuffling layer fills a pool per size class and hands blocks out in random order, and `DieHard`'s randomised placement (E. D. Berger and B. G. Zorn, "`DieHard`: Probabilistic Memory Safety for Unsafe Languages", PLDI 2006, <https://doi.org/10.1145/1133981.1133985>), applied here from outside the allocator by freeing a seeded share of each size class's pool in a seeded order; the shuffle is the Fisher-Yates shuffle of [`super::shuffle`].

provenance.name: shuffling-allocator
provenance.purpose: for its size classes and shuffling layer and to judge whether it could be used; not taken, for the reasons above. No code copied.

modules.cost: linear in the size of the kernel's Rust sources: one parse and one walk per file.
modules.does: [`check`] reads the kernel's crates under `projects/engines/geometry/crates`, parses every Rust source of their `src` and `tests` folders as Rust ([`scan`]), and returns every [`Problem`]:
guarantees: **Code, not text.** Every file is parsed by `syn`, Rust's grammar as the compiler's procedural macros read it: a call or a constant in a comment, a doc comment or a string literal is never counted, and a call inside a macro whose arguments are expressions (`assert!`, `println!`, `vec!`, ...) is.

**The named function checks the golden.** A golden's `check` passes only when its function (its path through inline modules included) exists in the target's file and calls the store's check with the golden's id itself, directly or inside a closure, not through a helper.
**It never passes by accident.** A folder it cannot read, a crate with no files, a file it cannot parse, or a store whose current edition has no golden is a problem, not a pass.
**Every problem names its file**, relative to the workspace root with `/`, and a line where one applies.
**Deterministic.** Files are read in path order; problems are sorted.
modules.job: The golden store against the repository: every golden is checked where the store says, every golden check in the code is in the store, no golden digest hides outside it, and every pinned file is unchanged.

method.text: a syntax-tree walk with `syn`'s visitor (`syn::visit`), the way `cargo-semver-checks` and clippy read Rust as syntax rather than text; the call and import forms above are this check's written grammar, as the map's headers have theirs (chapter 26.3 and the merge gate of 28.8, `projects/engines/geometry/architecture/28-testing.md`). `syn`: D. Tolnay, <https://github.com/dtolnay/syn> (a dependency, MIT OR Apache-2.0).

modules.cost: linear in the message, one compression per 64-byte block; the state is a fixed 112 bytes or so and nothing is allocated, except the 64-character `String` of [`hex`].
modules.does: [`Sha256`] takes a canonical byte stream piece by piece and gives its 32-byte digest; [`sha256`] hashes one buffer; [`hex`] writes a digest as the 64 lowercase hexadecimal digits the golden store keeps, and [`Digest`] reads them back. The hashing itself is the `RustCrypto` project's `sha2` crate. Before this module, each crate's golden tests carried a hand-written copy of `geom-num`'s implementation, which chapter 21 left to the golden store's piece (G19) to replace with one; every copy now uses this one, and every digest they pinned is unchanged, since SHA-256 is one function whoever computes it.
guarantees: **The digest FIPS 180-4 defines.** For every message, in whatever pieces it is written, the digest is the standard's SHA-256. The tests check the standard's examples (the empty message, "abc", the two-block 448-bit and 896-bit messages and one million "a"s) in pieces of every size around the 55-, 56- and 64-byte padding edges, and every message length from 0 to 130 bytes against one call.

**The same digest on every target and build.** `sha2` picks a processor's SHA instructions where it has them (x86 SHA-NI, the Arm SHA-2 extension) and portable 32-bit code elsewhere, WebAssembly included; each computes the one function FIPS 180-4 defines, so the choice changes speed, never bits. The kernel's goldens pass on every leg of `kernel.yml` with it.
**No panic.** Writing, finishing and formatting never panic; [`Digest::from_hex`] refuses anything but exactly 64 hexadecimal digits with `None`.
modules.job: SHA-256, the hash of every golden digest: the one implementation every kernel test hashes with.

method.text: NIST FIPS 180-4, *Secure Hash Standard* (2015), <https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/180-4/upd1/final>, computed by the `sha2` crate (`RustCrypto`, MIT OR Apache-2.0, a dependency, not a port). Chapters 21 and 28.13 of the kernel architecture (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/28-testing.md`) name SHA-256 as the golden hash. The test vectors are NIST's examples, <https://csrc.nist.gov/projects/cryptographic-standards-and-guidelines/example-values>.

modules.cost: one shuffle is linear in the number of inputs; [`order_free`] runs the case `shuffles + 2` times (once for a single input or none) and copies the inputs once per run.
modules.does: [`Orders`] makes seeded permutations; [`order_free`] runs a case on its inputs in the given order, in the reverse order and in `shuffles` shuffled orders, and returns the one digest they all give, or an [`OrderError`] naming the first permutation that gave another.
guarantees: **Seeded and portable.** A seed gives the same permutations on every target, 32-bit and 64-bit: the shuffle is `rand`'s Fisher-Yates over [`SplitMix64`], which draws each index as a 32-bit value for slices shorter than 2^32 elements, so the word stream and the permutation do not depend on the width of `usize`. A golden in the tests pins the first permutations.

**Every permutation can come.** Durstenfeld's form of the Fisher-Yates shuffle with unbiased bounded draws gives each of the n! permutations of n inputs with equal probability, so a failure is not limited to orders a hand-written list happened to try.

**The given order is always run first, then its reverse**, so a case that fails in its own order fails as such, and every case of two or more inputs meets at least one other order whatever the seed: for two inputs, the reverse is the only other order, so both are run.
**No panic.** An error names the permutation and both digests.
modules.job: The input-shuffle hook: a case whose contract says the order of its inputs does not matter is run on its inputs in their own order and in seeded shuffled orders, and every run must give the same canonical output, bit for bit.

method.text: R. Durstenfeld, "Algorithm 235: Random permutation", *Communications of the ACM* 7(7), 1964, <https://doi.org/10.1145/364520.364540>, the modern form of the Fisher-Yates shuffle (Knuth, *The Art of Computer Programming*, volume 2, section 3.4.2, Algorithm P), as `rand`'s `SliceRandom::shuffle` implements it (a dependency, MIT OR Apache-2.0), driven by this crate's [`SplitMix64`].

provenance.name: rand
provenance.purpose: to confirm that its shuffle draws 32-bit indices below 2^32 elements, which makes it portable. No code copied.

modules.cost: linear in the size of the store for a parse; a lookup scans the current edition's goldens.
modules.does: [`Store::parse`] reads the store's JSON text (`golden/store.json` in this crate's folder, [`STORE_PATH`]) into typed records and checks the rules below; [`Store::embedded`] parses the copy compiled into this crate, which every golden test reads, on every target (WebAssembly test runs have no file system); [`Store::expected`] gives the digest a golden must reproduce in the current edition.
guarantees: **Nothing ambiguous parses.** Unknown fields, a missing field, a digest that is not 64 lowercase hexadecimal digits, a malformed id or edition label, a golden with both or neither of `check` and `file`, a `check` in another crate than its id names, two goldens with one key in an edition, two editions with one label, no open edition, an open edition that is not the last, a history record whose digest equals the value that replaced it, an unknown kind, an empty piece or reason: each is a [`StoreError`], never a silent choice.
**One answer per key.** [`Store::expected`] finds the golden by id and operation versions in the current edition, or says that it is not there.
**Deterministic.** Records keep the file's order; maps are `BTreeMap`s; nothing reads a clock.
modules.job: The golden store: every golden digest of the kernel, keyed by kernel edition, golden and operation versions, with the record of every change.

method.text: golden hashes per edition and operation version, chapter 28.13 of the kernel architecture (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/28-testing.md`), with the editions of 26.2 (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/26-how-it-grows.md`) and the rule for goldens before the first edition in 32.12 (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/32-decisions.md`). The records are JSON (RFC 8259, <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8259>), read with `serde`.

modules.cost: constant per draw. The memory of earlier draws is capped at [`HISTORY`] coordinates and [`HISTORY`] points of each dimension, overwritten in a fixed rotation.
modules.does: a [`GridSampler`] draws coordinates, 2D points and 3D points from any [`Entropy`]: a seeded [`crate::SplitMix64`] in a property test, or a fuzzer's bytes through [`crate::ByteSource`] in a fuzz target. It remembers what it drew, so later draws can repeat or nearly repeat earlier ones.
guarantees: **Always on the grid.** Every value is a valid [`Coord`], magnitude at most [`COORD_MAX`] = 2^40 − 1, whatever the entropy, so any input decodes to a legal test case.
**Everything reachable.** Every grid coordinate, and so every grid point, can be drawn.
**The same entropy gives the same values** on every target: integer arithmetic only, one fixed decision order, and no hash maps.
**One entropy word per decision at most.** No draw loops or rejects, so a fuzzer's bytes map to a test case in one pass, and a short input simply reads zeros at its end.
modules.job: Grid test data: coordinates and points on `geom-num`'s grid, aimed at the hard cases.

method.text: the generators of section 28.5 of the kernel architecture, "aimed at the hard cases" (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/28-testing.md`), after `SolidCraft`'s fuzzer (evidence report 11, `projects/kit/notes/G01-evidence/11-vetting-suggested-projects.md`, `SolidCraft`), with Manifold's fuzzer as the counter-example whose coordinates stay between 0.1 and 10 (evidence report 01, `projects/kit/notes/G01-evidence/01-manifold-mesh-booleans.md`, section 4). Each coordinate is one of: full range (2 in 8 draws); small, in −16..=16; one of the extremes ±(2^40 − 1), ±(2^40 − 2), 0 and ±1; snapped to a coarse sub-grid (1 mm, 2.5 mm, 0.01 mm at the building step, 1 mm at the mechanical step, 2^20 steps, 625 steps) so coincident faces and shared edges are common; snapped and then moved by exactly one step, so near-coincidences are common; a repeat of an earlier coordinate; or an earlier coordinate moved by one step. Each point is fresh (half the draws), a repeat of an earlier point, an earlier point moved one step along one axis, a point on the line through the two latest points (so the next point of a triangle is often collinear with the first two), or a point on the line through two earlier points. A point on a line is exactly on it while it stays in the frame.

modules.cost: linear in the length of the source and of the run's output.
modules.does: the guard itself is `kernel.yml`, which runs every golden on every target and build mode whenever `rust-toolchain.toml`, `Cargo.lock`, the workspace manifest or anything under the kernel changes, so a toolchain or dependency change that moves a result fails there. This module proves that the guard trips. [`perturb_sin`] rewrites `libm`'s `sin` so that every result has its last bit flipped, a one-ulp change no test of a tolerance would see; the binary `guard` builds `geom-num`'s determinism golden against that copy of `libm` (Cargo's `[patch.crates-io]`, given with `--config`) and [`verdict`] reads the run: the golden `geom-num/determinism`, which hashes every function of `geom_num::math::unproven` and so `libm::sin`, must report a digest that differs from the store's.
guarantees: **The change is one bit, in one function.** [`perturb_sin`] renames `libm`'s one `pub fn sin(x: f64) -> f64` and puts a function of that name beside it that returns the same result with bit 0 flipped. It refuses a source with no such function or with two, so a new `libm` that moves the function fails the proof loudly instead of proving nothing.

**A trip counts only for the right reason.** [`verdict`] accepts a run only when it failed, Cargo used the patch (it warns when a patch is not used, and that warning is refused), and the golden printed its line saying its digest differs from the store's. A run that failed to build, or failed for any other reason, proves nothing and is refused.
**Deterministic.** Both functions are pure: the same text gives the same answer.
modules.job: The toolchain and dependency guard's proof (chapter 28.13, "The toolchain guard"; piece G20): a deliberate change to the numeric code the kernel depends on must fail a golden.

method.text: Cargo's documented `[patch]` table for overriding a dependency with a local copy (<https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/overriding-dependencies.html>), set from the command line (<https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/config.html#command-line-overrides>), and the seeded-violation pattern of the kernel's merge gate (G12): each gate is shown to fail on a violation planted on purpose.

modules.cost: linear in the map's records, the licence texts and the notes, plus sorting them.
modules.does: [`build`] takes the map as a value ([`crate::map::Generated::map`], the records `MAP.json` holds), the hand-kept licence texts under `projects/engines/geometry/notices/` ([`notices`]) and the method notes under `projects/engines/geometry/methods/` ([`methods`]), and returns the text of both files with every [`Problem`]: a ported source with no licence text, a licence text no port uses, a method note that breaks its template, a record whose method note credits another source, or a map whose headers are incomplete. [`repo`] reads the inputs from a workspace on disk and writes or checks the committed files; the binary `provenance` (`cargo run -p geom-test --bin provenance -- check`) runs it in CI.
guarantees: **One text per input.** Sources, files and notes are written in a fixed order (sorted by class, name, link and path), with `\n` line ends, no timestamps and no absolute paths, so the same tree gives the same bytes on every target.

**Every record is in the ledger.** Every `port`, `port-method` and `depend` source of the map is a row of `PROVENANCE.md`, with every file that takes it and what each took, and every method note is listed with the records that name it.

**Every ported source carries its licence text and copyright lines.** Every source a `Source:` record ports, grouped by repository and commit, has exactly one licence text under `notices/`, for the same repository, commit and licence, and `NOTICE` reproduces it in full with the copyright lines each ported file's header copies; a port without one, a licence text no port uses, a licence that differs, and an origin file whose `Source:` record copies no copyright line for it are problems ([`Rule::Notice`]).

**Every source consulted is credited.** Every `Consulted:` record's source is in `NOTICE`'s credits, with its licence, link, method note and what each file consulted it for (rule 4: a PORT METHOD module "credits every source it consulted").

**Every method note keeps the procedure's record.** A note that breaks the template, holds code, is named by a record that credits another licence or repository, or does not record a module whose record names it is a problem ([`Rule::Note`]; [`methods`]).

**Nothing generated from an incomplete map passes.** When the map's headers have problems, a record may be missing, so the check reports it ([`Rule::Map`]) and the map's own check names each one. A source the map lists that no file records, and a file's record that no source of the map holds, are [`Rule::Map`] problems too, so no record leaves the ledger in silence.
modules.job: The kernel's source ledger and notices: `projects/engines/geometry/PROVENANCE.md` and `projects/engines/geometry/NOTICE`, generated from the map's provenance records, and the check that both committed files are current.

method.text: regenerate and compare, as the map does ([`crate::map`]) and as chapter 27 keeps every generated file honest ("Generated code and data have one home", `projects/engines/geometry/architecture/27-crates-folders.md`); the ledger's content is chapter 29.20's rules 4 and 5 and its `SourceRecord` (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/29-sources-licences.md`); the notice file follows the Apache License 2.0's NOTICE convention, section 4(d), of carrying attribution notices in one readable text file distributed with the work (<https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0>).

modules.cost: linear in the size of the notes, and in the number of records times the number of notes.
modules.does: [`parse`] reads one note ([`Note`]) and reports where it breaks the template; [`read`] reads every file of the folder, holding `TEMPLATE.md` to the same fields and sections; [`check_records`] compares each note with the `Consulted:` records whose `Method note:` line names it, and [`check_code_record`] checks that the note records each of those files.
guarantees: **The template's fields, once each.** A note opens with `# Method note: <title>`, and its table has one row for each of [`FIELDS`], each stating something and none left as the template's `<placeholder>`. `TEMPLATE.md` must have every field and section too, with placeholders, so the template and the check cannot drift apart.
**A copyleft source, pinned.** The licence is one chapter 29.2 classifies as method only (LGPL) or owner only (GPL), the classes rule 6 serves, and the pinned link names a full commit.
**The sections, in order, each with content.** [`SECTIONS`] appear as `## ` headings in that order, each followed by text; other sections may come between or after them.

**No code** (rule 6, step 3). A line that opens a fenced code block (three backticks or tildes, however indented), an indented code block (four spaces or a tab after a blank line) or an HTML `pre` or `code` element is a problem. Inline backticks, for the public names a note may use, are not.

**The record credits the source the note describes.** A `Consulted:` record naming the note gives the note's licence and links into the note's repository (or, off a code-hosting site, to the same file); otherwise the note has a problem, and stop and ask an owner (rule 1).

**The note records the code written from it.** Every file whose `Consulted:` record names the note appears, by its path, in the note's `Code written from it` field (rule 6, step 5: the module, the session, and that the source was not in its context).
modules.job: The method notes of the method-only procedure: every note under `projects/engines/geometry/methods/` read, held to the template, and matched to the records that name it.

method.text: chapter 29.20, rule 6, the method-only procedure (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/29-sources-licences.md`); headings, fences and indented code blocks as `CommonMark` 0.31.2 defines them, sections 4.2, 4.4 and 4.5 (<https://spec.commonmark.org/0.31.2/>), and tables as GitHub Flavored Markdown's table extension (<https://github.github.com/gfm/#tables-extension->).

modules.cost: linear in the size of the files, and in the number of ports times the number of files to match them.
modules.does: [`parse`] reads one licence-text file ([`Notice`]); [`read`] reads every file of the folder; [`match_ports`] groups the map's `port` sources by repository and commit and pairs each group with its licence text ([`Port`]), which `NOTICE` reproduces.
guarantees: **The file says what it is the licence of.** A licence-text file opens with `Key: value` lines: `Name`, `Link` (the source's repository pinned to a full commit), `Licence` (an SPDX expression on chapter 29.2's allow-list, since only allowed code is ported) and `Licence file` (the origin's licence file, pinned to the same repository and commit), and optionally `Project`; then an optional `Credit:` section and a required `Licence text:` section that runs to the end of the file. A missing, repeated, unknown or empty key, an unpinned link and a missing or empty text are problems.

**One licence text per ported source, used.** Every group of `port` records with one repository and commit has exactly one licence-text file with that repository and commit, the same licence as every record of the group, and every licence-text file belongs to a group; every origin file a port names has at least one copyright line in its record, a run of links sharing the lines after it ([`crate::ledger::origins`]); anything else is a [`Rule::Notice`] problem.
**Exactly as written.** The credit and the licence text are kept byte for byte, apart from `\r\n` read as `\n` and blank lines at the end of the file.
modules.job: The hand-kept licence texts of ported sources: one file per source under `projects/engines/geometry/notices/`, matched to the ports the map records.

method.text: chapter 29.20, rule 4, on notices (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/29-sources-licences.md`); the Apache License 2.0, section 4(a) and (d), which ask that a redistribution carries the licence and the attribution notices (<https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0>), as the MIT licence asks that its notice be included.

modules.cost: linear in the size of the output.
modules.does: [`provenance`] writes the ledger as Markdown tables, one per class of chapter 29.1 the code takes (PORT, PORT METHOD, DEPEND), and one of the method notes; [`notice`] writes the notices as plain text: each ported source with its ported files, the origin files and copyright lines each header copies, any further credit and the licence text in full; then the credits of every source consulted; then the published crates.
guarantees: **Deterministic text.** Sections and rows are written in a fixed order (ported sources by name, credits by name then link, uses by file, notes by path), with `\n` line ends and one final newline, from nothing but the inputs.
**Valid tables.** A table cell never holds a line break or an unescaped `|`: line breaks become spaces and `|` is written `\|`, as GitHub Flavored Markdown's table extension asks.

**Nothing dropped.** Every source of the map is written, with every file that uses it; a ported source with no licence text is still listed in `NOTICE`, with a line saying its text is missing (the check fails on it, [`crate::ledger::notices::match_ports`]).
modules.job: The text of `PROVENANCE.md` and `NOTICE`, written from the map's sources, the licence texts and the method notes.

method.text: tables as GitHub Flavored Markdown 0.29's table extension defines them (<https://github.github.com/gfm/#tables-extension->); the notice layout of the hand-kept file G05 wrote, which it replaces, and chapter 29.20, rule 4 (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/29-sources-licences.md`).

modules.cost: one build of the map, one read of each licence text and note, and one read and at most one write of each generated file, plus the ledger's own cost ([`crate::ledger::build`]).
modules.does: [`read`] builds the map of a workspace root ([`crate::map::repo::read`] and [`crate::map::build`], with the known gaps) and reads every file directly under the licence texts' folder and the method notes' folder; [`check`] builds the ledger and compares both files with the committed ones; [`write()`] builds it and writes each file whose bytes differ.
guarantees: **The map's own reading.** The records come from the map built exactly as the map's check builds it, so the ledger and `MAP.json` can never disagree about a header.

**Every file, in a fixed order.** Each folder is listed in sorted order; a missing folder is an empty one; a file that is not UTF-8, and a folder or symbolic link inside either folder, are reported, never skipped.
**`check` changes nothing**; `write` changes only `PROVENANCE.md` and `NOTICE`, and each only when its bytes differ.
**I/O failures are errors, not passes**: [`MapError`], which the binary turns into exit code 2.
modules.job: The ledger on disk: reading a workspace's map, licence texts and method notes, and writing or checking the committed `PROVENANCE.md` and `NOTICE`.

method.text: regenerate and compare, as [`crate::map::repo`] does for the map (chapter 27, "Generated code and data have one home", `projects/engines/geometry/architecture/27-crates-folders.md`).

modules.cost: linear in the expression's length to parse; O(n log n) in its operands to canonicalise.
modules.does: [`Expr::parse`] reads an SPDX licence expression as Cargo manifests carry it. [`Expr::permissive`] says whether it can be met with permissive licences alone, and [`Expr::canonical`] writes it in one form per meaning, so two records can be compared. [`records`] reads the licence records of a crate header: the list items after its `Licences` line, each of the form ``- <expression>: `package`, `package` and `package`.``
guarantees: **Exact grammar, or an error.** An expression with an unknown character, an unbalanced parenthesis, a missing operand or a stray operator is an [`ExprError`], never a pass.

**Permissive means every licence of one way to comply is permissive.** An `OR` needs one permissive branch, an `AND` needs both, and `WITH` may add only an exception in [`EXCEPTIONS`], which grant permissions and take none away. So `MIT OR Apache-2.0 OR LGPL-2.1-or-later` is permissive, taken under MIT or Apache-2.0, and `MIT AND GPL-3.0-only` is not. The permissive licences are exactly [`PERMISSIVE`]: the list the development crates may take (MIT, Apache-2.0, BSD, ISC, Zlib, Unicode). The Unlicense is not on it (chapter 32.6 takes it only beside another licence), nor is MPL-2.0, which is ours and is checked separately.

**One form per meaning.** [`Expr::canonical`] flattens nested `OR`s and `AND`s and sorts and deduplicates their operands, so `MIT OR Apache-2.0`, `Apache-2.0 OR MIT` and Cargo's legacy `MIT/Apache-2.0` compare equal.
modules.job: Licences: whether a package's licence expression is permissive, and the licence records every development crate keeps in its header.

method.text: the SPDX license expression grammar of the SPDX specification 2.3, annex D (<https://spdx.github.io/spdx-spec/v2.3/SPDX-license-expressions/>), by recursive descent, with its precedence (`WITH` binds tightest, then `AND`, then `OR`) and Cargo's legacy `/` read as `OR` (<https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html#the-license-and-license-file-fields>). Recursion is bounded: nesting deeper than [`MAX_DEPTH`] parentheses is an error.

modules.cost: linear in the size of the source files read, plus sorting the crates, modules and sources.
modules.does: [`build`] reads an [`Input`] (each crate's manifest and every `.rs` file under its `src/`) and returns the map as JSON text with every [`Problem`]: a crate or module header that lacks a field of the grammar in `projects/engines/geometry/HEADERS.md`, a provenance record that is incomplete or takes more than chapter 29.2 allows, a link to outside code that nothing credits, or an error kind without a doc comment. [`repo`] reads the input from a workspace on disk (the crates under `projects/engines/geometry/crates`, and the facade `engine-geometry` and its binding crates under `projects/engines/crates`) and writes or checks the committed map; the binary `map` (`cargo run -p geom-test --bin map -- check`) runs it in CI. The map lists each crate's job, layer, invariants, sections, family, status and published dependencies; each module's job, what it does, guarantees, method with its links, cost and family; every provenance record, merged into one entry per source; and every error kind of each kernel crate.
guarantees: **One map per source tree.** The text depends only on the files read: crates in name order, modules in path order, fields in a fixed order, object keys sorted, list items in header order, no timestamps, no absolute paths (every path is relative to the workspace root, with `/`), and `\n` line ends. The same tree gives the same bytes on every target.
**Every problem names its file and field.** A [`Problem`] carries the file's path, the [`Rule`] (the field of the grammar) and what to write; nothing stops at the first problem.

**Known gaps are visible, exact and cannot rot.** A problem listed in [`GAPS`] (or the gaps a test passes) by its file, rule and exact message is not reported, but the map lists the gap with its reason; any other problem in the same file and rule is still reported, and a gap that no longer occurs is itself a problem ([`Rule::GapStale`]), as the scaffold check's header gaps work.

**One record per source.** Records are merged by how the source was taken and the source's link without its fragment, so one file at one commit is one source whatever line range a header shows; two headers that give one source different licences are a problem in each, not a silent choice (29.20, rule 1).
**The map is built even when headers are incomplete**, with `null` or empty fields, so a person can regenerate it and read what is missing; the check fails on any problem.
modules.job: The map for people and AI: `projects/engines/geometry/MAP.json`, generated from the crate and module headers of every crate of the geometry kernel, and the check that every header is complete and the committed map is current.

method.text: regenerate and compare, the way the kernel keeps every generated file honest (chapter 27, "Generated code and data have one home", `projects/engines/geometry/architecture/27-crates-folders.md`), and the way Clippy's `cargo dev update_lints` and rust-analyzer's tidy tests keep their generated lint lists and module documentation current; headers are read by the written grammar ([`header`]), never by guessing, as rustc's tidy reads its error-code registry rather than the compiler's messages (<https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/1731faea0da5b4ebf881d8e53f98066c17a74711/src/tools/tidy/src/error_codes.rs>). rustdoc's JSON output would give the same doc text with resolved items, but it needs a nightly compiler and its format changes with every breaking release (`FORMAT_VERSION` 61 at <https://github.com/rust-lang/rustdoc-types/blob/2e63bdc44b94e86fe12d6e0034d1ed9c2ac6e9dc/src/lib.rs>), so the map reads the source, which the pinned stable toolchain can always do. Each crate's `Cargo.toml` is parsed by the `toml` crate (MIT OR Apache-2.0, <https://docs.rs/toml/0.9.6/toml/>), the TOML 1.0 reader of the toml-rs project that cargo's own manifest reading is built on; piece G12a put it in place of a line reader (chapter 29.1).

provenance.name: rustc's tidy
provenance.purpose: for reading a catalogue from one registry and its lists of known exemptions. No code copied.

provenance.name: `rustdoc-types`
provenance.purpose: for what rustdoc's JSON format holds and how it is versioned, to decide not to use it. No code copied.

modules.cost: linear in the expression's length, times a search of the tables, which are fixed.
modules.does: [`of`] reads a licence as a provenance record writes it (an SPDX expression, or `public domain`) and returns its [`Class`]: on the allow-list (code may be ported), readable but never ported, readable only under the method-only procedure, readable only with an owner's yes, or never read. A licence identifier the table does not classify is an error naming it, so a record cannot pass with a word that is no licence (`TBD`, `unknown`, a file name).
guarantees: **Chapter 29.2's table, exactly.** [`ALLOWED`] is 29.2's allow-list ("these SPDX identifiers, and no others, may appear ... in a ported file"), with `Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception` its one exception form. LGPL in any version, with or without exceptions, is read only under the method-only procedure (rule 6); GPL in any version, with or without exceptions, is not read unless a kernel owner allowed it, and then under rule 6; AGPL, non-commercial terms and custom terms (any `LicenseRef-`) are never read. [`READABLE`] are the documentation and data licences 29.2 and rule 9 name, and `public domain`, which 29.2 takes as PORT METHOD only.

**Real identifiers only.** Every identifier in the tables is on the SPDX License List 3.29.0, deprecated forms included, as consulted below; an identifier outside the tables is [`Unclassified`], never a pass, and adding one needs a row in 29.2 first (rule 1: a source not in the ledger gets a row; rule 11: an unclear licence is a reason to stop and ask).

**A choice takes the most permissive way; a conjunction the strictest.** An `OR` is read as its most permissive operand (rule 3: "we take the permissive option"), an `AND` as its strictest (rule 1: "the strictest applies"), and an unclassified identifier anywhere makes the whole expression unclassified.
modules.job: Chapter 29.2's licence classes: what the kernel may do with code under a licence, read from a provenance record's licence expression.

method.text: chapter 29.2's table and allow-list and 29.20's rules 1, 3, 4 and 6 (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/29-sources-licences.md`), applied to the parse tree of an SPDX license expression ([`crate::licence::Expr`], SPDX specification 2.3, annex D, <https://spdx.github.io/spdx-spec/v2.3/SPDX-license-expressions/>).

provenance.name: SPDX License List 3.29.0
provenance.purpose: to check that every identifier in the tables below is a real SPDX licence identifier, and to list the deprecated GPL, LGPL and AGPL forms and the non-commercial licences.

modules.cost: linear in the number of tokens, times a search of the crate's error type names.
modules.does: [`find`] reads one source file's tokens ([`crate::map::rust`]) and returns every public enum that is an error type, declared at the top level of the file, with its doc comment, whether it is `#[non_exhaustive]`, and each variant's name, shape and doc comment. An enum is an error type when its name contains `Error` (`NumError`, and chapter 22's `ErrorKind`, `OpErrorDetail` and `IntersectError` when they arrive), or when its crate implements a trait named `Error` for it or names it as the error of a `Result<_, E>` anywhere ([`crate::map::items`]), so a family's own detail enum is found whatever it is called. Items under `#[cfg(test)]` are skipped whole.
guarantees: **Found or reported.** A public error enum inside a function, an inline module or any other block that is not a `#[cfg(test)]` item is reported ([`Rule::ErrorEnum`]): error enums are declared at the top level of a module file, where the map finds them.
**Every kind explained.** An error enum or a variant without a doc comment is reported ([`Rule::ErrorDoc`]), because the catalogue of 26.3 explains every error the kernel can return.

**Only real code.** The scan runs on tokens, so an enum inside a comment, a string or a doc example is never found; `pub(crate)` and private enums are not part of the crate's interface and are not listed.
modules.job: Finding a kernel crate's error kinds: the public error enums in its source, with every variant and its doc comment.

method.text: a single pass over the token stream at nesting depth zero, reading attributes (`#[...]`), outer doc comments and `pub enum` items, with bracket depth counted over `()`, `[]` and `{}`, the way Clippy's development tool finds `declare_clippy_lint!` items with a token cursor rather than a full parser (<https://github.com/rust-lang/rust-clippy/blob/3583eb8a9ae1161bd7d80907acfa09b3612a93f9/clippy_dev/src/parse/cursor.rs>). Item syntax follows The Rust Reference on enumerations (<https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/enumerations.html>) and attributes (<https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/attributes.html>).

provenance.name: Clippy's `clippy_dev` token cursor
provenance.purpose: for the approach of finding declarations with a token cursor. No code copied.

modules.cost: linear in the length of the header for each field read.
modules.does: [`Header::parse`] takes the `//!` lines that open a file. [`Header::blocks`] splits them into paragraphs, lists and provenance records. [`crate_fields`] reads a crate header's summary, job, layer, invariants, sections, family and status; [`module_fields`] reads a module header's summary, what it does, guarantees, method, cost and family. Each returns the fields it found and a problem for every required field that is missing, malformed or a placeholder ([`PLACEHOLDERS`]).
guarantees: **The written grammar, exactly.** Every label, form and rule here is the one `projects/engines/geometry/HEADERS.md` states, and its seeded fixtures (`tests/map_seeded.rs`) hold each one. A field counts only when written in that grammar, with one of its closed set of labels, so a header cannot pass by mentioning a word in passing or by a label that denies the field (`What this module never guarantees:`).

**G09's four crate fields, found where G09 finds them.** Job, Layer, Invariants and Sections are located as the scaffold check in `engine-geometry` (`tests/scaffold/header.rs`) locates them: paragraphs are runs of non-blank lines, sentences open a paragraph or follow ". ", the same labels count, the layer is the first `Layer` sentence whose word is `Development` or a number, and the invariants follow the first line that opens a paragraph with `Invariants`. So a crate header states a field for one check exactly when it states it for the other (one difference: this reader skips a leading byte-order mark, which G09's does not). This reader then checks what the fields hold, which G09's leaves to its crate table: a job and every invariant state something, and the layer is in range and fits the crate's kind.
**Deterministic and total.** No input panics; every field is the first one written, in header order, and a module field written twice is a problem rather than a silent choice.
modules.job: Reading a file's `//!` header: its blocks, and the crate and module fields of its grammar.

method.text: line classification and block grouping as in `CommonMark`'s two-phase parsing strategy (block structure first, inline text after, <https://spec.commonmark.org/0.31.2/#appendix-a-parsing-strategy>), restricted to what headers use: paragraphs, `- ` list items with indented continuation lines, fenced code blocks, and the line-level provenance records of chapter 29.20 (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/29-sources-licences.md`). Sentence splitting and the crate fields' positions follow G09's reader so the two checks agree.

modules.cost: linear in the number of tokens, plus one forward look per `impl`, `fn` and `Result`, each to the end of its header.
modules.does: [`scan`] walks one file's tokens ([`crate::map::rust`]) and returns its [`Items`]: whether it declares any item other than `mod` and `use` lines (a crate root that does is a module too, with a module's fields); every function with a body that is not part of a trait implementation (a module that defines one implements an algorithm, so `Method: none` does not fit it); every type a trait implementation of `Error` is for, and every type a `Result<_, E>` names as its error (so an error enum is found by what it is, whatever its name); and every outer doc comment (so a link to outside code in an item's documentation needs a credit as one in the header does). Items under `#[cfg(test)]` are skipped whole.
guarantees: **Only real code.** The scan runs on tokens, so text in comments, strings and doc examples is never read as an item; `fn` in a type (`fn(&[u8]) -> u8`) is not a function.
**A trait implementation is told from an inherent one by its `for`.** `impl Trait for Type` bodies are trait implementations; `for<'a>` (a higher-ranked bound) is not that `for`.
**Total.** No input panics, and every step moves forward, so the scan ends.
modules.job: What a source file declares, read from its tokens: whether it holds code, the functions it defines outside trait implementations, the types it uses as errors, and its doc comments.

method.text: a single pass over the token stream with a stack of open braces, as the error-kind scanner ([`crate::map::errors`]) reads items, after the item grammar of The Rust Reference: implementations (<https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/implementations.html>), functions (<https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/functions.html>) and the `Result` type's parameters (<https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/result/enum.Result.html>).

modules.cost: linear in the length of the text written.
modules.does: [`Value`] is a JSON value whose objects are ordered maps; [`Value::to_text`] writes it as JSON text indented by two spaces, with `\n` line ends and a final newline.
guarantees: **One text per value.** Object keys are written in byte order (a `BTreeMap`), arrays in their own order, and nothing depends on the platform, a clock or a hash seed, so the same map is the same bytes on every target.

**Valid JSON.** Strings are escaped as RFC 8259 section 7 requires: `"` and `\` with a backslash, control characters below U+0020 as `\b`, `\f`, `\n`, `\r`, `\t` or `\u00XX`; every other character is written as its UTF-8 bytes, as section 8.1 asks of JSON exchanged between systems. The tests read every text back with `serde_json`.
**No floating point.** Numbers are unsigned integers, so no rounding or formatting choice can differ between targets.
modules.job: Writing JSON deterministically: one text per value, the same bytes on every target.

method.text: the JSON grammar of RFC 8259 (<https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8259>), written by recursive descent over the value; recursion is as deep as the value is nested, which the map builds at most six levels deep.

modules.cost: linear in the length of the text.
modules.does: [`find`] lists the links in a text: web addresses (`https://…` and `http://…`, bare, in `<…>` or in a Markdown link), DOIs written `doi:10.<registrant>/<suffix>`, and repository paths in backticks under [`REPO_LINK_ROOTS`] that end in `.md` or `/`. [`view`] reads a web address on a code-hosting site into the repository it names, the revision it names and whether it shows code. [`is_code`] says whether an address points at source code, [`is_pinned`] whether it names a full commit, [`repository`] which repository or file it belongs to (so a credit line can be matched with a link elsewhere), and [`source_key`] which source it is (one file at one revision, whatever line range it shows).
guarantees: **Every link once, in order.** A link that appears twice is listed once, at its first place.
**Trailing punctuation is not part of a link.** A sentence's `.`, `,`, `;` or `:` after an address, and the `>` or `)` that closes it, are left out.

**A DOI is a whole DOI.** `doi:10.` must be followed by a registrant code (digits, with sub-divisions after full stops), a `/` and a suffix that is not empty; a `doi.org` address is a link only when its path is such a DOI.

**Every code host's layout, read by its revision slot.** A link is on a code-hosting site when its host is one of [`FORGE_HOSTS`], starts with one of [`FORGE_HOST_PREFIXES`] or ends with one of [`FORGE_HOST_SUFFIXES`], or when its path or query has one of the layouts below, on any host. It is pinned when the revision slot of its layout, and only that slot, is a full commit name: 40 hexadecimal digits for SHA-1 or 64 for SHA-256, in lower case. - GitHub's layout, shared by Gitea, Forgejo, Codeberg, Gitee, Bitbucket, sourcehut and `SourceForge`: `<owner>/<repository>/<view>/<revision>/<path>`, a view one of [`VIEWS`] (Gitea's `src/commit/<revision>`, `src/branch/…` and `src/tag/…` included); `raw.githubusercontent.com/<owner>/<repository>/<revision>/<path>`; and gists, `gist.github.com/<user>/<id>/<revision>`. - GitLab's, on any host: `<group>/…/<repository>/-/<view>/<revision>/<path>`. - Gitiles' (`*.googlesource.com` and any Gerrit host): `<repository>/+/<revision>/<path>`, and its other `+` commands. - cgit's (hosts starting `cgit.` or `git.`, or a `cgit` path segment): `<repository>/<view>/<path>?id=<revision>`; without an `id`, GitHub's revision slot. - gitweb's, on any host: `?p=<repository>;a=<action>;f=<path>;hb=<revision>`.

**Conservative about code.** An address is code when it shows a file, folder, commit or diff in a repository on a code-hosting site, when it is a gist, or when its last path segment, or a value in its query, ends in one of [`CODE_EXTENSIONS`] (`.rs.html` and other source pages included). A project's home page, a paper or a documentation page is not.
modules.job: Links in header text: finding them, telling a link to source code from a link to a paper, reading where a link points inside a repository on a code-hosting site, and whether it is pinned to a commit.

method.text: URI syntax per RFC 3986 (<https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3986>), reduced to what a header holds: an address runs from its scheme to the first space, quote, backtick, `<`, `>`, `)` or `]`; its query is split at `&` and `;`. The DOI syntax is ISO 26324's, as the DOI Foundation states it (<https://www.doi.org/the-identifier/what-is-a-doi/>): a prefix `10.` and a registrant code, a `/`, and a suffix. The code-hosting layouts are those of npm's `hosted-git-info` (its templates for GitHub, Bitbucket, GitLab, gists and sourcehut, consulted below), Gitiles' view commands (consulted below), gitweb's `p`, `h` and `hb` parameters (gitweb.conf(5), <https://git-scm.com/docs/gitweb.conf>), and cgit's `id` parameter as cgit sites write it. A commit is pinned when it is a full Git object name (Git's hash-function transition, <https://git-scm.com/docs/hash-function-transition>).

modules.cost: linear in the header's and the doc comments' length, times the number of records for the credit check.
modules.does: [`read`] parses a header's provenance records ([`crate::map::header::Block::Record`]) into [`Record`]s and its licence line, and reports every record that is incomplete or takes more than chapter 29.2 allows, and every link to source code in the header's other text or in the file's doc comments that no record credits.
guarantees: **A `Source:` record is the whole notice, of code 29.2 lets us port.** It reads `Source: PORT from <name>, <licence>,` with a licence met by 29.2's allow-list ([`classes::Class::Allowed`]), a link pinned to a full commit, at least one copyright line (a line before `Changed for Spare Kit:` that opens with `Copyright`, `©`, `(c)` or `SPDX-FileCopyrightText:`, as the REUSE specification writes copyright notices), and a `Changed for Spare Kit: ` line that says what changed; the header carries an `SPDX-License-Identifier:` line met by the allow-list whose expression is that licence or has it as an `AND` operand. Anything else is a [`Rule::Source`] or [`Rule::Spdx`] problem.

**A `Consulted:` record names a real licence and a read 29.2 allows.** It reads `Consulted: <name>, <licence>, <link>, <what for>`, the link a web address or a DOI; the licence is classified by [`classes`] (an identifier 29.2 does not classify is a problem); a link on a code-hosting site is pinned to a full commit; and code under a licence 29.2 never lets us read (AGPL, non-commercial or custom terms) is a problem, while LGPL code, and GPL code an owner allowed, carry a `Method note:` line naming the method-only procedure's note under `projects/engines/geometry/methods/` (rule 6). Anything else is a [`Rule::Consulted`] problem.
**A module that ports nothing is ours.** Without a `Source:` record, an `SPDX-License-Identifier:` line, if any, is `MPL-2.0` (29.20, rule 4: "A PORT METHOD module is MPL-2.0 and ours").

**Every link to outside code is credited.** A link to source code ([`links::is_code`]) anywhere else in the header or in the file's doc comments needs a `Source:` or `Consulted:` record in the same header for the same repository (on a code-hosting site) or the same file (elsewhere), and a commit named by an abbreviated name (the word "commit" and its first seven to 39 hexadecimal digits) is a source read but not credited with a pinned link; either is a [`Rule::Uncredited`] problem.
modules.job: The provenance lines of a header: `Source:` for a ported file, `Consulted:` for a source a module consulted, `SPDX-License-Identifier:`, and the rule that every link to outside code is credited.

method.text: the header forms of chapter 29.20, rule 4, the `SourceRecord` it proposes and the classes of 29.2 (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/29-sources-licences.md`); SPDX license expressions per the SPDX specification 2.3, annex D (<https://spdx.github.io/spdx-spec/v2.3/SPDX-license-expressions/>); the `SPDX-License-Identifier:` line per its annex E (<https://spdx.github.io/spdx-spec/v2.3/using-SPDX-short-identifiers-in-source-files/>); the copyright notice's opening words per the REUSE specification 3.3 (<https://reuse.software/spec-3.3/>), with `(c)` added because an origin's lines are copied exactly, however they open.

modules.cost: one listing of each folder under the crates' `src/` folders, one read of each manifest and source file, and one listing per component of each repository path a header links to, plus the map's own cost ([`crate::map::build`]).
modules.does: [`read`] lists the crate folders under `projects/engines/geometry/crates` of a workspace root, and the facade `engine-geometry` and its binding crates `engine-geometry-*` under `projects/engines/crates`, and reads each one's `Cargo.toml` and every `.rs` file under its `src/` into an [`Input`], with every repository path the headers link to that exists. [`check`] builds the map and compares it with the committed `MAP.json`; [`write()`] builds it and writes `MAP.json` when its bytes differ. Both return every problem.
guarantees: **Every file, in a fixed order.** Folders are listed in sorted order and walked without recursion, at most [`MAX_DEPTH`] folders deep, so the input, and so the map, is the same on every system. A file that is not UTF-8, and a symbolic link (or Windows junction) under a crate's `src/` that is a folder or a `.rs` file, or that is a crate folder itself, are reported, not skipped.

**A link into the repository exists as written.** A path a header links to is recorded as existing only when every component is found with exactly that name, so the answer is the same on a file system that ignores case as on one that does not.
**Paths are the repository's.** Every path in the input is relative to the workspace root and uses `/`, so the map holds no absolute path and reads the same on Windows.
**`check` changes nothing**; `write` changes only `MAP.json`, and only when its bytes differ.
**I/O failures are errors, not passes.** A folder or file that cannot be listed or read stops the run with [`MapError`], which the binary turns into exit code 2.
modules.job: The map on disk: reading a workspace's crates, and writing or checking the committed map.

method.text: the default target layout of Cargo, which chapter 27's "one folder per crate, folder name = crate name" and the crate manifests on this branch follow: the library root `src/lib.rs`, the binary roots `src/main.rs` and `src/bin/`, and modules under `src/` (<https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/cargo-targets.html#target-auto-discovery>); a manifest that moves a target's root is reported by the map's manifest rule.

modules.cost: linear in the length of the source, for the lexer and for the walk over its tokens.
modules.does: [`tokens`] splits a source file into [`Token`]s: identifiers, punctuation (each delimiter included), literals, lifetimes and outer doc comments (`///` and `/** */`), each with its text and byte offset. Plain comments, inner doc comments (`//!`, `/*! */`) and whitespace are dropped. The item scanner in [`crate::map::errors`] reads the tokens.
guarantees: **Comments and literals never look like code.** Text inside a comment, a string, a raw string (any number of `#`), a byte or C string or a character literal is never an identifier or punctuation token, and block comments nest as Rust nests them: the lexer is the one `syn` parses with, which follows rustc's.

**An error, never a guess.** A comment or literal that does not end, and a delimiter that does not close, is a [`LexError`] naming the byte offset where the lexer stopped, so a file the lexer cannot read is reported, not mapped from a wrong reading.
**No recursion and no panics** here: groups are opened with an explicit stack, and every offset is the lexer's own.
modules.job: Rust source as tokens, for the map: the language's lexical grammar, from the standard lexer, so that items are found without being misled by comments, strings or character literals.

method.text: the `proc-macro2` crate's lexer (MIT OR Apache-2.0, <https://docs.rs/proc-macro2/1.0.107/proc_macro2/>), with its `span-locations` feature for byte offsets: the lexical grammar of The Rust Reference (<https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/tokens.html>, <https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/comments.html>) as `syn` reads it. It gives a doc comment as the attribute it means, `#[doc = "..."]`, with the comment's span on every token, so a `#` whose span covers a comment in the source is that comment, read from the source text with its markers dropped. Piece G12a put the crate in place of a lexer written here (chapter 29.1, the owner's direction of 2026-10-22: use well-known permissive crates rather than hand-rolling).

modules.cost: linear in the size of the metadata.
modules.does: [`packages`] reads `cargo metadata` and returns the package of every kernel crate, in name order, and [`cargo_args`] writes them as the `-p` arguments the workflow (`.github/workflows/kernel-quality.yml`) gives `cargo miri nextest run` and `cargo miri test --doc`. nextest runs each test in its own Miri process, splits the tests into partitions, one CI job each, and stops a test that reaches its budget (the `default-miri` profile in `.config/nextest.toml`): such a test passed every step Miri interpreted, and the job's report names it.
guarantees: **Every kernel test suite, with nothing to keep in step.** The scope is every kernel crate in the metadata, so a new crate or test file runs under Miri the week it lands, and no list of test names or files is kept anywhere. A test that cannot run under Miri at all (one that starts a process or reads the repository) says so where it is written, with `#[cfg_attr(miri, ignore = "<why>")]`.
**The development crates are left out** (`geom-test`, `geom-fuzz`, `geom-gen`, `geom-bench`): they never ship, and their tests start processes and read files, which Miri's isolation refuses.
**A plan that runs nothing does not pass.** Metadata without any kernel crate, or with a package that has no name or manifest path, is an error.
modules.job: The weekly Miri run's scope: every kernel crate, whose test suites Miri interprets.

method.text: the `packages[]` of `cargo metadata --format-version 1` (<https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-metadata.html>); a kernel crate is a package whose manifest is in the kernel's crates folder, as [`crate::deps`] defines it. nextest's Miri support and partitions are documented at <https://nexte.st/docs/integrations/miri/> and <https://nexte.st/docs/ci-features/partitioning/>.

modules.cost: linear in the size of the output files, plus one read of each mutated source file and of each unviable mutant's log.
modules.does: [`read_run`] reads one cargo-mutants output directory (`mutants.out`, or one shard's), checking that the run is whole; [`judge`] puts the runs of one gate together and decides, mutant by mutant, under the rules of section 28.8:
guarantees: **A gate that cannot see everything fails.** A run that did not finish, a failed or missing baseline, a mutant with no outcome or two, totals that disagree with the outcomes, a shard missing from the full run or two shards that overlap are each a failure or a [`RunError`], never a smaller set of mutants judged.
**Untested is never caught.** An unviable mutant counts only when its log shows a compiler error at a source location; any other failed build fails the gate.

**28.8's rules, exactly.** In the foundation set a missed mutant passes only as `equivalent`; elsewhere also as `harmless`, or as `known` when the base branch's ledger already kept it; a timeout only as `hangs`. A ledger entry that matches more mutants than it counts, or a caught or unviable one, or (in the full run) fewer, fails as stale.
**Reasons follow the code.** Entries are keyed by the mutated line's text, so editing that line puts the mutant before the gate again.
modules.job: The mutation gate: judges cargo-mutants' results against the quality ledger.
