modules.cost: a blossom is O(p²·d) rational operations for dimension d; a point one blossom; insertion and refinement one blossom per new control point; elevation C(p + t, p) blossoms per new control point, which this reference accepts because it runs on small cases only. The rationals grow with the knots' and points' binary expansions; no recursion.
modules.does: a [`Spline`] holds a degree, a knot vector and control points as exact rationals, in homogeneous form for a rational curve (w·P and then w), converted exactly from the doubles a kernel curve holds: every finite double is a binary fraction, so nothing rounds. Everything else comes from one function, the blossom of a polynomial piece: the symmetric, multi-affine function of p arguments whose value at (u, …, u) is the piece at u. De Boor's algorithm computes it, taking its r-th argument at its r-th level. [`Spline::homogeneous_point`] is the blossom at (u, …, u); [`Spline::point`] divides by the weight. A new knot vector over the same domain, finer or of higher degree, gets its control points from the dual functional property: control point i of a spline of degree q is the blossom of any of its pieces in that point's support, at the q knots that follow knot i. [`Spline::insert`] and [`Spline::refine`] read the original pieces' blossoms that way. [`Spline::elevate`] reads the blossom of each piece seen as a polynomial of degree p + t, which is the mean of the original blossom over every choice of p of its p + t arguments, on the knot vector with each distinct knot repeated t more times.
guarantees: **Exact.** Every value is an exact rational; nothing rounds, so each result is the exact result of the operation on the doubles given.

**Independent of the kernel.** Written from the definitions below, without reading `geom-nurbs`'s code (chapter 28.9: a different author, a different agent session), and by a different method: blossoms, where the kernel follows The NURBS Book's algorithms as `NLib` implements them. It shares no code with the kernel and calls none.

**Refused, never guessed.** Malformed input (knots out of order, counts that do not match, a weight that is not positive, a value that is not finite), a parameter outside the domain, a knot that cannot be inserted and a curve that cannot be elevated are typed [`ReferenceError`]s.
modules.job: The reference implementation of NURBS curves (chapter 28.9): evaluation, knot insertion, refinement and degree elevation in exact rationals, to check `geom-nurbs` against.

method.text: C. de Boor, "On calculating with B-splines", *Journal of Approximation Theory* 6 (1972), 50–62, <https://doi.org/10.1016/0021-9045(72)90080-9>, for the recurrence; L. Ramshaw, "Blossoms are polar forms", *Computer Aided Geometric Design* 6 (1989), 323–358, <https://doi.org/10.1016/0167-8396(89)90032-0>, for the blossom, the dual functional property and degree elevation as the mean of the blossom over the choices of its arguments; and H.-P. Seidel, "A new multiaffine approach to B-splines", *Computer Aided Geometric Design* 6 (1989), 23–32, <https://doi.org/10.1016/0167-8396(89)90003-4>, for de Boor's algorithm as the blossom with one argument per level.

modules.cost: one run of the property per case, plus shrinking after a failure, at most about 41 property runs per coordinate (a binary search over at most 2^40 magnitudes). One read of proptest's process-wide configuration per [`run`] or [`first_value`].
modules.does: [`run`] runs a proptest property from a [`Seed`] resolved and printed by [`crate::seed::resolve`], so a property test has the same seed rules as every other seeded test. [`config`] builds the proptest configuration it uses. [`first_value`] draws one case from a seed. [`coord`], [`p2`] and [`p3`] are proptest strategies for grid coordinates and points.
guarantees: **The seed decides every case, or nothing runs.** [`config`] fixes the seed, the generator (`ChaCha20`) and every runner setting that changes which cases are drawn or how they shrink, so proptest's runner variables (`PROPTEST_RNG_SEED`, `PROPTEST_RNG_ALGORITHM`, `PROPTEST_CASES`, `PROPTEST_MAX_SHRINK_ITERS` and the other limits) cannot change a run: `SPAREKIT_SEED` is the one override. That is why [`run`] drives proptest's `TestRunner` directly; the `proptest!` macro re-reads those variables after its configuration is built. Two settings cannot be fixed that way, so [`run`] and [`first_value`] refuse to draw anything, with [`Failure::Environment`], while either is in force: - `PROPTEST_MAX_DEFAULT_SIZE_RANGE`. proptest 1.12 reads it once per process into `Config::default()`, and every collection strategy of default size (`any::<Vec<T>>()`, `any::<String>()`, `vec(s, SizeRange::default())`) takes its size from there when the strategy is built, before [`run`] sees it (`collection.rs`, `impl Default for SizeRange`). A runner's own `max_default_size_range` is never read. So a seed printed in a shell with the variable set would draw other cases in a shell without it. Strategies with explicit sizes (`vec(s, 0..=n)`) never read it. - Forking and timeouts (`PROPTEST_FORK`, `PROPTEST_TIMEOUT`, read when another crate in the build turns on proptest's `fork` or `timeout` feature). A forked case runs in another process, and a timeout lets a clock decide a result (28.19).

**The same cases on every target.** These strategies draw exactly one 64-bit word from proptest's `ChaCha20` stream per coordinate and make the coordinate from it with [`crate::rng::SplitMix64`], in integer arithmetic only. proptest's own samplers are not used for them: proptest 1.12 samples a `usize` range as a `u64` on 64-bit targets and as a `u32` on 32-bit ones (`num.rs`, `sample_uniform!`), so `proptest::sample::select`, for one, reads the stream at different offsets on wasm32 and on x86-64, and every later value of the case differs. A strategy a caller builds from proptest's samplers keeps that weakness; a test whose cases must replay across targets draws from these strategies or from [`crate::grid`].

**No files.** Failure persistence is off: a run never reads or writes `proptest-regressions` files, so its result depends only on the seed and the code. A failure becomes a permanent fixture by the route of 28.16, not by a file proptest keeps.
**A failure carries its replay.** [`Failure`] names the property, the seed, the minimal failing input after shrinking, and the `SPAREKIT_SEED` value that replays it.

**Grid strategies stay on the grid and shrink towards zero.** Every value has magnitude at most [`COORD_MAX`]. A coordinate shrinks by binary search from its drawn value towards zero, whichever kind of value was drawn, so for a property that fails exactly when |v| ≥ k (k > 0) the minimal failing coordinate proptest reports is ±k.
modules.job: Property tests run from a seed: proptest with the seed discipline, and grid strategies that draw the same cases on every target.

method.text: proptest (MIT OR Apache-2.0, <https://github.com/proptest-rs/proptest>), the Hypothesis-style property tester the kernel's tests use (28.2). Its runner draws each case from a `ChaCha20` stream seeded by `RngSeed::Fixed`, and shrinks a failure to a minimal case. A coordinate shrinks with proptest's own `num::i64::BinarySearch`, which halves the distance towards zero while the property still fails and backs off when it passes: bisection, as in Knuth, *The Art of Computer Programming*, volume 3, section 6.2.1 (<https://www-cs-faculty.stanford.edu/~knuth/taocp.html>).

modules.cost: linear in the size of the file.
modules.does: [`Ledger::parse`] reads the ledger file (`projects/engines/geometry/quality-ledger.json`, [`LEDGER_PATH`]) strictly. The mutation gate ([`crate::mutants`]) matches every surviving mutant against [`Ledger::survivors`]; the coverage gate ([`crate::coverage`]) matches every `coverage(off)` mark against [`Ledger::coverage_off`].
guarantees: the file is read strictly, so a typo cannot drop an entry silently. An unknown or missing field, a wrong type, an empty or short reason, an unknown kind or tool, an absolute or backslashed path, a zero occurrence count and two entries with one key are all [`LedgerError`]s, never a smaller ledger.
modules.job: The quality ledger: every surviving mutant the kernel keeps, with why, every `coverage(off)` mark, with the proof it cites, and every foundation line still waiting for its proof.

method.text: JSON (RFC 8259, <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8259>) read with `serde_json` into its value tree and checked field by field.

modules.cost: one parse of every file of the crates that ship and of the model, and one type check of each instance's body, again when what it read changes (see [`mono`]); the analysis runs on a thread with [`ANALYSIS_STACK`] bytes of stack, because the checker recurses over syntax trees.
modules.does: [`analyse`] reads every crate that ships (the kernel crates under `projects/engines/geometry/crates` and the facade `engine-geometry` and its binding crates, [`sources`]) with `syn` ([`model`], [`resolve`], [`macros`], [`cfg`]), together with a model of the standard library and `libm` written as Rust ([`stdlib`]), and builds the call graph of the program as the compiler copies it: one instance for each instantiation of each generic function, closures as types of their own ([`mono`]), each body type-checked as rustc does it, with inference variables ([`typeck`], over [`index`], [`ty`] and [`infer`]), so every call reaches what the compiler would call. It finds the graph's recursive cycles, named by the functions they run, and the kernel's recursive types ([`graph`]); reads every `Recursion:` statement of the module headers ([`statement`]); and checks each cycle against them ([`check`]): a cycle without a stated bound, a statement that names no cycle or not exactly one, a bound constant that disagrees, a test that is missing or does not reach its cycle, and code the analysis cannot read are all [`Problem`]s. [`stack`] runs the tests on the small stack. The binary `recursion` lists the cycles, checks them, and runs the tests:
guarantees: **Every cycle is listed.** The call graph holds every call Rust can make in a build that ships ([`typeck`] states the routes, [`mono`] the treatment of generic parameters left open, and [`stdlib`] what the standard library may call back); a strongly connected component of it with a cycle is a recursive cycle ([`graph`]). Code the analysis cannot read, or whose types it cannot infer where a call depends on them, is a problem, never skipped, so the check cannot pass over code it did not see.
**A cycle without a stated bound fails**, and so does a statement that is not true to the code ([`check`]); CI runs the check in the merge gate (`.github/workflows/kernel-gate.yml`).
**Each stated bound is run** by its test on the small stack, in debug and in release, and the stack's limits are shown in force by probes ([`stack`]).
**Deterministic**: the same tree gives the same report, in the same order.
modules.job: The recursion check (piece G13; chapter 28.8): every recursive cycle in the crates that ship, each with its depth bound stated in a module header and tested on a small WebAssembly stack.

method.text: a whole-program call graph from source by monomorphisation, as rustc's collector builds it from MIR (<https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/backend/monomorph.html>), here from `syn`'s syntax trees with name resolution and type inference as rustc's type checker performs them (<https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/type-inference.html>); cycles as strongly connected components (Tarjan, "Depth-first search and linear graph algorithms", SIAM J. Computing 1 (1972), <https://doi.org/10.1137/0201010>). The rule that input-driven recursion carries a stated bound because wasm32 has no guard page follows solidcore's (G01 evidence 13, `projects/kit/notes/G01-evidence/13-vetting-smlib.md`).

modules.cost: linear in the size of the attributes; no recursion beyond the nesting of `all`, `any`, `not` and `cfg_attr` as written.
modules.does: [`effective`] expands every `#[cfg_attr(predicate, attributes...)]` whose predicate is not known to be false into the attributes it adds, and [`ships`] says whether an item, statement or expression with those attributes is compiled into the crates that ship. A predicate is read in three values: `test`, `doc`, `doctest`, `kani` and `miri` are false (test, documentation, proof and interpreter builds are not what ships); every other option (`feature = "..."`, `target_arch = "..."`, `debug_assertions`, ...) is unknown, because some build that ships may set it. `all`, `any` and `not` combine them as Kleene's strong three-valued logic.
guarantees: **Over every build that ships, never one.** Code is left out only when its predicate is false in every build of the crates that ship, so the call graph is the union of every feature and target, and code behind a feature or a target is analysed like the rest.
**A predicate it cannot read keeps the code.** A `cfg` or `cfg_attr` whose arguments do not parse is unknown, never false, so unreadable configuration never hides code.
modules.job: Which code ships: `#[cfg(...)]` and `#[cfg_attr(...)]` read for the recursion check.

method.text: the conditional-compilation grammar of The Rust Reference (<https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/conditional-compilation.html>), its `cfg_attr` expansion (<https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/conditional-compilation.html#the-cfg_attr-attribute>), evaluated in Kleene's strong logic of indeterminacy (S. C. Kleene, *Introduction to Metamathematics*, 1952, section 64; <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-valued_logic>).

modules.cost: linear in statements times cycles, plus one breadth-first search of the call graph per test.
modules.does: [`check`] matches each statement ([`crate::recursion::statement`]) to the cycle or recursive type it names, and reports:
guarantees: **Every cycle is bounded or reported**, and every statement is checked against the code it names, so a bound cannot outlive its cycle or silently cover a cycle that grew.
**Names are resolved as the code resolves them**: relative to the statement's module, from `crate::`, or through its `use` declarations ([`crate::recursion::resolve`]).
**Deterministic.** Problems come in statement and cycle order.
modules.job: The recursion check's rules: every recursive cycle has a stated depth bound, and every statement is true to the code.

method.text: matching of named sets against strongly connected components; reachability by breadth-first search (Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, *Introduction to Algorithms*, 3rd edition, section 22.2); the module-header grammar of `projects/engines/geometry/HEADERS.md`.

modules.cost: linear in instances and edges for the components, plus one breadth-first search per cycle.
modules.does: [`cycles`] finds the strongly connected components of the call graph over instances ([`crate::recursion::mono`]) that hold a call cycle (more than one instance, or an instance that calls itself), names each by the functions and derived implementations its instances are copies of (a closure counted as the function it is written in), and joins components that share a function into one [`Cycle`], since a statement names functions as written. Each cycle carries a shortest path round it, with the file and line of each call and how it was found. [`type_cycles`] finds the kernel's structs, enums and unions that contain themselves, through any field type: their drop glue recurses over their nesting.
guarantees: **Every cycle.** A function that can be re-entered while it runs lies on a closed walk of the instance graph, which lies inside one strongly connected component, and every component holding a closed walk is reported, unless none of its instances belongs to a crate that ships (the bound tests exercise cycles; the standard library's model is not checked).

**Every recursive type.** A type that contains itself through its fields' types, at any depth and through the arguments of the standard library's types (`Box<T>`, `Vec<T>`, `Option<T>`), lies on a cycle of the field graph and is reported.
**Deterministic.** Cycles come in the order of their first member's name, members and paths in a fixed order.
modules.job: The recursion check's cycles: the recursive cycles of the instance call graph, named by the functions they run, and the kernel's recursive types.

method.text: strongly connected components by Tarjan's algorithm (R. E. Tarjan, "Depth-first search and linear graph algorithms", SIAM J. Computing 1 (1972), <https://doi.org/10.1137/0201010>), from `petgraph`, whose implementation is iterative; components joined by union-find over shared names (R. E. Tarjan, "Efficiency of a good but not linear set union algorithm", J. ACM 22 (1975), <https://doi.org/10.1145/321879.321884>); shortest cycle paths by breadth-first search (Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, *Introduction to Algorithms*, 3rd edition, section 22.2).

modules.cost: building is linear in implementations and nodes; a lookup tries the implementations filed under the heads of the receiver's auto-dereference steps (at most [`DEREF_DEPTH`]), each by one unification; bounds of blanket implementations are checked to depth [`BOUND_DEPTH`].
modules.does: [`Index::new`] resolves every implementation's self type and trait and files it by the head of its self type ([`Head`]); every function's signature in types ([`Sig`]); every node's name (`geom_num::wide::I256::mul`, `<geom_num::wide::I256 as Mul>::mul`). Given an inference table ([`Infer`]), [`Index::probe`] finds what `receiver.name(...)` calls as rustc's method lookup does; [`Index::select`] which implementation of a trait a type uses (operators, `?`, `for`, conversions); [`Index::normalize`] resolves associated types; [`Index::assoc_fns`] finds what `Type::name` names.
guarantees: **The compiler's lookup.** Method lookup tries the receiver's auto-dereference steps in order (references, `Deref` implementations, an array unsized to a slice), at each step the receiver by value and then by reference, and at each of those inherent methods before trait methods; the first that has a candidate whose receiver unifies wins. Traits need not be in scope (code that compiles names only methods it may call, so this only adds candidates when two traits offer one name, and then both are kept).

**Over-approximate where types are open.** Where unresolved variables let several implementations apply, every one of them is a candidate and none is committed to; a blanket implementation applies when its bounds may hold (a bound on a type not known yet may).

**Generic receivers.** On a receiver whose type is a generic parameter, an `impl Trait` or a projection, a method of one of its bounds is a [`Pick::Bound`]: the trait's default body for it, and the blanket implementations, are what it may run from here (other implementations are checked from their own instances, [`crate::recursion::mono`]). On a trait object, a [`Pick::Dyn`]: every implementation of the trait may run.
**Deterministic.** Every table is ordered and candidates come in implementation order.
modules.job: What a call may reach: the recursion check's tables of implementations and signatures, and its method lookup, trait selection and projection normalisation.

method.text: Rust's method-call resolution (The Rust Reference, <https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions/method-call-expr.html>; the rustc dev guide, <https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/method-lookup.html>); trait selection by unification of implementation headers with their bounds checked (<https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/traits/resolution.html>); projection normalisation (<https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/traits/goals-and-clauses.html#normalization>); class hierarchy analysis for trait objects (J. Dean, D. Grove and C. Chambers, ECOOP 1995, <https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-49538-X_5>).

modules.cost: a unification is linear in the size of the two types; finding a variable's root follows its chain of unions (no path compression, so undo stays simple).
modules.does: [`Infer`] holds the inference variables of one reading of one body: general ones, and the integer and floating-point ones an unsuffixed literal gets. [`Infer::unify`] makes two types equal by binding variables, and fails, binding nothing, when they cannot be; [`Infer::resolve`] gives a type with every bound variable replaced. [`Infer::snapshot`] and [`Infer::rollback_to`] let the checker try a unification (does this implementation apply?) and undo it. [`Infer::default_numeric`] gives the literal variables nothing else fixed their defaults, `i32` and `f64`, as the compiler does.
guarantees: **Unification is all or nothing.** A failed [`Infer::unify`] leaves the table as it was.
**No infinite types.** A variable is never bound to a type that holds it (the occurs check).
**Literal variables stay numeric.** An integer variable binds only to an integer type or a variable, a floating-point one only to a floating-point type or a variable.
**`!` and unknown types bind nothing.** Unifying with [`Ty::Never`] (which coerces to any type) or [`Ty::Unknown`] succeeds without binding, so a variable keeps the type its other uses give it.
modules.job: Inference variables for the recursion check's type checker: one table per body checked.

method.text: first-order unification with union-find over variables (J. A. Robinson, "A machine-oriented logic based on the resolution principle", J. ACM 12 (1965), <https://doi.org/10.1145/321250.321253>; R. E. Tarjan, "Efficiency of a good but not linear set union algorithm", J. ACM 22 (1975), <https://doi.org/10.1145/321879.321884>), with an undo log for snapshots, as rustc's `InferCtxt` keeps one (<https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/type-inference.html>); integer and float variables and their defaults from The Rust Reference (<https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions/literal-expr.html>).

modules.cost: matching is linear in the invocation's tokens for each rule tried, times the speculative parses of repetitions; transcription is linear in its output. Recursion follows the nesting of token groups in a macro's rules.
modules.does: [`read`] says what an invocation in a function body means for the call graph. The standard library's formatting macros (`format!`, `write!`, `panic!`, `assert_eq!`, ...) become their argument expressions, each with the formatting trait its placeholder calls (`{}` Display, `{:?}` Debug, `{:x}` `LowerHex`, ...), read from the format string by [`format_traits`]; `vec!`, `matches!`, `assert!`, `debug_assert!`, `dbg!` and `addr_of!` become the expressions they evaluate; macros that only make literals (`concat!`, `stringify!`, `line!`, `cfg!`, `include_str!`, ...) run nothing. A `macro_rules!` macro of the crates read is expanded by its own rules ([`expand`]): its matchers are matched fragment by fragment with `syn`'s parsers, with repetitions, and its transcriber is filled in, `$crate` included. [`expand_items`] does the same for invocations in item position.
guarantees: **What runs is read, or the invocation is reported.** An invocation is either read as above, or, for an outside macro the check does not know, read as comma-separated expressions or as statements when its tokens parse so, or else reported as unread ([`MacroRead::Unread`]); it is never skipped.

**Expansion is the compiler's.** Rules are tried in order and the first whose matcher matches the whole input is used; fragments are parsed by the same grammar `syn` gives the compiler's fragment kinds; a transcription whose repetitions do not agree in length is an error, as in the compiler.
**Terminates.** Expansion depth is limited to [`EXPANSION_LIMIT`], the compiler's default recursion limit.
modules.job: Macros for the recursion check: what code a macro invocation runs.

method.text: The Rust Reference, "Macros By Example": matching, fragment specifiers, repetitions, transcription and `$crate` (<https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/macros-by-example.html>); `std::fmt`'s format string grammar (<https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fmt/index.html#syntax>).

modules.cost: one parse of every file the module tree reaches; linear in the number of items; no recursion (modules and function bodies are queued).
modules.does: [`load`] parses each crate from its root file and follows its module tree as the compiler does: `mod name;` from `name.rs` or `name/mod.rs` beside its parent (or from a `#[path]`), inline `mod name { ... }`, and the items of function bodies, which get a scope of their own. It records every item that ships ([`crate::recursion::cfg`]): functions, methods of inherent and trait implementations, trait methods with default bodies, structs, enums, unions, traits, type aliases, constants, statics, `use` declarations and `macro_rules!` macros, and expands every macro invocation in item position ([`crate::recursion::macros`]). Each function body, and each implementation a `#[derive]` writes, is a [`Node`] of the call graph.
guarantees: **The compiler's module tree.** A file is read only when a `mod` declaration that ships reaches it, by the reference's rules for `mod` files and `#[path]`, so code the compiler does not build is not analysed and code it builds is.

**Nothing unread passes silently.** A module file that cannot be found or parsed, an item form the reader does not know, and a macro in item position that cannot be expanded are each a [`Problem`]; the check fails on any problem.
**Deterministic.** Crates, modules and items are numbered in the order the files declare them, so node ids and every listing are the same on every run.
modules.job: The program the recursion check reads: every crate that ships, parsed by `syn`, as modules, items, implementations, generic parameters and function bodies.

method.text: The Rust Reference on modules and the `path` attribute (<https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/modules.html>), on items and associated items (<https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items.html>), and on derive (<https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/attributes/derive.html>); parsing by `syn` (<https://docs.rs/syn/3.0.9/syn/>).

modules.cost: one check of each instance's body, plus one more each time something it read changed.
modules.does: Rust compiles one copy of a generic function for each instantiation of its type parameters, and a closure is a type of its own whose body belongs to the copy of the function that writes it. [`analyse`] builds the call graph over those copies ([`Inst`]): its roots are every function, method, trait default body and derived implementation of the crates that ship and of the bound tests, a generic one with its parameters left open ([`Ty::Param`]: the copy that stands for every instantiation from outside the crates read). It checks each body ([`crate::recursion::typeck`]) and adds, for every call, the copy the call reaches with the generic arguments the checker inferred, queueing new copies. A body is checked again when something it read grows: the hidden type a callee's `impl Trait` result turned out to be, or the callables coerced to closure trait objects and function pointers anywhere, which a call through one may run. Each check of a body replaces that body's edges and problems.
guarantees: **Every copy a call can reach is an instance**, with the generic arguments the call fixes; a type nested deeper than [`crate::recursion::ty::MAX_DEPTH`] is cut to an unknown part, and a function with more than [`MAX_COPIES`] copies is reported, so the graph is finite.

**Generic parameters left open.** Dispatch on a receiver of a bare generic parameter reaches the trait's default body and blanket implementations, never the other implementations ([`crate::recursion::index::Pick::Bound`]), and a call through a bare generic callable reaches nothing. This loses no cycle: a cycle runs concrete copies, and every implementation and closure is a root of its own (a non-generic one is checked with its exact types, a generic one through its own open copy), from which the checker follows the cycle with types whose heads are known, dispatching exactly; and a cycle whose every copy is generic and that passes through a bare parameter's implementation would need a type that contains itself. What it avoids is the false cycle a generic implementation would form with its own copy at a nested type (`Vec<Vec<T>>`'s `clone` calling `Vec<T>`'s). Callables an open parameter stands for come from outside the crates read, and recursion through them is their caller's.

**A fixed point.** Hidden result types only become known and the callable sets only grow, and a body is checked again only when something it read changed; a body checked more than [`MAX_RUNS`] times is reported.
**Deterministic.** Instances are numbered in the order they are found, the work list is first in, first out, and every table is ordered.
modules.job: Instances: the recursion check's call graph over functions as the compiler copies them, one per instantiation of their generic parameters, and the work list that builds it.

method.text: monomorphisation as rustc's collector performs it (<https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/backend/monomorph.html>), here over the source with the checker's types, closures as types (The Rust Reference, <https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/types/closure.html>); chaotic iteration to the least fixed point with a work list (P. Cousot and R. Cousot, POPL 1977, <https://doi.org/10.1145/512950.512973>; F. Nielson, H. R. Nielson and C. Hankin, *Principles of Program Analysis*, Springer 1999, section 1.6).

modules.cost: each lookup is linear in the number of `use` declarations it follows, memoised per module, name and namespace; no recursion (lookups use an explicit work list).
modules.does: [`Resolver::resolve`] follows a path as the compiler's name resolution does: `crate`, `self`, `super` and `Self`; generic and const parameters; the items of a function body's scope, then of its module; `use` declarations, renamed, grouped, `self` and glob, and the re-exports they lead through; the other crates read by name, the standard library's model among them under its names `core`, `alloc` and `std` ([`crate::recursion::stdlib`]); and the standard prelude, from the model's `prelude` module. Later segments step into modules, enum variants and associated items. [`Resolver::ty`] turns a written type into a [`Ty`], expanding type aliases and `Self`, and [`Resolver::trait_ref`] a bound into a [`TraitRef`] with its associated-type bindings (`Fn(A) -> R` as `Fn<(A,)>` with `Output = R`).
guarantees: **Every alternative.** A name defined twice in one namespace (as under `#[cfg]`s that are both kept, [`crate::recursion::cfg`]) resolves to both, so a call reaches every function it may name in some build.
**Terminates on any input.** `use` cycles and glob cycles are cut by a visited set; alias expansion stops at a fixed depth ([`ALIAS_DEPTH`]).

**Outside is outside.** A path is an outside path only when it starts at a crate that is neither read nor modelled (or, without a model, at the standard library or its prelude); a path that resolves nowhere resolves to nothing, and the type checker reports it.
modules.job: Name resolution for the recursion check: what a path in the kernel's source names, and what type a written type is.

method.text: The Rust Reference on paths, namespaces, `use` declarations and the preludes (<https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/paths.html>, <https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/names/namespaces.html>, <https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/use-declarations.html>, <https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/names/preludes.html>); visibility is not checked (code that compiles only names what it may see, so ignoring visibility only adds alternatives).

modules.cost: two builds of each crate's bound tests for `wasm32-wasip1` and their runs, and four builds and runs of the probe crate.
modules.does: [`run_bound_tests`] runs each crate's `tests/recursion.rs` for `wasm32-wasip1`, in debug and in release, linked with a shadow stack of [`STACK_BYTES`] in linear memory (`-C link-arg=-zstack-size=...`) and run by a WebAssembly engine whose own stack for WebAssembly frames is limited to [`ENGINE_STACK_BYTES`] ([`Runner`]), and checks that every test a statement names ran and passed. [`probes`] builds a small crate whose tests overflow each of the two stacks and requires them to trap with the small limits and pass with [`CONTROL_BYTES`], so a limit that was not applied fails the check instead of letting every bound pass.
guarantees: **A named test that did not run is a failure**, as is one that failed or a run that trapped, so a test skipped, ignored or renamed cannot pass the check.
**The limits are shown to be in force**: the probes trap with them and pass without them, in the same build and runner as the bound tests, or the check fails.
**Nothing outside steers the build**: each run starts without the variables that change the compiler, its flags or the target (`SCRUBBED_ENV`), builds in its own folder and uses `--locked`.
modules.job: The small WebAssembly stack: every stated bound's test run there, and probes that show the stack's limits are in force.

method.text: wasm-ld's `-z stack-size` (<https://lld.llvm.org/WebAssembly.html>); wasmtime's `-W max-wasm-stack` (<https://docs.wasmtime.dev/cli-options.html>); Node's `worker_threads` `resourceLimits.stackSizeMb` and `node:wasi` (<https://nodejs.org/api/worker_threads.html>, <https://nodejs.org/api/wasi.html>); cargo's target runner (<https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/config.html#targettriplerunner>); libtest's output lines (`test <name> ... ok`).

modules.cost: linear in the length of the header.
modules.does: [`read`] finds the `Recursion:` paragraph of a file's `//!` header and reads the list after it. Each item states one cycle (or one group of recursive types) in four labelled parts, the first on the item's first line and each other at the start of a line of its own:
guarantees: **Read as written, or reported.** A part that is missing, written twice, empty, a placeholder ([`crate::map::header::PLACEHOLDERS`]) or malformed is a [`Problem`] naming the file, the line and what to write; a `Recursion:` paragraph without a list, or written twice, is one too. A statement is never read from text that is not in this grammar.
**Header only.** Only the `//!` lines that open the file are read, as the map reads headers (`projects/engines/geometry/HEADERS.md`).
modules.job: The `Recursion` field of a module header: each recursive cycle's stated depth bound.

method.text: the header grammar of `projects/engines/geometry/HEADERS.md` (paragraphs, `- ` list items with indented continuation lines, labels before a colon), which this field joins.

modules.cost: three more crates for the loader to parse, about 5 000 lines; their instances are checked only when kernel code calls them.
modules.does: the kernel's crates call `core`, `alloc` (and `std` in tests) and `libm` constantly, and the standard library calls kernel code back through what it is handed: closures (`Option::map`, `Iterator::fold`, `sort_by`) and trait implementations of kernel types (`sort` runs `Ord::cmp`, `Vec::clone` runs `Clone::clone`, formatting runs `Display::fmt`). Their real source is not read; instead [`CORE`], [`LIBM`] and [`RAYON`] are Rust written from their documented signatures, which [`sources`] gives the loader as three crates of role [`Role::Model`]: `core` (also answering to `alloc` and `std`, [`crate::recursion::resolve::MODEL_ALIASES`]), `libm` and `rayon` (`geom-pool`, the one kernel crate that depends on it, runs its tasks on a rayon pool: `in_place_scope` runs its closure and `Scope::spawn` its body). A function of the model that calls back has a body that makes exactly those calls (`Option::map` calls `f`; `Map`'s `next` calls its closure; `[T]::sort` calls `T::cmp`); one that calls nothing back has the body `loop {}`. The type checker reads the model's bodies as it reads the kernel's, instance by instance, so a callback reaches exactly the closure or implementation the call was handed.
guarantees: **Never less than the library calls.** Each modelled function's body calls every closure it is handed and every trait method of its type parameters that the documented function may call; adapters that defer a call (an iterator's `map`) keep the closure in their result and call it where the library does (in `next`). By parametricity, code that does not know the kernel's types reaches kernel code only through the values and bounds it is handed (J. C. Reynolds, "Types, abstraction and parametric polymorphism", IFIP 1983; P. Wadler, "Theorems for free!", FPCA 1989, <https://doi.org/10.1145/99370.99404>), so these are all the calls it can make into the kernel.

**What is not modelled is reported.** A path into the standard library that names nothing in the model resolves to nothing, and the type checker reports it as code it cannot read; the model is extended rather than guessed.
modules.job: The recursion check's model of the standard library, of `libm` and of the part of `rayon` that `geom-pool` calls: Rust source the check reads in place of theirs, so a call into them is checked as any other call is.

method.text: the standard library's documented signatures and behaviour (<https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/>, <https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/>, <https://docs.rs/libm/0.2.16/libm/>, <https://docs.rs/rayon/1.12.0/rayon/>), written as stubs: a library model, which the type checker reads as ordinary code, under parametricity as above.

modules.cost: each operation is linear in the size of the types it touches; recursion follows the nesting of a type, which [`MAX_DEPTH`] bounds for every type an instance is keyed by.
modules.does: [`Ty`] is a type of the program: a primitive, a struct, enum or union of the crates read (the standard library's model among them, [`crate::recursion::stdlib`]) with its arguments, a reference or raw pointer, a slice, array or tuple, a generic parameter left open, a trait object, a return-position `impl Trait`, a projection not yet resolved, a function pointer, one closure, one function item, the never type, an inference variable of the body being checked, a `_` written in the source, or a type the checker could not infer ([`Ty::Unknown`]). [`TraitRef`] is a trait with its arguments and its associated-type bindings (`Iterator<Item = u64>`; `Fn(A) -> R` is `Fn<(A,)>` with `Output = R`).
guarantees: **One type per value.** As in Rust, every expression of one instance has exactly one type; what the checker does not know yet is an inference variable, and what it cannot learn is [`Ty::Unknown`], which the checker reports wherever a call would depend on it.
**Finite.** [`Ty::cut`] replaces everything nested deeper than [`MAX_DEPTH`] by [`Ty::Unknown`], so instances, which are keyed by types, are finitely many.
**Deterministic.** Types are ordered (`Ord`), so every table keyed by them iterates the same way on every run.
modules.job: Types for the recursion check's type checker: Rust's types as far as a call graph needs them, with inference variables.

method.text: the type grammar of The Rust Reference (<https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/types.html>), with closures and function items as types of their own (<https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/types/closure.html>, <https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/types/function-item.html>), and inference variables as in rustc's type checker (<https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/type-inference.html>).

modules.cost: one pass over each instance's body, each expression's lookups as [`Index`] costs them, and at most [`MAX_SETTLE`] rounds over the obligations. The checker recurses over the syntax tree, so its depth is the nesting depth of the source's expressions; [`crate::recursion::analyse`] runs it on a thread with a large stack.
modules.does: [`body`] checks the body of one instance ([`crate::recursion::mono`]) as rustc's type checker does, in one pass over the source with inference variables ([`Infer`]): every expression gets a type, from the signatures and field types the source writes (the standard library's model among them, [`crate::recursion::stdlib`]), literals, and what unification learns; an expected type flows down into each expression (a `let` annotation, a parameter's type, a closure bound's parameters). Every call is recorded with what it calls:
guarantees: **Every call is an edge, or the code is reported.** A call whose target cannot be known (a receiver whose type cannot be inferred, a path that resolves to nothing, a method no type has, a syntax form the checker does not read) is a [`Problem`]; the check fails on any.

**Precise where the program is.** A call reaches exactly what the compiler would call for the instance's types, through the standard library's model, apart from what [`Index::probe`] and [`crate::recursion::mono`] state for generic receivers and trait objects.
**Deterministic.** One pass in source order (closure arguments after the others, as rustc checks them), obligations in the order they were made.
modules.job: The type checker: every call one instance's body makes, as edges of the call graph.

method.text: Hindley-Milner inference with bidirectional checking as rustc's typeck performs it (<https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/type-inference.html>, <https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/ty-module/instantiating-binders.html>), with deferred obligations (<https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/traits/resolution.html>) and default binding modes for patterns (RFC 2005, <https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/2005-match-ergonomics.html>); expression, pattern and statement semantics from The Rust Reference (<https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions.html>, <https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/patterns.html>), its operator traits, `?`, `for` loops, coercions (<https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/type-coercions.html>) and drop scopes (<https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/destructors.html>).

modules.cost: a handful of integer operations per word. [`SplitMix64::below`] draws one word, and draws again with probability below `n / 2^64`, so fewer than two words on average.
modules.does: [`SplitMix64`] turns a [`Seed`] into a stream of 64-bit words. [`ByteSource`] turns a fuzzer's bytes into the same kind of stream. Both implement [`Entropy`], so one builder (for example [`crate::grid::GridSampler`]) makes test data from a seed in a property test and from coverage-guided bytes in a fuzz target.
guarantees: **The same words on every target.** `SplitMix64` is wrapping 64-bit integer arithmetic only, so a seed gives the same stream on every target, in every build profile.

**Every word, once per period.** The state is a counter advanced by an odd constant, so it visits all 2^64 values once per period, and the output function is a bijection of the state, so over one period every 64-bit word is returned exactly once.
**Unbiased bounded draws.** [`SplitMix64::below`] returns each value in `0..n` with exactly equal probability over the generator's period.

**Test only, and independent of the kernel.** The kernel has no randomness (28.17); this is not the counter-based generator chapter 27 plans for `geom-num`, so a change there never changes a test's inputs. It is not cryptographic and must never seed anything that ships.
**[`ByteSource`] never fails.** Past the end of its bytes it yields zeros, so every input, including the empty one, decodes to some test case.
modules.job: `SplitMix64`, the deterministic generator behind every seeded test input, and [`Entropy`], the source of words that test-data builders draw from.

method.text: `SplitMix64` of Steele, Lea and Flood, "Fast Splittable Pseudorandom Number Generators", OOPSLA 2014 (<https://doi.org/10.1145/2660193.2660195>), with the constants of Vigna's reference implementation `splitmix.c` (<https://prng.di.unimi.it/splitmix.c>, public domain): the golden-ratio increment `0x9e3779b97f4a7c15` and Stafford's "Mix13" output function (<https://zimbry.blogspot.com/2011/09/better-bit-mixing-improving-on.html>). The unit tests check it against 50 outputs of that reference implementation. Bounded draws use Lemire's multiply-and-reject method, "Fast Random Integer Generation in an Interval", ACM Transactions on Modeling and Computer Simulation 29(1), 2019 (<https://doi.org/10.1145/3230636>).

provenance.name: S. Vigna, `splitmix.c`
provenance.purpose: for the generator's constants and the 50 reference outputs the unit tests check. No code copied.

modules.cost: linear in the file's length: one parse, one walk of the tree and one of the tokens. The span locations `proc-macro2` keeps for the file are released when the scan returns.
modules.does: [`scan`] parses a Rust file with `syn`, the parser Rust's procedural macros use, and reads every token's line from `proc-macro2`'s span locations. From the syntax tree and the tokens it finds:
guarantees: **The language's own grammar.** Comments, strings, raw strings, character literals and nested block comments are told apart by `proc-macro2`'s lexer, and items by `syn`'s parser, so a brace or a word inside a string or a comment is never read as code.
**An error, never a partial answer.** A file that does not parse as Rust is a [`ScanError`] naming the line, because a gate must not pass on a file it could not read.

**What a test reaches is read from its tokens.** [`references`] walks token trees, not expressions, so code inside any macro's arguments is read as the compiler will expand it in the common case; it follows only the file's own items, by name, and when two items in different modules share a name it follows both, which can only find more.

**A comment is a comment.** A citation is read only from a line that starts with `//` and is not inside a string literal that spans lines; the walk up from a mark passes only over such lines and over the lines of other attributes, and stops at anything else.
modules.job: Rust source, read for the quality gates: which lines are test code, whether a file has code that runs, where its branches are, every `coverage(off)` mark with the proof it cites, whether a file defines a cited proof, and what a test reaches in its own file.

method.text: `syn` 3 (MIT OR Apache-2.0, <https://docs.rs/syn/3.0.9/syn/>) parses the file into its syntax tree, walked with `syn::visit`; `proc-macro2` 1 (MIT OR Apache-2.0, <https://docs.rs/proc-macro2/1.0.107/proc_macro2/>) with its `span-locations` feature gives each token's lines outside a procedural macro. The attribute forms are the Rust Reference's (<https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/attributes.html>, conditional compilation at <https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/conditional-compilation.html>); `coverage(off)` is the unstable `coverage` attribute (<https://doc.rust-lang.org/unstable-book/language-features/coverage-attribute.html>).

modules.cost: linear in the text's length times the number of markers, all of them short.
modules.does: [`scan_text`] reads one file's text and returns every [`Hit`]: a Numerical Recipes routine name, macro, variable name, author or step-control constant; a copyleft licence's notice text; a statement that code was taken, ported, adapted or copied from a copyleft source; or an Autodesk hatch pattern or linetype name or description. [`repo`] scans every file of the kernel's crates and the facade's, with its named exemptions, and the binary `source-scan` (`cargo run -p geom-test --bin source-scan -- check`) runs it in CI.
guarantees: **Every marker of [`markers`] is found, wherever it is**: in code, a comment, a string or a data file, matched by words, so punctuation, line breaks inside a phrase and comment marks (`//!`, `#`, `*`, `;`, `--`) do not hide it. A routine name is found as a part of an identifier (`ST_pythag`, `smosPythag`), with or without a trailing number or the precision prefix of the book's variants (`tqli2`, `dpythag`); a variable name as a word or a part; a phrase also when it is written as one identifier (`numerical_recipes`, `takenFromCgal`); a description also when a string literal escapes its backslashes (`/\\/\\/`); and a constant as a value however its decimal literal is written (`1.89e-4`, `0.000189`, `.000189`, `1.89E-04_f64`).

**A taken-from statement needs a taking phrase and a banned source.** A hit needs a taking phrase ([`markers::TAKING`], its two words at most [`markers::TAKING_GAP`] words apart) followed within [`markers::WINDOW`] words by a copyleft source's name ([`markers::COPYLEFT_SOURCES`]), with no negation in the [`markers::NEGATION_REACH`] words before the phrase and in the same clause (a clause ends at `.`, `!`, `?`, `;`, `:` or `,`), so "no code is taken from OCCT" is not a hit, and "based on CGAL's widening", "No tests. Taken from CGAL." and "Not tested: adapted from CGAL" are.
**Each hit names its line, category and marker**, in the order they occur; one marker on one line is reported once.

**Words, not meaning.** A marker spelt with look-alike characters, split by punctuation inside a word, built at run time, written as an expression or a hexadecimal float, named after the phrase that takes it ("CGAL, from which this was taken"), or paraphrased is not found: rule 7 leaves the rest to review.

**Deterministic.** The same text gives the same hits on every target: words are runs of Unicode letters, digits and `_`, compared after lower-casing, and numbers are compared as the doubles Rust parses them to, which is exact and the same everywhere.
modules.job: The banned-source scanner: finds the markers that show code in the kernel's crates may come from a source chapter 29 bans: Numerical Recipes, copyleft code, and Autodesk's hatch patterns and linetypes.

method.text: matching words and short phrases of a written marker list, the method of license scanners such as `ScanCode` (Apache-2.0), whose rules are lists of words matched against a file's word sequence (<https://scancode-toolkit.readthedocs.io/en/stable/explanations/license-detection-reference.html>); the markers and their sources are chapter 29.20, rules 2 and 7 (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/29-sources-licences.md`), and [`markers`]; number literals as the Rust Reference's float literal grammar (<https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/tokens.html#floating-point-literals>), which C's matches for the forms the markers take.

modules.cost: constant tables.
modules.does: holds the tables [`crate::scan::scan_text`] matches, each with where it comes from. Nothing else in the repository's scanned crates may hold these markers, so this file is one of the scanner's named exemptions ([`crate::scan::repo::EXEMPT`]).
guarantees: **Every marker has a written source.** Each table below says which rule of chapter 29.20, or which evidence report, names it; a marker found only by memory is not here.

**Distinctive markers only.** Common words that a routine, pattern or licence shares with ordinary text (Brent, Jacobi, golden, spline; CENTER, HIDDEN, BRICK; a bare "Triangle", the GPL constraint solver Frontier, the GPL repository offsets-and-remeshing and the proof tool Gappa, which runs only as a separate program) are left out, so a hit is a reason to look, not noise. The phrases of taken-from statements need both a taking phrase and a copyleft source's name within [`WINDOW`] words, with no negation just before.
modules.job: The banned-source scanner's markers: the words, phrases, names and values that show code may come from a source chapter 29 bans.

method.text: chapter 29.20, rules 2 and 7, and chapter 29.4 and 29.6 on Numerical Recipes (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/29-sources-licences.md`); the Numerical Recipes markers evidence report 13 found in `SMLib`, `NLib` and solidcore (routine names, macros, the step-control constants and the variable names of the Cash-Karp step), and the Autodesk pattern and linetype names and descriptions evidence report 12 found reproduced in `CADCraft` (`projects/kit/notes/G01-evidence/13-vetting-smlib.md`, `projects/kit/notes/G01-evidence/12-vetting-cadcraft.md`); the hatch pattern names Autodesk's own customization guide shows, `ANSI31` among them (<https://help.autodesk.com/cloudhelp/2025/ENU/AutoCAD-Customization/files/GUID-A6F2E6FF-1717-44B6-A476-0CA817ADD77E.htm>) and AR-B816 (<https://help.autodesk.com/cloudhelp/2017/ENU/AutoCAD-LT/files/GUID-79B99823-7600-4CAB-BD12-04D5103D90CB.htm>).

modules.cost: one listing per folder and one read of each file, plus the scan's own cost, linear in the files' total size.
modules.does: [`files`] lists every file under the kernel's crates folder and under each facade crate (`engine-geometry` and its binding crates), skipping build output; [`check`] scans each with [`crate::scan::scan_text`] and returns every [`Finding`]: a hit, a file that cannot be read as a file, or an exemption that no longer applies.
guarantees: **Every file, every kind.** Every regular file under the scanned folders is read, whatever its name or extension (source, manifest, data, fixture), in every reading [`readings`] gives: as UTF-8 with any invalid byte replaced, so a marker in ASCII is found even in a binary file; as UTF-16 when the file opens with a UTF-16 byte-order mark; and, when it holds a zero byte, again with its zero bytes dropped, so text stored as UTF-16 without a mark is read too. A file's hits are those of all its readings. Folders named `target` (build output) are the only ones skipped. A symbolic link or junction is reported, never followed or skipped, and so is a folder deeper than [`MAX_DEPTH`].

**Exemptions are named, few and cannot rot.** A file in [`EXEMPT`] (or the list a test passes) is not reported, but each exemption must name a file that exists and still holds a hit; otherwise the exemption itself is a finding. Only the scanner's own marker tables and its seeded tests are exempt.
**Deterministic order.** Files are scanned in path order and findings sorted by file, line and text, with paths relative to the workspace root and `/`, the same on every system.
**I/O failures are errors, not passes**: [`MapError`], which the binary turns into exit code 2.
modules.job: The banned-source scan of a workspace: every file of the kernel's crates and of the facade's, scanned, with the scanner's own files as named exemptions.

method.text: the same walk as the map's ([`crate::map::repo`]): sorted listings, no recursion, links reported; the scope is the code chapter 29.20's rule 7 covers, every crate of the kernel (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/29-sources-licences.md`).

modules.cost: constant time; one environment read per [`resolve`], none for [`fixed`].
modules.does: a [`Seed`] is a 64-bit value that decides every input a seeded test draws. [`resolve`] picks a test's seed, the value of the environment variable [`ENV_VAR`] (`SPAREKIT_SEED`) when it is set and the test's fixed default otherwise, and prints it as `seed: <hex>` before the test draws anything. [`fixed`] prints a seed that a test must use whatever the environment says, because its assertions depend on that seed (a golden hash, a recorded case).
guarantees: **Every seed is printed.** [`resolve`] and [`fixed`] print one line that starts `seed: ` and is followed by exactly 16 lowercase hexadecimal digits, then the test's label, where the seed came from and how to replay it. Rust's test harness shows a passing test's output only with `--nocapture`, and always shows a failing test's, so every failure carries its seed (28.5: "Every generator prints its seed, so any failure replays exactly").

**Any printed seed replays exactly.** Setting `SPAREKIT_SEED` to the digits [`resolve`] printed makes it return the same seed, and the generators in [`crate::rng`] then give the same inputs on every target. A seed [`fixed`] printed replays by itself: the test always uses it.

**A seed is never invented here.** It is the test's fixed default or the value of `SPAREKIT_SEED`; nothing reads a clock or the operating system's random source. Pull requests run with the fixed defaults; a nightly job sets `SPAREKIT_SEED` to a fresh value, and the printed line logs it (28.17).
**A malformed override is an error, never ignored.** A run that asked for one seed and silently got another would replay the wrong case, so [`resolve`] returns [`SeedError`] instead.
modules.job: Seeds: where every random choice in a test comes from, and how a failure is replayed.

method.text: the replay discipline of sections 28.5 and 28.17 of the kernel architecture (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/28-testing.md`): "Every generator prints its seed, so any failure replays exactly", and "Seeds belong to test generators only, and every one is printed". The environment variable mirrors the seed variables of proptest (`PROPTEST_RNG_SEED`, <https://github.com/proptest-rs/proptest>) and bolero (`BOLERO_RANDOM_SEED`, <https://github.com/camshaft/bolero>), with one name for every Spare Kit test, so one value replays any of them.

modules.cost: linear in the file's length and the run's output.
modules.does: gate 1 (chapter 30.3) asks that every merge gate fail on a seeded violation, the pattern of the kernel's merge gate (G12) and of the toolchain guard (G20, [`crate::guard`]). Most gates already meet it in their own tests (gate 1's record in chapter 32 lists each). The gates here are the ones whose verdict is an outside tool's: rustfmt, Verus, Kani, libFuzzer, `ClusterFuzzLite`, Gungraun's Callgrind comparison and Wasmtime's fuel. [`VIOLATIONS`] holds one planted violation for each: a file of the kernel, one line in it found exactly once ([`Violation::anchor`]), the line it becomes, and the text the tool prints when it catches it. The binary `trip` writes the changed line into the working tree, runs the gate's own command, restores the file byte for byte, and asks [`verdict`] whether the run failed for that reason. Each workflow job runs it with its real check, so a job that could no longer fail (a tool that stopped checking, a command that checks nothing) fails instead. The two count gates run it last, comparing the planted run with the pull request's own run measured just before; the `ClusterFuzzLite` gate runs it in a job of its own, `clusterfuzzlite-seeded`, because its actions build a fresh clone of the pull request, which a planted line never reaches.
guarantees: **Each violation is real and small.** One line changes, and the change breaks exactly the property the gate checks: a line rustfmt would format differently; a sign the Kani harness for signs asserts; a carry the Verus twin's proof of addition asserts; a bound the limb proofs assert; orient2d's exact path answering `Positive` whatever its points, which breaks the antisymmetry every orient2d harness checks (a sign flipped everywhere would not: the fuzz target holds orient2d to its laws, not to an oracle); the carry the wide-integer fuzz target compares with big integers under cargo-bolero's libFuzzer, and which `ClusterFuzzLite`'s own build and fuzzing must report through whichever target meets it first (each target's law names its own break, "broken law: "; its address sanitizer reports the abort that follows); and `Sign::of_i128` reading its argument through an opaque copy (`core::hint::black_box`), the same answer for more work, which both count gates must report as a rise of more than 5% on its benchmark.

**An anchor found once, or no run.** [`apply`] refuses a file that holds the anchor line other than exactly once, so a refactor that moves it fails `tests/attack_g43.rs` (which checks every anchor in the repository) and the job, loudly, instead of planting nothing.

**A trip counts only for the right reason.** [`verdict`] accepts a run only when the command failed and printed every line [`Violation::caught`] names: the tool's own words for a found violation. A build error, a missing tool or any other failure proves nothing and is refused.
**Line ends kept.** The anchor is matched on a line with its line end set aside, so a Windows checkout's CRLF files work the same, and the line end is kept.
modules.job: Seeded violations for the gates that run an outside tool on the kernel's own code (gate 1, piece G43): each such gate is shown to fail when a violation is planted on purpose.

method.text: the seeded-violation pattern of the kernel's merge gate (chapter 28.8, `projects/engines/geometry/architecture/28-testing.md`; pieces G12 and G20, `guard`): plant one violation, run the real tool as the gate runs it, and require the tool's own report of that violation. Gate 1's condition is chapter 30.3's (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/30-build-order.md`).

crates.summary: Spare Kit geometry kernel, development only: the shared test support every kernel test uses.

invariants: Entities live in arenas addressed by 32-bit typed indices: no pointers, no reference counting between entities, no identity by memory address (8.2).
The builder assigns indices in persistent-name order, so a body's arenas depend only on what it contains, never on how it was built (8.2, proposed).
A body is immutable after building; an edit makes a new version (8.2).
Ordered containers only: maps that can be iterated are ordered by stable keys (8.2, 21).
Indices are never persisted; references and files hold persistent names (8.2, 20.1).
Each edge has one primary geometry; pcurves are derived and checked against it, never kept in loose agreement by a growing tolerance (8.1).
Attributes are keyed by persistent name and never decide shape (8.4).
